rationale: The cannabinoid arm had at least one fall in 4 of 31 participants versus 3 of 30 on placebo. Both formulations contained strawberry extract and neither assigned raw fruit. The count is people with a fall, with no recurrent-event rate or strawberry estimate.

High-dose leaf extract prolonged mouse rotarod latency and shortened pole turning. The reported cell-line experiment overlaps the poster. Leaves and test performance provide no transferable raw fruit and spontaneous fall direction.
A strawberry odor item showed nominal group discrimination and did not enter the final three-item panel. The grouping is freezing status. The study does not compare eaten fruit or falls.

Daily fruit and vegetable consumption is associated with lower adjusted odds of prior-year falls (OR 0.55). No strawberry identity, separate fruit estimate or Parkinson population.
Case-control dietary comparisons use aggregate fruit frequency, with cases defined by fractures after falls. There is no species-specific or recurring Parkinson fall contrast.
Seasonal strawberry consumption is observed in the underlying diet and microbiota cohort. Diet is measured rather than assigned and no fruit-only or fall outcome is reported.

The food-related dermatology entries discuss strawberry alongside other possible reaction triggers. The definitions provide no inspectable fruit-specific outcome comparison or fall frequency. Descriptive clinical terms are separate.

The older-adult survey reports strawberry-flavored supplement preference. The falls findings printed on the same page are from a separate vitamin D analysis. There is no assignment or falls estimate for the strawberry exposure.

The grouped strawberry, cherry and grape report compares overeating-related responses by food-addiction status. Preparation and individual fruit are unresolved. No fall outcome or Parkinson population is reported.

Early operant performance in irradiated rats favored a 2% strawberry extract diet. Later comparisons did not separate and irradiated controls were depleted. The assay records bar presses and cannot estimate Parkinson falls.

The separate 1.5 Gy operant experiment reports no difference at six months and a favorable strawberry extract comparison at twelve months. Full figures remain open. The assay is not a fall-frequency proxy.

Drug-induced learned taste avoidance in irradiated rats favored both berry diets in the amphetamine condition, with no reported change in the lithium condition. Cohort linkage with the later same-dose operant work is unverified.

Poison-center reports include tremor and weakness after whole kernels. The same investigator observed no tremor in four experimentally exposed dogs. The overlapping series and trial are one lineage. Neither studied expressed oil, resting phenotype or Parkinson disease.

Thirteen Australian field cases described hindlimb weakness, recumbency and pain after reported raw or roasted kernels. The case series differs from the US poison-center lineage. It supplies no separate rest-tremor outcome.
Pure macadamia-oil application did not significantly change skin flare or erythema in the author abstract. The comparison involved skin application and no tremor assessment.
The published conservation consultation records traditional uses of the kernels for food and trade. No pressed oil preparation, symptom or comparative response is described.

The dissertation reports the registered oil-blend comparison. Eight people entered the macadamia arm and seven contributed interpretable hydrogen transit. The groups did not differ significantly in transit response. No movement outcome or pressing grade.

Seventeen participants per family-history group ate the same macadamia-oil meal. Postmeal metabolic responses did not significantly differ across groups. Pressing grade and tremor were unreported, and no oil-free comparator was included.

The distinct BRAVO comparison enrolled 125 and stopped early. It used macadamia-oil placebo against omega-3 and planned affect and cognitive assessments. The official registry has no posted results or Parkinson tremor outcome.

Protocol compares macadamia and coconut oils in a skin-absorption and metabolic context. Target enrollment was 16. Results and actual participant counts are absent from the official record. No food intake or tremor measure.

555 were randomized and 245 completed. Cognition, mood and resilience did not show clear group-by-time effects. The 2019 protocol, 2021 outcomes and later trainee analysis share a cohort. No untreated arm, pressing grade or rest observation is established.

One person reported less numbness and tingling after unrefined oil. A copied version and serving clarification duplicate the report. The record supplies no diagnosed Parkinson disease, movement endpoint or verified cold pressing.

The paper and reports describe two crossover samples of 16 and eight healthy students with separate figures. Acute alertness and fatigue contrasts do not estimate tremor. Outcome reports and the registry belong to the same family, and grade is unreported.

The abstract reports cerebellar staining and oxidative or inflammatory biomarker changes in a potassium-dichromate rat model. Full dosing, pressing grade and denominators remain unverified. The accessible text gives no interpretable motor or tremor result.

The Methods specify room-temperature hydraulic pressing. Comparative physicochemical and fatty-acid results establish process differences. The body and abstract attribute one percentage to different comparators. No participant or motor measure.

Eight of eleven historical Parkinsonian cases had tremor. Injected drug in oil and wax and oral belladonna lowered amplitude without materially changing incidence or rate. No oil-only exposure. The 1951 Ebin review is the same study family.

The 200-person clinical series covered several diagnoses. The author describes possible relief of painful rigidity with the injected drug and gives no individual tremor estimate or oil-only comparison.
Three of six animals received the drug dissolved in injected peanut oil. The reported effect is on levodopa-induced dyskinesia. Rest tremor appears in model description without an oil-only contrast.

Both diets contained peanut oil. The low rod yielded longer retention under the low-alpha-linolenic acid diet, the high rod and traction comparisons were inconclusive or unchanged, and some learning measures were weaker. No resting-tremor assessment.
The peanut-plus-rapeseed blend was the comparison for salmon-palm oil, with several dietary fatty acids changing. The fish-oil blend reduced general activity or changed habituation.

Six of sixty participants with peanut allergy reported reactions after crude oil, including two observable or measurable reactions. None reacted after the refined oil. Outcomes are acute allergy signs, with no identifiable rest-tremor response.

One trial assigned 129 healthy adults to eight weeks of peanut, olive, safflower oil or no study oil. The analyzed denominator for the activity result is unverified. Its companion paper reports no significant change in general activity, and neither report assessed tremor.
Measured fatty acids, tocopherols and phytosterols in specified cold-pressed oil. Availability of measured composition supplies no observed symptom contrast.
The table associates peanut-oil massage with infantile paralysis. This row identifies no direct witness, measured response or comparable oral route.

Metformin-treated outpatients consumed dietary oils including groundnut. The reported glucose and lipid outcomes do not record tremor or an acute hypoglycemic movement phenotype.
Shared diet in 16 patients includes cantaloupe. Supplement S2 and body Figure 4 score composite motor change. No fruit-level contrast, preparation or separate tremor estimate.
Same cohort as PMID23661325. Adjusted occurrence RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.72–1.38) combines four cucurbits. The indication is diagnosis occurrence and there is no separate raw-fruit comparison.
GliSODin favored memory in the restraint stress experiment. The supplemented mice were assessed for spatial learning and tissue endpoints.
A ripe pickling-melon versus muskmelon juice contrast concerns glycemia in people with diabetes. Neither a resting-tremor nor isolated raw flesh effect was reported.

Crossover exposes volunteers to servings of separate unripe melon landraces or cucumber. Measured appetite and food reward without a tremor assessment.
The separate survey describes food experiences. Participant overlap with the crossover is unverified and its published outcomes do not inform rest tremor.

Mahlouji lists historical tremor and melon together only at the review level in separate tables. The Dadmehr textual analysis concerns a broader condition. Shared textual sources are plausible and no independent first-person response is established.
Rock melon is a named exposure in a registered crossover. Planned outcomes are glycemic index and load, and as of the review no results were available.
The capsule protocol lists frailty and quality-of-life outcomes. Registry results are absent and a named raw-fruit or resting-tremor comparison is not planned.
In mobility-limited older women, motor and fatigue differences are inconclusive. Capsules contain a Vauclusien melon extract and wheat gliadin.
Healthy men trained during a human supplement trial. The dried melon concentrate comparison did not give a clear between-group physical-fatigue difference or a separate tremor outcome.
A 61-participant healthy-adult comparison registered as NCT01767922 reports stress and fatigue. The proprietary freeze-dried concentrate and its endpoints cannot inform the frozen tremor outcome.

Regulatory review records tremor at the highest essential-oil toxicity exposure. The original case protocol and identity of the 2000 pamphlet animals remain open. Acute intoxication and toasted-fruit intake differ.
Oral methanolic fruit extract shortened experimenter-imposed bar posture. The assay did not score tremor.
Fresh leaf oil changed open-field and maze behavior in healthy mice. Separate five-animal limit screen disclosed no overt toxicity and gave no tremor count.

Oil group III shortened the bar posture relative to reserpine-only group II descriptively. Group IV was levodopa/carbidopa. Figures do not annotate the oil versus model comparison, and there was no item-level tremor.
Roasting changed the volatile profile, including lower fennel estragole. Full time, heat and sample-specific composition are open. No biological outcome was tested.
Cultivated and wild accessions differ greatly in starting volatiles, with a separate quantitative estragole estimate. The study has no roasting condition or symptom outcomes.
Whole crushed seed pellets lowered home-cage crossings and increased open-field center crossings. Toasting and resting tremor were outside the experiment.

The acute Table 1 records no convulsions or tremors in either fenchone or vehicle group. Methods and later table sample counts differ. The isolated compound comparison leaves the culinary Parkinson direction open.
A different methanolic extract had no reported deaths and no separately reported tremor outcome in the author abstract.
Boiled leaves and a separate claim about the fruit are documented under broad falij use. No firsthand fennel rest-tremor outcome or Parkinson diagnosis is identified.
Generalized seizure followed exposure to an unknown amount of fennel essential oil in cake in a person with epilepsy. No frozen outcome was recorded.
Repeated injections of leaf-and-stem juice were associated with convulsions. Route and dose units vary in the paper. No tremor outcome matches the claim.
Anethole given before rotenone improved rotarod and selected stride results. Resting tremor appears in the introduction as a disease feature.
Concentrated fruit extract reduced rotarod retention and grip in healthy mice. This does not identify a tremor phenotype.
Peri-lesion oral methanol extract favored coordination and grasp. Post-lesion-only comparisons were inconclusive. Neither was a tremor measurement.
Conference abstract gives rotarod, open-field and passive-avoidance results. Extract dosing and specific effect sizes remain open. The 2024 paper tests a separate in vivo challenge.
Oral fruit extract under LPS improved late coordination with no clear early result. No tremor assessment exists in the studied outcome set.
Tremors followed contaminated produce in cattle. Nitrate was measured in green and white plant waste and ruminal contents. No toasted seed or Parkinson exposure was isolated.
Fennel was held in a bundled seasoning oil during frying comparisons. The study measures aroma and composition without a separate fennel contrast.
The February conference abstract reports a concentration change in five people; the November Figure 4 lacks a plotted denominator. Treat the reports and Nomoto citation as one family for this review.
The clinical pilot assessed the separate rest item under cabergoline. No fruit was compared or measured.

Three people had lower UPDRS after antibiotic addition, with qualitative improvement in rest tremor or rigidity. Four were unchanged. The report gives no separated values for the item and the exposure is a different inhibitor.
The authors describe general motor improvements after itraconazole addition. One concentration and no separately reported resting-tremor change.
Whole fruit components and juice affected felodipine in a crossover. The food matrix effect cannot establish a comparable effect on cabergoline or symptoms.
Fresh white pulp changed measured exposure in healthy volunteers taking different calcium antagonists. No Parkinson drug or outcome was tested.
Grapefruit was listed in the mixed menu eaten by both Parkinson groups. No isolated ingredient or separate rest result.
The delay and severity description refer to an aggregate of induced signs. Timing of acute rat signs cannot specify resting-tremor severity.

Mean induced seizure tremor onset delayed in the drug-plus-juice arm versus drug plus water. The tested table comparator is the challenge-only arm. The stated denominator refers to the two beverage arms with nine rats each.
The registry concerns aroma and immediate brain signals or subjective responses. It gives no posted results.
The flavored drink observation does not describe a resting-tremor change. Regular grapefruit consumption, and added-sugar tremor, are different reports.
Injected isolated naringin and tissue degeneration in a rat model. No separate symptom sign.
The pretreatment and post-lesion comparisons separate tissue preservation from restoration in mice. No symptom measure.
Oral isolated limonin and general motor activity, with the exact task outcome requiring full methods.
The original isolated injection changed rod and pole behavior. Those tasks assess other motor functions, without a resting-tremor score.
The ground-soybean adjunct comparison gives longer ON and less dyskinesia. The abstract does not separate resting tremor or compare refined oil.
Spirography improved after both active octanol formulations. The pooled adverse-tremor and inconsistent six-hour results cannot isolate soybean oil.
Only the drug comparator varies against a shared oil vehicle. The prespecified essential postural tremor timepoint was inconclusive and later signals favor the drug.
Acoustic voice measures favored the active drug over the soybean-oil placebo. No oil-free placebo identifies a soybean oil effect and the refining grade is unspecified.

At day seven, 2.1 versus 4.7 (estimates read from Figure 4a) in highest oral whole-plant methanol-extract versus vehicle groups, eight mice per group. Fresh petioles carry identified extract compounds. Their effective dose and mediation in the mouse trial are unresolved.
The fresh petiole analysis found apigenin and luteolin also measured in the experimental extract. Chemistry supports an exposure link and supplies no independent symptom result.

Pharmaceutical butylphthalide compared off-medication tremor pooled across three types. The purported composite exceeds the stated maximum and nearly reproduces a quality-of-life row. The separate rest result cannot be interpreted.
One public contributor reported previous tremor, uncertain diagnosis and general benefit with seed extract, coffee and mannitol. No tremor change was attributed to a single exposure.

Two prints of one cohort's turkey frequency versus pooled self-reported tremor graphic. The tile is extremely close to zero on the positive side. Cooking, separate rest item, adjusted estimate, uncertainty and analyzed denominator are unverified.

Tremor returns in qualitative Figure 2 and 3 timelines after protein challenge in two participants. The third revised-load participant has no figure and the lower-load comparison has a different protocol. The authors give no specific rest score or baked exposure.

Five participants reported worsening general symptoms on an 80 g protein breakfast. Three also reported dyskinesia or restlessness with the high-carbohydrate meal. The balanced meal favored pegboard performance. No individual rest result or food ingredient is reported.

The author abstract separates a shorter response under the unusually high protein formula from inconclusive usual-allowance comparisons. There is no separate observed tremor subtype or comparable food preparation.

The Parkinson group showed supine hypotension and worsening of an aggregate motor score after a shared liquid meal. The twenty denominator refers to the Parkinson group rather than the sixteen controls.
Postprandial OFF time was shorter during the assigned low-protein product diet. The comparison supplies no separate rest measurement and cannot estimate an isolated baked-turkey effect.

An independently identifiable anecdote describes worse perceived medication effect during one holiday with repeated leftover turkey. Stronger attribution would require timing or food controls and a separately observed symptom. The quoted question counts as no additional observed event.

Two copies of one graphic for the same cohort give a small inverse tile for unspecified olive oil and pooled self-reported tremor. There is no pairwise estimate, uncertainty, grade or separate rest item. The 2017 composite symptom analysis overlaps and has no separate tremor result.
Exact oil grade administered by injection improved rotarod and activity under toxin exposure. An acute tremor observation was outside the comparative endpoints.
The ketogenic recipes use extra-virgin olive oil. During the early phase, 12/24 versus 3/23 reported worsened tremor or rigidity. This is a bundled diet comparison with a combined adverse endpoint.
The oil association addresses Parkinson case status, with no within-disease separate tremor estimate or confirmed grade.

Registered total scale and related white-seed enzyme formulation trail. Clinical use of the exact formulation and outcomes remain unverified.
An isolated compound with a registered total motor scale, unknown overall status and no posted results. There is no culinary-comparator premise.
Unheated brown powder added to cooked broccoli changes urinary metabolite recovery in healthy adults.

Original bar, grip and coordination figures assess leaf extract. No rest-tremor rating or culinary seed comparison.
Relative glucosinolate signals declined after roasting. No measured Parkinson symptom or preparation-equivalent human dose.
The processed mustard adjunct raises measured urinary sulforaphane metabolite recovery. The study has no human Parkinson or rest-tremor outcome.

Relative to high-oleic sunflower, DHA shortened the composite working-memory response time by 0.36 SD (95% CI 0.14 to 0.58). This shows the relative assigned diets, with an uncertain preparation and no oral sunflower-only or Parkinson estimate.
High-oleic sunflower capsules served as active comparator for conjugated linoleic acid. Trail Making and Serial Sevens yielded no clear between-arm change. No cold pressing or Parkinson cohort.

Oral sunflower seed oil improved novel-object discrimination at both doses versus water in scopolamine-treated mice, both p<.001. The preparation is unverified and the model tests recognition memory without a Parkinson mechanism or executive task.

Both high-fat arms had poorer chronic spatial maze performance. A standard chow contrast changes dietary fat and energy, and there is no conventional-fat sunflower group or Parkinson disease pathology. The oil processing is unverified.

Figure 2 shows sunflower and chow near overlapping. The omnibus result and saturated-arm caption cannot assign a signed sunflower contrast. Author overlap with the original ECO member and later high-fat work leaves the experiment lineage open.

The progressive dopaminergic-loss experiment tests behavior after common tamoxifen injection in sunflower oil. There is no edible exposure contrast or separate executive measure. The later gene-expression report uses the same model but a different schedule.
Rotenone in carrier was contrasted with carrier. The difference in social recognition is a toxin-model observation; injection, common oil and different task prevent sunflower attribution.

The combined saline plus oral oil vehicle made more working-memory errors at 72 hours than untreated controls (p=.0127). Additional reference-memory errors occurred at 72 and 96 hours. The handling and saline schedule, no pressing grade and the non-Parkinson control comparison leave no transferable sign.
The reported culinary oil use has no measured neurologic outcome. Separate medicinal or ceremonial uses of the plant are contextual and do not supply an independent oil effect.
Modeled ALSFRS-R decline was 4.91 in the oil arm and 3.00 on RT001, with relative difference 1.90 (95% CI −1.39 to 5.19). The overall ALS score does not establish its swallowing item's direction.

The reflux total rose 0.33 (95% CI −2.4 to 3.1) in 18 safflower completers. Alternate allocation, shared vocal training and aggregate reflux reporting limit the inference. No separately reported swallowing item.
The earlier independent singer cohort averaged a 1-point reflux-total decline in seven safflower completers, with interaction p=.509. The separate swallowing item was unreported.

The six-month blinded safflower comparison reports caudate measurements and motor totals. The European results and two trial updates summarize this same trial family. No separate swallowing or grade verification.
Safflower and triheptanoin crossed over for Glut1 episodic movement counts. Neither swallowing nor a verifiable cold-pressed grade was reported.
The estimated swallowing safety difference favored maximum triheptanoin (−0.9, 95% CI −1.6 to −0.3) relative to MCT or periods without treatment. The study did not assign safflower.

The safflower-and-carnauba wax formulation had smoother texture. The panel spat out samples. Attendance ranged from 6 to 12 per session, with no unique participant count or swallowed test for the formulation.
The safflower-fed amyloid group showed an inflammatory gene response. Swallowing was unmeasured. Sample and overlap with the same lab's other reports require full methods.
A cold-pressed safflower diet supplies an exact processing match, in an aged mouse immune comparison. It supplies no swallowing measure. Total cohort size not established from this extract.
People swallowed capsules, and subsequent blood draws measured triglycerides. The test was designed to bypass or vary exposure to oral fat sensation, without a swallowing assessment.
This distinct protocol used two swallowed safflower capsule loads. Lipids were measured. Cohort overlap with the investigator's prior study remains unclear.

A safflower crossover measured lipids and inflammatory markers. Those endpoints supply no swallowing direction. This is the registered lipid cohort already in the assessment ledger.
Safflower in yoghurt was the control for total allergy symptom and lung measures. No isolated throat event or clinical swallowing effect was reported.

The author reports improved spatial retention in the strawberry extract arm after irradiation. The measured result is maze learning. Same-dose pathway studies share authors and design elements, with unresolved cohort independence.

Aberdeen community study identifies severe gait abnormality in 84 of 214 clinically assessed people. Separate repeated falls and strawberry exposure are unreported. The index is a locator to this report.

One serious fall in each of the selected corn-oil-only placebo and fish-oil-only groups (1/71 and 1/109). These sparse counts cover serious events. The journal pooled placebo row also includes a cellulose comparator.
33/164 in pooled corn-or-soy placebo versus 42/238 on DHA, p=.60. Oil-specific allocation is unknown, recurrent outcomes are absent and population has Alzheimer dementia.

The corn-oil arm was slower on the Timed Up and Go relative to fish oil in the six-month comparison. The timed mobility task does not count falls. A fish oil benefit could explain the relative contrast.
Gait and single-leg balance comparisons are imprecise. The parent and secondary reports share both a mixed-oil control and the same participants. No fall-frequency result.
Equal-parts soybean and corn oil capsules accompanied maltodextrin. Gait and balance tasks are named. No reported fall-frequency estimate in accessible abstract and supplement.

The corn-oil formulation contributes to rat adiposity and lipid contrasts. The companion linkage and fall endpoint are unavailable.

The MVP baseline program relies on participant-reported diagnosis. A small inverse graphical sign links pooled non-fried fish and self-rated slowness. This figure gives no species, grilling, separate clinical bradykinesia assessment, pair-specific estimate or interval.

Parkinson participants took capsules of dried common-sage leaf. The actual comparator was vitamin E. The report mentions cognition and salivation but contains no apathy scale or named apathy analysis. A secondary assessment timetable was absent.

One mild constipation event among 106 active participants and two among 100 placebo participants. This sparse safety count is from purified bilberry and black currant, with no raw blueberry or Parkinson constipation measure. Protocol and secondary publications share this family.

No adverse events were listed in the acute whole-blueberry pharmacokinetic crossover, with 18 at risk in each condition. This duration and reporting cannot substitute for longitudinal constipation severity in Parkinson disease.

The Parkinson trial uses wild blueberry powder and registers motor outcomes. No constipation severity outcome or comparative results were available.
The direction for pooled fresh fruit uses a constructed constipation category, with missing or nondaily bowel reports and no blueberry-specific estimate. It cannot isolate the frozen food.
A pooled berry item in the dietary study had a lower total Parkinson symptom score. The constipation comparison concerns overall dietary scores and supplies no separate raw-blueberry estimate.
The study measures bowel diaries but blueberries are one part of a shared mixed meal. There is no isolated blueberry estimate.

Some participants reported more constipation during a blueberry and grape seed extract adjunct. Neither exact counts nor isolation of blueberry from other ingredients and concurrent treatment is verified in the original abstract.
The live and sterilized preparations combine processing and fermentation differences. Stool-form changes do not establish a raw-blueberry constipation effect, and chronic constipation was excluded.

New drooling occurred immediately while the child had oral and facial swelling and other symptoms of a likely allergic reaction. Positive allergy testing corroborates the exposure history. No oral challenge or Parkinson saliva or swallowing outcome was available. Acute allergy supplies no directional estimate for changes in chronic Parkinson drooling.

Both active syrup groups report more drooling events than placebo, with 17/40 versus 15/40 between active arms. Neither raw fig nor a matched addition of fig was assigned. The child ADHD population and lack of drooling grades leave no transferable efficacy sign.
Drooling and dysphagia were observed in secondary parkinsonism. The reported medication response concerns other symptoms. The case gives no paired dietary and salivary comparison.
Two continuing apomorphine users described less drooling after stimulation. No raw-fig comparison or graded drooling outcome was reported.
The crossover compares levodopa with and without an add-on. Table 1 shows one lower, one higher and four unchanged drooling item scores. It did not test raw fig.
The Japanese and English-language validation groups give separate ordinal distributions for combined saliva and drooling. The translation study did not assign fruit exposure.

Fifteen each received powder, placebo and a separate yeast arm. Day-20 constipation severity was 49.13 versus 65.86 for ginger and placebo, with baseline imbalance and a crude change difference of −11.79 points. The reported table threshold concerns arm comparisons, and the crude contrast has no adjusted uncertainty. The same rhizome and same symptom permit minimal transfer across preparation and population.

The ginger capsule group began higher and ended at 1.09 versus 1.80 on the constipation domain, p=.016. The adjusted result applies to a separate overall score. Registry and paper identify one trial. The same symptom and rhizome permit a minimal link, with no direct dietary Parkinson result.

The adjusted constipation-severity changes were −24.15 and +11.39 on a 100 mm scale. Gingerol-standardized tablets and relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis limit exposure and population transfer. The older clinical outcomes paper and newer review repeat the same trial family.

The pulverized-rhizome group went from 1.06 to 0.38 on the constipation item and placebo from 0.98 to 1.04, reported p<.001 at end. A treated thyroid cohort and a capsule preparation limit transfer to the culinary Parkinson question.
PAC-SYM and stool frequency favored the extract in 55 completers, while stool consistency was inconclusive. Funding, attrition imbalances and inconsistent extract amounts limit extrapolation.

Among adults with functional dyspepsia, the registered ginger extract trial reported a 2.9-point difference in constipation score changes, with 80 randomized. Steaming, extraction and diagnostic setting limit transfer.

Composite IBS responders were numerically more frequent with placebo and there was no clear group difference. Difficulty passing stool was reported without arm-specific counts. The trial gives no separate efficacy estimate for constipation.

One constipation adverse event was reported with extract versus zero listed on placebo. The small event count and unset severity leave a safety lead, with no interpretable change in the frozen symptom.

Six Parkinson patients reported easier defecation and faster mean colonic transit under a shared formula. Ginger, ginseng and pepper were assigned together, and efficacy significance was pooled with multiple system atrophy observations.
Secondary first defecation was around six hours earlier with ginger after cesarean delivery. Long-term symptom severity outside surgery was unmeasured. Trial and registration are one source family.
Ginger capsules versus placebo yielded a 12.6-hour earlier secondary first stool after surgery. The comparison uses perioperative recovery and does not assess a chronic symptom.
Ileus occurred in 23 patients per arm and time to first flatus was similar. Stool timing was incomplete. Enhanced recovery alone was the comparator and the outcome differs from chronic constipation.
The trial compares two capsule strengths and prioritizes ghrelin. Gut transit and GI symptoms are listed as other outcomes. Recruitment is active and there are no reported results.

The public bilingual record compares standardized powder tablets with placebo. It prioritizes total MDS-UPDRS and gives no separate constipation outcome. Recruitment is listed complete and results remain unavailable.

Applied gingerol suppressed spontaneous contraction in isolated rat distal-colon longitudinal muscle. This is a lower-motility observation under laboratory conditions without a stool or severity measurement or evidence of exposure at the same concentrations after eating ginger.

A participant reports regular bowel movements with a smoothie containing ginger and other ingredients and reports using cereal as an alternative. Dose, the role of ginger and the contributor's diagnosis are unresolved.
A person reporting IBS-C describes less stomach pain with tea and chews and no clearly perceived constipation relief. No comparative symptom measure or verified exposure composition.
A public report describes no stool during two weeks after switching from a helpful aloe preparation to ginger. Pre-existing constipation and stopping aloe prevent separating effects.

Separate replies describe bowel regularity while taking powdered capsules and later worsening after illness with unspecified ginger. The source links a cross-post and the known gingerol experiment. No independent diagnosis or comparable exposure.
Randomized stable-angina trial of powdered lemon-balm leaf capsules vs placebo reports favorable adjusted depression contrast, though baseline symptoms were low and adjusted CI was unreported.

Randomized type 2 diabetes trial (60 assigned, 44 completers) reports BDI-II change -3.91 vs -0.04 for lemon-balm extract capsules vs placebo (adjusted p=.001), with higher extract baseline and trial-length wording discrepancy.
Randomized trial of formulated phospholipid lemon-balm extract vs placebo in adults with emotional distress/poor sleep reports favorable DASS-42 group-by-time depression contrast.
Postpartum capsule trial reports smaller day-14 EPDS rise under lemon balm (+1.9 vs +6.2, p=.004); both arms rose from low baselines and attrition/table denominators are unresolved.
Randomized active-comparator trial adding dried-leaf lemon balm to egg isolate found no clear difference on HAM-D (8.4 vs 10.1) or BDI-II (11.0 vs 10.5), supplying a key competing null result.

Retrospectively registered burn-injury trial comparing brewed Melissa vs black tea shows favorable marginals, but Table 3 p=.002 is within-arm, Table 5 differences are undefined, and early discharges were replaced.
Aqueous leaf extract trial had severe-depression counts 3/28->3/28 vs 10/27->6/27 with baseline imbalance and no verified between-group change.

Adolescent PMS family (PMID29369810, IRCT2014060717998N1, PMID26339667) and CABG HADS report (IRCT2014071918531N1) have unreconciled test statistics, missing baselines, or overlapping cohort ambiguity.

Includes pooled PD survey (ECBN260617), Serbian/Wroclaw surveys, dialysis inhalation null (PMID40082838 p=.84), acute calmness Lemcog null (PMID41782777), multi-herb blends (Nepeta, IBS, STW5, Ze185), pending brewed-tea registries (UMIN000055134, IRCT20190204042617N2, NCT05422599), and mixed rodent assays.

Randomized depression trial adding nigella oil extract to sertraline vs sertraline alone reports DASS-21 endpoint means 18.6 vs 23.4 (p<.001), with a one-point discrepancy between printed change and means; oil co-treatment outside PD.
Ground nigella seed capsule trial favored a post-treatment premenstrual composite mood domain rather than depression severity; depression inventory was used for screening only.
Crushed nigella seed capsule placebo comparison showed no clear between-arm Bond-Lader mood difference.

Combined nigella-ajwain-lime in hypothyroidism (PMID39086868, BDI-II p=.79) and nigella-flax in MS (IRCT20140617018126N6, n=35) were inconclusive; hemodialysis HADS (IRCT20200411047027N1) remains unreported; rat toxin models (rotenone, manganese) are preclinical proxies.
Placebo-controlled trial of proprietary nigella oil extract (BCO-5) in non-restorative sleepers reports improved PSQI and sleep components at 45 and 90 days; proprietary oil outside PD.

Separately registered 7-day double-blind placebo-controlled actigraphy trial at the same site reports improved sleep efficiency, latency, and duration with BCO-5 oil extract (corrigendum corrects placebo p value).
Postmenopausal nigella extract placebo comparison reports PSQI 7.2->6.6 vs 11->9.5 (overall p=.45) with conflicting narrative scores and unverified ground-seed identity.

Active crossover (PMID42819242) favored melatonin over nigella oil; multi-herb chronic insomnia formula (PMID41623556, p=.27) was inconclusive; nasal drops (NCT05494164) and pending oil registry (NCT06950424) give no ground-seed insomnia estimate.

Randomized tart-cherry concentrate trial favored treatment-mean mental fatigue by 9.5 points (95% CI 2.5 to 16.5, p=.009), with inconclusive treatment-by-repetition (p=.257); concentrate and non-PD session fatigue limit transfer.
Randomized ulcerative-colitis trial (35 completers) found inconclusive secondary IBD fatigue severity and impact differences for tart-cherry concentrate versus placebo.
Acute tart-cherry concentrate crossover (PMID27989253, n=27, p=.690) and 2-week cherry-apple juice crossover (PMID20438325, n=15) both found inconclusive fatigue comparisons.

Multiple athlete trials found null fatigue contrasts: marathon VAS (PMID41677899, n=35), sprint fatigue (PMID41683264, n=40), rugby crossover (PMID32672095, n=11), pretraining (Swinbourne 2015), cyclist muscle fatigue (PMID39141644), soccer well-being (PMID31188696), and cycling exhaustion (PMID30932750).

Endurance/time-trial studies (PMID27231439, PMID30617467, PMID36678258), sleep trials (PMID22038497, PMID23732552), fibromyalgia pain (Elliot 2010), unresolved cherry-cocoa report (10.59841/an-najat.v3i4.3456), and pending UMIN000057292 do not measure clinical fatigue after dried cherries.

Early-Parkinson observational study (PMID34127758) found non-significant correlations between plasma ALA and body bradykinesia (age-adjusted rho=-.230 p=.171; sex-adjusted rho=-.151 p=.372) without dietary correlation or oil contrast.

Randomized flaxseed omega-3 plus vitamin-E PD trials (PMID28342967, PMID30554092) lacked an oil-only arm and separate bradykinesia score, and found no clear Part III effect (-1.9 vs +3.1, printed p=.05).

Older-adult FAB motor series was null (PMC10056498 p=.140); maternal-separation rat locomotion was null (PMID39374840 p=.595); rotenone open-field activity (ijbcs.20170603.01) and purified ALA models (PMID40269665, PMID40946953) do not measure clinical bradykinesia.
Small human flaxseed-oil trial (DOI10.23937/2474-3631/1510010) found an inconclusive final Beck anxiety comparison (p=.31) with low baseline anxiety, no change interaction, and unverified pressing.
PD flaxseed omega-3 plus vitamin-E trials (PMID28342967, PMID30554092) report aggregate UPDRS/Part I scores without an isolated anxiety item or oil-only comparison.

Maternal-separation rats (PMID39374840) showed mixed EPM vs null light-dark and higher amygdala inflammation; haloperidol poster (SBFIS2024-P259-PAIVA) showed no isolated oil benefit; rotenone mouse EPM (INDJ/2017/34206) is a remote animal proxy.

Registered 3-oil hemodialysis trial (NCT02103556, PMID25238699, n=50) compared flaxseed, olive, and active mineral oil; Rome III fell within all arms with an inconclusive between-oil interaction (p=.15) and no inactive control or verified pressing.

Lipid trial (sjams.2018.v06i01.047) logged 2/57 vs 5/55 constipation adverse events vs active liquid paraffin without severity scores; plasma ALA did not associate with PD Wexner constipation (PMID34127758); solvent-extracted oil in rats (PMID25889554) was nonmonotonic.

Single-blind oral flaxseed-oil osteoarthritis trial (DOI10.36347/sjams.2019.v07i09.031) reports lower rest and movement pain, limited by inconsistent dosing, unverified cold-pressing grade, and non-PD cohort.
Same-group single-blind RA flaxseed-oil report (Vyas-2020-IJHCR-397) reports lower rest/movement pain (p<.001) with numeric inconsistencies and unverified independence from the 2019 report.

Competing randomized trials show null pain contrasts: ACL surgery flaxseed vs corn oil (PMID36398219, KOOS 87.6 vs 87.3, p=.96), RA flax vs linoleic acid (PMID7597378, n=22), and cyclic mastalgia vs vitamin E (PMID33407941, p=.142).

PD flaxseed omega-3 plus vitamin-E trials (PMID28342967, PMID30554092) report total UPDRS without pain items; vitamin-D add-on (PMID42529699) has baseline imbalance and endometriosis report (PMID39759908) conflicts on ethanol extract vs oil.

Placebo-controlled menopause trial of fresh-sage-tip extract (PMID33615001) favored secondary POMS fatigue (p=.029, no arm-by-time table; sleep-exhaustion item unchanged); multiplicity and non-PD extract limit transfer.
Dry sage extract menopause trial (IRCT2015111713940N2) found an inconclusive post-treatment exhaustion contrast versus placebo (p=.634).

Spanish-sage essential oil (PMID20937617, different species) eased acute task fatigue; mixed-extract trials (NCT02202629, NCT04804657), uncontrolled menopause series (PMC6686654, PMID21630133), FAERS15895309, and Newcastle PD (no fatigue data) give no isolated fresh-sage PD estimate.

Randomized oral dried thyme trial (PMID38039009) reports normal-range HADS anxiety in 40/53 vs 31/53 at 1 month (from 27/53 vs 30/53), but has implausible baseline SD, overlapping cutoffs, contradictory within-control test, and 86 triple-blind registry vs 106 double-blind paper.
Wild-thyme extract trial (PMID42930530) found null FDDQL anxiety (+3.21, 95% CI -4.17 to 10.60, p=.410) with paper-vs-registry discrepancies.

Oral thyme extract (PMID27419090), isolated carvacrol (PMID19909350), carvacryl acetate (PMID24036473 conflicting marble burying), injected essential oil (PMID40283944), and paraquat model (PMID40188599) test extracts/terpenes in rodents.
Randomized knee-osteoarthritis trial of turmeric rhizome extract with volatile oil (PMID29316908) reports gait speed change +0.08 vs +0.01 m/s (p<.05) with a conflicting intergroup figure.
Randomized trial of water-dispersible turmeric extract in chronic knee pain (PMID34045905) reports 80-meter walk-time change -11.0 vs -6.8 s (Mann-Whitney p=.0011).

Competing trials show null 4-meter gait speed in healthy aging (PMID29951592 p=.9), null 40-meter walk for Curcugen (PMID35010916 p=.604), placebo-leaning older-adult pilot (NCT03085680 n=17), baseline-imbalanced PMID40361833, tamarind blend, and null curcumin-alone rotenone rats (PMID40208367).
Open-label randomized trial of oral Nigella sativa oil in acute COVID-19 (PMID36425571) reports day-4 fatigue in 12/30 vs 25/30 (adjusted OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.48).

Ground nigella seed arms showed mixed/null day-10 fatigue (PMID36142070) and null PMS physical domain (PMID41267796); nigella-flax MS fatigue was null (DOI10.34172/hpp.44662); massage, sprint bar, pending lupus mix, and rodent swim tests do not isolate ground seed.

Controlled mouse experiment (7/group; DOI10.1016/j.bjp.2018.03.007) reports higher evoked thermal and mechanical pain thresholds with whole walnut oil (55% linoleic acid; mechanical fold below tramadol), bridged chemically to cold-pressed extraction profiles (PMID30065427, PMID30651416).

Pain rose in an uncontrolled advanced-cancer mixed-oil ketogenic diet (PMID21794124); NCT00938340 recorded diarrhea without pain; walnut hydrosol caused hypoglycemia (PMID27335580); ACTRN12622000083796 puts cold-pressed walnut oil in placebo without results; green-walnut injection (PMID41596967) is non-oil.

Single medullary thyroid carcinoma case (PMC1673758) replaced antidiarrheal drugs with high-dose ground nutmeg and dropped secretory diarrhea from 6.7 to 2.6 stools/day; uncontrolled drug-replacement diarrhea case, not clinical constipation.

1976 constipation letter (PMID942762) lacks verified full text; rat ethanol/petroleum-ether/aqueous extract studies measure dry stool output, induced diarrhea (aqueous null), or charcoal transit proxies rather than clinical constipation.
Randomized functional-dyspepsia trial (IRCT2013101214980; companion SF-36 report same cohort) reports lower week-4 epigastric pain with ground anise powder versus cornstarch placebo (0.38 vs 2.05).
Randomized IBS trial (NCT02364830) reports favorable abdominal pain response for enteric-coated anise oil capsules versus placebo; oil formulation and IBS etiology limit transfer.

Acute COVID anise+rock-sugar sachet trial (IRCT20120506009651N3) prints an ambiguous RR 0.55 event label with control discrepancy; Ushaq capsule composition (PMID42935088) is pending; rotenone anethole and methanolic mouse models are preclinical proxies.

Randomized crossover in 24 adults with medication-induced xerostomia (PMID33314461) reports easier subjective swallowing in 8/24 after spat-out cold-pressed roasted-kernel sunflower oil rinse vs 2/24 after water (unadjusted p=.031; saliva flow favored water).

Parkinson surveys (10.1111/ger.70049, PMID30028552) link dry mouth with swallowing complaints without oil assignment; MVP-2017 total PRO-PD was null (+2, p=.787); infant oral-oil aspiration cases (PMID30094029) flag aspiration caution without swallowing severity comparison.
Randomized older-adult pilot of distilled cumin essential oil (PMID42088310) had inconclusive group interactions on both simple and complex attention despite descriptive numerical differences.

Analytical roasting studies confirm cuminaldehyde retention without cognition outcomes; UK PD survey (PMID30662706) was null after correction; synthetic odor EEG and mouse avoidance/spatial memory do not test clinical attention.

Triple-blind randomized abdominal-surgery trial (PMID38965524) reports earlier first postoperative defecation with oral Cuminum cyminum extract capsules versus placebo; surgical ileus recovery and extract differ from chronic PD constipation.

Multi-herb digestive mixture (jjnpp-148163) favored week-1 constipation (p=.049) and was null at week 2 (p=.152) with 10% mix in control; IBS oil drops (PMID24829694) lacked control; UK PD survey null; rat wet-stool vs slowed charcoal transit (PMID25002800) oppose.

Randomized 36-adult meal crossover (NCT03879213, 2026 publication) reports fewer six-hour post-meal spatial working-memory errors and better strategy (p<.05) after whole freeze-dried red raspberry powder.

Black-raspberry Alzheimer pilot (NCT05680532) omitted executive subscales; four-berry drink (PMID31698695) and multicomponent capsules (PMID33467530) do not isolate raspberry; mouse studies split between high-fat benefit and AD-model null (PMID36450698).

Randomized chemoradiotherapy trial (64 completers; two 2025 articles and 2026 abstract share one cohort) reports better post-treatment Penetration-Aspiration Scale scores with nanocurcumin vs placebo (2.91 vs 3.72 from equal 2.91 baselines).

Randomized chemoradiotherapy abstract (PMID34161952) reports lower grade 3 dysphagia with two bio-enhanced turmeric doses (25% and 20%) versus placebo (60%); radiation injury and extract differ from neurologic PD dysphagia.

Oral-fibrosis trial (IJPSR 2018) had sparse counts (4/50->0/50 vs 4/50->4/50) with discordant printed p-value; PD multi-supplement registry (NCT02445651) notes pill-swallowing difficulty without isolated turmeric severity data.

Randomized open-label trial in 80 students (PMID25085020) reports menstrual weakness falling 6.65 to 2.88 with fennel soft capsules vs 6.39 flat on no medication (p=.001); abstract prints a conflicting control value and no-treatment control leaves expectancy open.

Fennel essential oil dysmenorrhea fatigue was inconclusive (ijpr.2010.18 overall p=.08 with differential dropout); 2007 extract abstract gave p=.058 without direction; crushed-seed menopause survey (n=10) and Tlemcen honey survey lack controlled fatigue data.
Randomized pediatric chemotherapy-mucositis trial (IRCT2016061813691N7, n=60) reports faster local pain reduction with topical summer-savory extract gel plus routine care vs placebo gel.

Randomized oral dried summer-savory leaf powder trial in knee osteoarthritis (IRCT2013112515542N1, 39 analyzed of 60) found an inconclusive between-group pain change (-2 vs -0.5, p=.38) with high attrition.

Summer-savory extracts and seed fractions attenuated rodent formalin/writhing nociception (PMID12241981, PMID22095089), whereas isolated carvacrol showed no clear thermal hyperalgesia effect in 6-OHDA Parkinson-model rats (PMID29489959).
Randomized functional-dyspepsia trial (IRCT2013101214980) favored ground anise powder over cornstarch on week-12 SF-36 vitality; generic vitality and dyspepsia differ from Parkinson fatigue severity.

Randomized IBS trial (NCT02364830) reports lower tiredness with enteric anise oil vs placebo (3.15/2.74 vs 3.94/3.54, three-arm p<.001, disputed by a later review); menopause ground-anise trial (NIUM-ANISE-BEGUM) omitted fatigue.

Double-blind RCT in 66 OAB outpatients (NCT03532789, Phytomedicine 2020) reports lower OABSS (6.33 vs 9.73, p<.001), urgency-frequency item (2.82 vs 4.18, p<.001), and USS (2.67->1.64) for topical cinnamon vs placebo patch; daytime frequency null (p=.79).
Oral Cinnamomum cassia bark powder lowered cyclophosphamide-cystitis 24-hour void counts in mice (controls 62 vs unexposed 10); acute chemical cystitis voids differ from perceived PD urgency.

Oral true cinnamon reduced cystitis bladder-distension responses but modestly increased them in uninflamed rats (nutraceuticals3010012); uncontrolled Kampo series (PMID18203522) and PD survey (PMID30662706) give no isolated ground-cinnamon urgency estimate.
Parkinson ginger registrations (Ginger-PD NCT07882108, IRCT20251028067794N1, NCT05001217) have no posted dyskinesia severity results.

Patent WO2024101890A1 reports lower mouse AIM AUC for dried-rhizome extract with unverified route/n/masking, while isolated zingerone (PMID21769642) did not suppress hindlimb stiffening and Duzhong Fang used a multi-herb formula.

Curcumin older-adult pilot (NCT03085680) tracked walking speed without freezing counts; MVP-2024 plots an unquantified pooled-spice tile; ZAZ2 tested multi-herb granules on composite UPDRS; rodent gait/beam assays (PMID35966793, PMID36742141) recorded no freezing.

Randomized within-person nursing-home study (PMID26094950, n=39) found more frequent seated postprandial hypotension with full vs half rice serving, but omitted arm estimates, brown-rice grade, standing test, and lightheadedness severity.

Parkinson glucose and mixed-meal studies (PMID27239112, PMID27393383, PMC12325557, PMID9399210, PMID8984127) document postprandial pressure drops or presyncope without isolating steamed brown rice or orthostatic lightheadedness severity.

Parkinson gum-chewing study (PMID20385891) sped swallowing without specifying flavor or drooling severity; healthy spearmint-gum studies (PMID22505903, PMID23372599, PMID7503931) measured stimulated saliva flow; NCT06313905 has no posted results.

Brewed lemongrass tea study (Leite 1986, n=50) found no clear dream-recall differences without PSG or PD; rat tea EEG (PMID3762195) found no slow-wave/REM changes; aroma/inhaler studies (Aoyama 2025, Kumboyono 2026) do not test brewed tea or dream enactment.

PENSA EGCG RCT (PMID40664536) found null 12-month olfaction (+0.1, p=.853); Kagoshima PD green-tea cohort (PMID42816813) found null hyposmia by frequency (p=.854) and volume (p=.519); acute coffee/caffeine trials were null.

CHRIS (PMID42830263) defined tea as black/herbal rather than green tea; NTP mouse extract gavage (NTP-TR-585, PMID20884815) reported nasal histopathology without smell testing; scent-training trials test inhaled odor.

Heated onion-peel extract trial (Cho 2024) gave baseline-imbalanced self-rated URI hoarseness (p=.038) with null overall WURSS (p=.164) and no intelligibility metric; allergy case (Albanesi 2019) had acute anaphylactic dysphonia; PD diet cohorts pool sofrito.

Boysenberry-apple trials (Lomiwes 2025, Shrestha 2026) measured throat irritation or a 7-item respiratory sum without acoustic loudness; MVP and Thai PD surveys pool berries without voice-volume contrasts; jam interviews and allergy cases omit loudness.

Grape-seed extract RCT (NCT03526406) favored simple finger tapping at 6-12 weeks (interaction p=.005) while complex tapping was inconclusive; seed extract and conflict with Concord juice pegboard block a signed raw-grape direction.

Concord grape juice crossover (PMID26864371) slowed grooved pegboard in phase one (63.2 vs 60.4 s; phase two null); mixed bilberry-grape juice pegboard (NCT00972972) was null (p=.41); aquatic-exercise juice added no functional benefit.

Exergame fish-vs-olive-oil trial (PMID30866834) gave null single- and dual-task stride interactions (p=.753, .537; grade unspecified); NCT05485402 gave null 4-m gait speed; stroke mouse footprints were null; PRIME whole-diet stride protocol (NCT07097103) awaits results.

Brewed green tea PD pilot (jbbs.2015.56020) and LRRK2/Kagoshima cohorts omit script size; Postuma 2017 caffeine RCT (PMID28954882) found no MDS-UPDRS-II item differences; healthy caffeine study (PMID17010462) tested pen velocity/fluency rather than letter size.

MVP cohorts (PMID29081890, PMID40732955) report composite PRO-PD without facial items or poaching; Phillips 2018 ketogenic meal plan included simmered chicken soup without isolating chicken or facial expressiveness; corticobasal case has no timed contrast.

PD menu (PMID32041265) listed chives without dose or separate dystonia outcome; meal-protein dystonia reports (PMID1866021, PMID839864) omit chives; onion/garlic/Chinese-chive animal and tissue studies do not test fresh common chives or Parkinson dystonia.

PD butylphthalide trial (PMID30988766) reported aggregate PDQ-39 with inconsistent adverse-event totals; celery-root mania case (PMID34370637) involved venlafaxine and St. John's wort; seed-extract safety (NCT06061926), Alzheimer composite (Gu 2024), and thyroid cases omit visual hallucination frequency.

Three-arm randomized placebo-controlled hemodialysis trial (n=16/arm, 12 weeks) reported Bonferroni-corrected Sniffin Sticks TDI delta +3.56 (500 mg, p=0.010) and +4.00 (1000 mg, p=0.002) vs +0.875 placebo, and discrimination delta +2.56/+3.31 vs +0.125 (both p=0.001); threshold and identification inconclusive.

Double-blind three-arm randomized placebo-controlled CKD trial (curcumin n=20, training n=19, placebo n=19) improved QOD (p=0.045), self-assessment (p=0.047), and normosmia shift (20% vs 0%, p=0.032), while training outperformed curcumin and Table 2 contains a pre/post Iran-SIT arithmetic discrepancy.

Double-blind 18-month Theracurmin RCT in nondemented older adults reported faster secondary Trail Making A time (32.6 to 24.9 s vs 30.5 to 28.4 s, p=0.04), without culinary turmeric or Parkinson participants.
Double-blind 12-week Longvida 2000 mg/day RCT in healthy adults aged 45-74 found identical Flanker attention scores across arms (8.3 to 8.5, arm-by-time p=0.97).
Double-blind 12-month BCM-95 RCT in older adults (n=96 analyzed) showed no clear differential change on the attention-containing cognitive battery (baseline to 12-month p=0.25).
Randomized 22-week adjunct glucoraphanin+myrosinase trial in schizophrenia reported inconclusive MCCB attention/vigilance changes (+2.56 high, +5.38 low vs +6.28 placebo, p=0.263).
Double-blind 12-week glucoraphanin capsule RCT in healthy older adults found Symbol Search p=0.03 alongside null Coding (p=0.83) and Stroop (p=1.0), without specifying plant source.
Eight-week pediatric ADHD methylphenidate adjunct RCT abstract favored sulforaphane on parent/teacher inattention (d=1.446/1.055), with full methods paywalled and botanical source unspecified.
Controlled freeze-dried strawberry intervention in older adults did not establish a clear direct attention improvement over placebo and did not test fresh raw fruit in Parkinson disease.
Combined oral dried fig plus olive oil rat scopolamine study measured maze memory and hippocampal markers with zero clinical visual hallucination outcome.
Multi-component plant-rich Parkinson diet study reported apathy change with inconsistent final group reporting and zero isolated raw-banana exposure.
Small open randomized whole-banana feeding trial outside Parkinson disease found inconclusive POMS2 vigor-activity and fatigue-inertia changes with no apathy scale.

Oral coriander seed powder trial in diabetes reported within-arm blood pressure decline without a clear between-arm placebo difference, dried leaf preparation, or standing orthostatic lightheadedness measure.
Healthy-adult raw romaine salad crossover (PMID:34261489) compared vascular measures against cellulose without any tremor outcome or Parkinson cohort.

Mouse Parkinson-model experiments (PMID:39264814, PMID:42015685) tested isolated lentinan or engineered carriers on pole and general behavioral assays without reporting rest tremor or cooked whole shiitake.

Acute rodent toxicology of isolated oral capsaicin (PMID:8887888) and dermal capsaicinoid gel (PMID:41674738) noted nonspecific toxic tremor without culinary paprika or Parkinson rest-tremor measurement.
Concentrated oral sowa extract in rodent alcohol withdrawal measured general coordination without Parkinson rest tremor or culinary dried dill weed.
ECHA 2012 regulatory dossier recorded occasional nonspecific body tremor in two rats after acute isolated carvone exposure without rest-tremor grading or culinary ground caraway.
Parkinson cannabidiol trial (PMID:25237116) delivered corn oil as the shared capsule carrier across all arms, preventing any isolated refined corn-oil rest-tremor contrast.

Oral methanol (PMID:24250488) and ethanol/alkaloid (PMID:22136413) Murraya koenigii leaf extracts inhibited reserpine- and haloperidol-induced rat orofacial dyskinesia (VCMs, tongue protrusions) and catalepsy without testing limb rest tremor or cooked culinary leaf.
Parkinson 57-person gluten-free diet trial reported an inconclusive composite motor outcome without isolating cooked wheat berries or a standalone rest-tremor item.

Parkinson vegetarian diet pilot (PMID:32041265) listed rosemary in a shared menu and reported aggregate UPDRS-III only; rosemary diterpene rodent studies (PMID:34434108, PMID:36526017) did not assess resting tremor.

Cross-sectional early Parkinson cohort (PMID:34127758, Supplementary Table S2) found a near-zero age-adjusted correlation between plasma alpha-linolenic acid and examiner-rated resting tremor (rho=0.059, p=0.728).

Parkinson RCTs of flaxseed-derived omega-3 plus 400 IU vitamin E (PMID:28342967, DOI:10.1016/j.clineuro.2018.12.006) co-administered vitamin E and reported aggregate UPDRS without an isolated resting-tremor item.

Isolated quercetin attenuated muscle tremor burst frequency in unilateral 6-OHDA Parkinson-model rats in a dose- and time-dependent manner, but quercetin is ubiquitous across foods and no raw-apple preparation was tested.
Intraperitoneal quercetin nanoemulsion (20 mg/kg) reduced harmaline-induced essential tremor severity in mice (n=8/arm, p<0.0001), using an essential-tremor model and non-apple isolated nanoemulsion.
Isolated cardamonin improved open-field, pole-climbing, and catalepsy outcomes in reserpine/haloperidol mice without evaluating rest tremor or ground culinary cardamom.
Isolated filbertone improved rotarod and treadmill performance in neurodegeneration mouse models without evaluating Parkinson resting tremor or cold-pressed hazelnut oil.

Accidental overdose and poison-center cases (PMID:39559662, PMID:24452991, PMID:26219944) report acute toxicosis with mixed upper-limb or intention tremor alongside delirium or hyponatremia rather than culinary intake or Parkinson rest tremor.

Double-blind 90-day 3-arm RCT in older adults with age-associated memory impairment (PMID29314866, PMC5779242, N=90 ITT) found 900 mg/day dried aqueous spearmint extract improved LSEQ ease of getting to sleep vs placebo (47.63 to 51.11 vs 49.83 to 45.48 mm, t(82)=2.91, p=.0046, d=0.805; overall p=.0170), while sleep quality (p=.4267) and ease of awakening (p=.9016) were null; industry-funded extract capsules in non-Parkinson older adults.

Competing larger 90-day double-blind RCT (PMID30802720, NCT02518165, N=142 healthy active young adults) of the same proprietary aqueous spearmint extract reported no statistically significant LSEQ or PSQI differences vs placebo; supplement tables unavailable.

30-day RCT of a proprietary water-extracted spearmint and green-tea blend in adults with subclinical sleep complaints (PMID33809544, PMC8000032, NCT03567343) had null primary sleep-onset latency and REM outcomes alongside an exploratory ISI coefficient of -1.0 point (95% CI -2.0 to -0.03, p=.044); green-tea co-ingredient prevents isolated spearmint attribution.

Oral aqueous Mentha spicata extract prolonged pentobarbital-induced sleep duration in rats (42.13 to 73.64 min, PMID30158996, PMC6106973) without changing sleep onset; drug-induced sedation is a remote proxy for clinical insomnia.

Randomized ITT trial (PMID41478596, IRCT20230616058497N1, n=68 adults with migraine) found 8 weeks oral flaxseed powder vs roasted wheat powder improved Insomnia Severity Index (-4.6 vs -1.6, p=.029) alongside headache severity; tested powdered seed rather than cold-pressed flaxseed oil in a non-Parkinson cohort.

Uncontrolled before-after pilot of roasted whole flaxseed in 46 students (DOI10.5455/jrtm.2022/97416) found shorter PSG sleep latency (14.8 to 10.39 min, p<.001), null global PSQI (9.61 to 8.74, p=.635), and an internal text-vs-table ESS conflict without a comparison group.

Randomized knee-OA trial (PMID42866378, PMC13657636, n=90) of topical 3% tarragon oil extract in sweet almond oil vs vehicle vs routine care lowered post-3-week WOMAC pain (10.13 vs 13.73 and 13.43, p=.001), while 1- and 3-week post-stop contrasts were null (p=.376 and .858), scent prevented blinding, and the 2021 registry conflicts on chronology, randomization, schedule and blinding.

Oral aqueous extract of shade-dried tarragon aerial parts for 4 weeks lowered formalin-evoked pain scores vs fructose-only control rats (PMID26170888, PMC4481084, p<.001); dried-aerial extract in non-Parkinson rodents.

Oral ethanolic tarragon extract PMI-5011 in high-fat-diet neuropathic mice (PMID20396384, PMC2852597) shifted tactile allodynia (1.20 vs 0.76 g), thermal latency (11.4 vs 15.7 s) and mechanical pressure threshold (12.3 vs 15.2 g) toward normal-chow values rather than measuring spontaneous pain.
Completed 5-arm dental-injection mucosal gel registry (IRCT20241115063712N1, target n=100) comparing tarragon extract vs jujube, combination, lidocaine and vehicle has no verified public results.

Haloperidol-exposed rat study (PMID33759084, DOI10.1007/s11011-021-00707-6) Figure 4 measured footprint stride length in cm: baseline ~9.1, disease control ~5.7, standard comparator ~8.4, and ascending oral methanolic Cucurbita pepo seed extract arms ~6.4, 7.3 and 8.0 cm; group counts and comparator footnotes are unverified from public figure/abstract.

Haloperidol-exposed mouse study (DOI10.1177/0976500X221150837; 6 mice/group) Figure 4 reported longer day-21 stride length for the two higher oral isolated p-coumaric acid arms vs untreated haloperidol controls (p<.05 and p<.01).

Roasted and pressed pumpkin seed oil (130 C and 150 C, DOI10.1002/ejlt.201700110) contained measurable p-coumaric acid (0.5-0.6 ug/g) and ferulic acid (0.9-1.8 ug/g), documenting constituent transfer into roasted oil without establishing food-to-extract dose equivalence or gait efficacy.

Randomized 30-day placebo-controlled trial in 86 university students (NCT05999071, DOI10.1108/nfs-08-2023-0193) reported lower anxiety with dried powdered Coriandrum sativum seed capsules vs starch placebo (p=.04); retrospective registration after completion, outcome-priority shift from secondary to primary, absent arm-level data, and seed-vs-leaf exposure limit inference.

Hydroethanolic cilantro-leaf extract fractions (strongest in aqueous fraction) showed anxiolytic signals in Swiss albino mouse elevated plus maze and light-dark box tests without rotarod deficit (DOI10.18203/2319-2003.ijbcp20202936).

Mouse elevated plus maze study of aqueous dried-cilantro-leaf extract (PMID26109787, 6 mice/group across 5 arms) reported more open-arm entries (19.50-29.17 vs 5.83 saline) but has internal abstract-vs-methods conflicts over oral vs injected route, extraction method, and p-value threshold, making it unusable for direction.

Patent-reported randomized crossover in 14 healthy men (WO2019230626A1, 28 days/arm) of commercial red-perilla water extract vs starch reported -0.24 fewer nighttime voids/night (p<.05) from a low 0.24 baseline, while daytime frequency and daily urine volume contrasts were null and table-vs-prose daytime SEs conflict; void frequency rather than urgency in a non-Parkinson sample.

Oral perilla extract for 2 weeks prolonged micturition inter-void intervals by 27% vs controls in female spontaneously hypertensive rats (PMID29268303) without altering maximum bladder pressure; extract and void interval rather than fresh shiso and urgency.

Controlled mouse experiment (Bian 2019; 10 mice/group across 5 groups) found oral volatile fractions from dry-fried (toasted) and raw huajiao reduced 20-min acetic-acid writhing vs vehicle (18.40 and 21.10 dry-fried, 19.50 and 27.20 raw vs 49.60 vehicle); full article body, fried-vs-raw statistical test, and botanical species voucher remain unverified.

Locally applied isolated hydroxy-alpha-sanshool reduced inflammatory mechanical hypersensitivity but did not reduce heat hypersensitivity in mice (PMID23652591); isolated constituent, topical route and evoked animal assay.

Competing null double-blind RCT (PMID26486374, NCT01890837, n=40 women with IBS) of multi-herb daikenchuto (Zanthoxylum, ginger, ginseng, maltose) found no significant abdominal or rectal-distension pain effect; multi-herb formula cannot isolate toasted Sichuan pepper.

Uncontrolled 9-woman xerostomia case series (PMC6392883, UMIN000027493) of mixed Zanthoxylum bungeanum oil, sesame oil, menthol and lemon oil capsules reported interview improvements in oral discomfort without a placebo or isolated attribution.

Double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial (PMID31835620, PMC6950039, NCT03673930; n=82 healthy adults aged 30-55) found 80 mg/day standardized Zanthoxylum armatum extract in MCT oil lowered day-56 cognitive-task mental fatigue vs sunflower-oil placebo (p=.006); baseline fatigue imbalance, extract vs ground culinary spice, and non-Parkinson sample.
Two healthy-gamer extract crossover registrations listing subjective fatigue (NCT07047105 completed, NCT07752329 planned) have no public posted results.

Randomized 4-arm functional dyspepsia trial (PMID40365186, PMC12068504; 104 randomized, 85 analyzed) reported greater week-8 constipation subscore improvement with aqueous Rhus coriaria extract (n=24, p=.002) and extract plus habit change (n=25, p<.001) vs omeprazole (n=25) in adjusted model 6 with zero adverse events; effect magnitudes/CIs omitted, active omeprazole comparator, extract vs ground sumac, non-Parkinson cohort.

Competing preclinical study (DOI10.3329/bjp.v9i4.20879) found crude Rhus coriaria extract suppressed castor-oil-induced diarrhea in mice and relaxed isolated rabbit jejunum; chemically induced diarrhea is a remote mechanistic proxy rather than constipation severity.

Published clinical case (PMID16258648, n=1 woman with focal eyelid dystonia/blepharospasm) reported dystonia severity rating falling from 4 at baseline to 1 at six months following transdermal capsaicin patch, while five healthy volunteers showed inconclusive blink-rate change (17 +- 3 vs 15 +- 5); uncontrolled case, topical isolated capsaicin vs oral ground cayenne, non-Parkinson focal dystonia.

Double-blind randomized placebo crossover (Tanaka 2008; 18 randomized, 17 analyzed) of oral chicken-breast extract drink (400 mg/day imidazole dipeptides x 29 days) lowered 4-h cycling fatigue VAS increase (+18.1 +- 15.8 vs +26.3 +- 18.1 mm, p<.05) and 4-h recovery increase (+9.8 +- 17.3 vs +20.1 +- 20.7 mm, p<.01), with null 2-h and next-day contrasts; extract drink vs poached chicken in healthy exercise fatigue.

Competing randomized crossover (DOI10.1248/jhs.55.56, n=30 healthy adults) of reconstituted freeze-dried whole-chicken soup vs placebo found inconclusive POMS routine fatigue change (-0.5 +- 0.9 vs +0.1 +- 0.8, p=.61).

Analytical chemistry (DOI10.3136/nskkk.66.210) confirms anserine and carnosine imidazole dipeptides are retained in heated chicken breast cuts; establishes exposure constituent bridge without symptom outcomes.
Culinary patent KR20050019309A describes subjective repeated-tasting fatigue impressions for Korean chicken baeksuk without controlled design or Parkinson measurement.

Randomized placebo-controlled 4-week trial (PMID19754931, PMC2757026, n=70 adults with stress/fatigue) found 10 mg/day coated proprietary cantaloupe juice concentrate (Extramel) yielded 26% higher day-28 FARD weariness improvement vs placebo with no reported adverse effects; proprietary coated concentrate vs raw cantaloupe, non-Parkinson sample.

Randomized placebo-controlled 84-day trial (PMID24949549, PMC4073155, NCT01767922, n=61 healthy adults) found 10 mg/day palm-oil-coated Extramel cantaloupe concentrate lowered day-84 secondary Prevost physical fatigue vs starch placebo (84.4 vs 93.2, p<.02; day-28 null).

Competing double-blind 12-week RCT (PMID21044831, n=38 women aged 50-65 with self-perceived fatigue) of melon SOD plus gliadin vs placebo found inconclusive MFI general (-1.6% vs -4.1%), physical and mental fatigue contrasts.

Two additional competing melon-extract RCTs were null on fatigue: SODB exercise trial (PMID32053942, Prevost physical fatigue intergroup null, trend p=.068) and 6-month GliSODin locomotive-syndrome trial (PMID35628874, n=46 completers, Chalder Fatigue -3.21 vs -0.59, p=.15).

Double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial (PMID31835620, PMC6950039, NCT03673930; n=82 healthy adults aged 30-55) found 80 mg/day standardized Zanthoxylum armatum extract in MCT oil improved acute Speed of Attention (p=.039) and lowered RVIP false alarms (p=.025) vs sunflower-oil placebo, while baseline false alarms were higher in the extract arm and name-to-face memory accuracy fell (p=.040).
Two healthy-gamer extract crossover registrations listing attention speed and accuracy (NCT07047105 completed, NCT07752329 planned) have no posted results.
Oral isolated thymoquinone in rotenone-exposed mice (PMID40951472, n=3/arm) increased open-field movement distance and speed vs rotenone control, while beam and hanging-wire tests were inconclusive.
Isolated thymoquinone improved catalepsy and locomotor scores in chlorpromazine-treated rats (PMID27180446).

Oral Nigella sativa seed oil (0.2 mL/rat) significantly reduced haloperidol-induced EPS movement disorders and oral dyskinesia alongside caudate astrogliosis (PMID27752803; item-level numeric tables behind paywall).
Higher doses of Nigella sativa seed extract reduced drug-induced catalepsy duration in mice (DOI10.4236/wjns.2014.44035).
Competing null hydroalcoholic Nigella seed extract haloperidol catalepsy experiment (PMID41438691) showed no significant single-plant catalepsy contrast.

Double-blind RCT of 2 g/day Cucurbita pepo seed oil vs wheat germ oil (18 vs 13 analyzed); depression item remained at median 0 vs rose 0 to 1 (unadjusted endpoint p=.046); active comparator, floor effect, unspecified pressing, non-PD cohort.

Oral pumpkin seed oil improved sucrose preference and reduced tail-suspension immobility in six-week chronic mild stress rats (2022 and 2024 reports grouped as one program); extraction grade unspecified and non-PD animal model.

Oral ethanolic Perillae Herba leaf extract shortened pentobarbital sleep latency in mice and increased total sleep in rats (thesis and 2017 article counted as one family); non-PD rodent model and extract rather than culinary dried shiso.

Oral fermented Perilla frutescens var. acuta leaf extract increased NREM sleep and slow-wave activity and shortened pentobarbital sleep latency in rodents (thesis and 2024 journal report counted as one family).

Inhaled Perilla frutescens essential oil shortened sleep latency and prolonged sleep duration via GABA_A and 5-HT signaling in PCPA-induced insomnia mice, paired with Traditional Chinese Medicine insomnia use context.
Eight-herb Jing Si concentrate vs placebo in functional dyspepsia (n=13/arm); median PSQI 14 to 12 (p=.207) vs 11 to 10 (p=.141) with no adjusted between-arm contrast and multi-herb confounding.
Registered perilla plus peppermint extract sleep trial in non-PD adults with no posted results.
Completed eight-herb perilla-containing long-COVID crossover listing day-28 PSQI without posted results.

low — Official registry planned MDS-UPDRS III and IV secondary outcomes for pharmaceutical butylphthalide versus placebo. The likely matching 2024 primary congress result reports cognition and general adverse events, with no dyskinesia item, Part IV result or fresh celery leaf exposure.

low — Healthy adults ate separated green celery leaves with bread. Apigenin appeared in plasma after ingestion but there was no levodopa, Parkinson population or dyskinesia rating. The 2009 report with shared author and identical pharmacokinetic estimates is a potential overlap.

low — Raw celery leaves contained 0.87 mg/kg 3-n-butylphthalide versus 0.29 mg/kg in raw stalks. This establishes a plant-part-specific chemical lead without a Parkinson population, consumption intervention, levodopa comparison or dyskinesia endpoint.

low — Pharmaceutical DL-3-n-butylphthalide in LPS-treated mice improved open-field and rotarod performance at 28 weeks. The abstract calls it dyskinesia, but the original methods measure locomotion and coordination without levodopa exposure or involuntary-movement scoring.

low — Oral whole dried celery methanolic extract improved certain motor behaviors in MPTP model mice. The preparation includes the whole plant, and none of the movement tests measures levodopa-induced dyskinesia.

low — Oral pharmaceutical DL-3-n-butylphthalide in people with Parkinson's was assessed with off-medication UPDRS Part III, sleep and quality-of-life scores. Its discussion of dyskinesia refers to a mouse locomotor study. No culinary leaf, levodopa pharmacokinetics or separate dyskinesia endpoint was reported.

low — People with Parkinson's received a multicomponent diet that listed celery without specifying the plant part. The study measured UPDRS Part III and could not estimate effects of fresh leaf or dyskinesia separately.
low — Hydrodistilled oil from shade-dried leaves contained 3-butylphthalide at 5.36% of oil composition. Neither fresh leaf ingestion nor a Parkinson motor endpoint was tested.

chervil in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome — The menu lists chervil and the motor examination includes facial expression. Plant preparation, isolated chervil exposure and facial expression item changes are unavailable.
sumac extract applied to Parkinson donor skin cells — The donor UPDRS scores characterize baseline disease. No facial item or change after eating sumac was measured.

ungraded canola in a Parkinson diet with motor complications tracked — Part IV changed by −0.79 versus −1.56 points between diet arms, p=.32. The four motor-complication items were not disaggregated and the oil was one menu ingredient.

perilla leaf extract and intestinal transit in a constipation mouse model — Leaf extract increased intestinal transit in activated-carbon-induced constipation. This was a distinct gastrointestinal model without Parkinson disease or fresh leaf consumption.
perilla seed oil and constipation ratings in a fixed-order pilot — Within-oil comparisons at weeks two and three favored oil. Endpoint p=.052, eight participants, nonrandom phases and no fresh leaf.

green-shiso and barley mixed tablet patent example — Table 3 reports mean subjective bowel improvement 2.8 for both mixtures among 10 women. The applicant narrative claims improvement. There is no isolated fresh-leaf or Parkinson comparison.

leaf-containing mixed formulation and bowel condition ratings — Two mixtures containing perilla leaf and other extracts score 4.50 and 4.75, with base mixture 4.25 and rice comparator 3.25. Four healthy women per arm and several component differences give no constituent-specific effect.

dried perilla leaf extract and constipation scores in otherwise healthy adults — Among 47 completers, stool days increased by 0.83 versus 0.80 per week and PAC-SYM changes did not differ. Registry maltodextrin and publication tapioca starch describe placebo differently. Fresh leaves and Parkinson constipation were untested.

completed Hou Gu Mi Xi comparison with disputed perilla in gastrointestinal disorders — Registry prose names perilla but the same registry arm list and primary protocol omit it. Defecation appears within a composite and no item result is available.

terminated Hou Gu Mi Xi post-gastrectomy trial with disputed perilla — Registry text and original protocol list discordant ingredients and amounts. No comparative bowel result is posted after termination.

perilla leaf extract and acute gastrointestinal symptoms in healthy adults — The crossover favored extract for overall postprandial discomfort but reported no clear bowel movement difference across visits. The acute extract and population differ from the frozen claim.

registered mixed perilla and ginger product for upper gastrointestinal symptoms — The Leuven scale covers upper gastrointestinal symptoms. General safety collection may provide event detail when results are released. No results, specific constipation outcome or isolated shiso arm are registered.

combined perilla and ginger extract in dyspepsia — The combined diarrhea and constipation score declined within the single arm after excluding seven early nonresponders. There is no constipation-only result, separate perilla exposure or Parkinson group.

perilla-containing clinical mixture with separate modification for dry stools — The author abstract gives 11 versus 14 and asserts significance. An independent comparison assuming all 60 per arm would not reproduce it. Full table, denominators, allocation and individual ingredient attribution remain unverified.

perilla seed oil and constipation ratings among female athletes — High-dose seed oil favored the selected lowest constipation score versus placebo (p=.020). Figure 4 and Methods use conflicting change signs. Official UMIN lists four arms including olive oil, with no olive result reported in the three-arm paper.

Parkinson constipation trial with unverified decoction composition — The 2026 original abstract has a response percentage but no response definition or itemized composition. Full-text access and whether the tested formula contained Perilla remain open.

purified perillaldehyde and gastrointestinal dysfunction in rotenone mice — The abstract reports a favorable broad gastrointestinal outcome. A constipation-specific endpoint or estimate was not verified, and the exposure was purified perillaldehyde.

ground whole hazelnut and mouse exploratory locomotion — Ground hazelnut increased open-field locomotion and rearing in high-fat-fed mice. The study did not use toasted oil, Parkinson disease or a freezing-of-gait measure.
