injected grapeseed oil drug carrier and an orofacial movement outcome — Grapeseed oil nanocapsules carrying haloperidol only partly attenuated acute vacuous chewing and all loaded formulations prevented excess chewing subchronically. The study counted involuntary jaw movements in rats. Speech, articulation and oral oil ingestion were unmeasured.

pepper-leaf tea and Insomnia Severity Index in primary insomnia — n=30. Day-14 ISI 5.33 with leaves and 5.60 with chamomile, p=.81. Leaves differ from ground peppercorns and the primary insomnia cohort does not identify PD.

oral three-botanical formula with black pepper and PSQI — 50 adults in a single-arm course reported mean PSQI 12.22 at baseline and 5.30 after week 4. The formula also contains gotu kola and lotus and the study includes no PD subgroup or isolated pepper estimate.

pepper extract and measured mouse sleep under acute caffeine challenge — Oral pepper extract plus caffeine increased non-REM sleep and lowered wake time versus caffeine alone. EEG gives no extract-only estimate and the intervention and outcome differ from ground pepper and clinical insomnia.

black-pepper-containing turmeric powder and a measured insomnia scale outside Parkinson disease — All 45 patients received multicomponent dietary advice and were offered Curcuma Latte, containing turmeric and black pepper. Thirty-two had lower Oviedo insomnia scores, with no control arm or pepper-specific dose, processing or outcome contrast. The cohort had rheumatic chronic pain, not Parkinson disease.

oral multiherb formula containing pepper fruit and PSQI in chronic insomnia — The n=60 open-label trial found within-arm improvement with all three active treatments and between-group post-treatment p=.27. Black pepper was one of twelve botanicals in one arm. No PD subgroup.

lovage in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome — The menu lists lovage and the motor examination includes gait. The paper reports no stride measurement or separate effect of fresh leaves.
cooked chervil soup allergy case — Acute allergy symptoms after cooked soup do not establish pain after eating fresh chervil.
methanol extract of culinary chervil in enzyme and cell assays — Keratinocyte inflammation and enzyme results are not pain severity outcomes.

rosmarinic-acid-rich lemon balm extract and cognitive composites in mild Alzheimer dementia — The report found no clear group difference on composite cognition and gives no separate intelligibility measure or fresh leaf exposure.

red raspberry vinegar and scheduled blood pressure in an incomplete eight-week trial — The deposited author abstract says blood pressure was measured; pressure and postural symptom results are absent. The comparison used vinegar and cranberry juice. The body remains open.

Himalayan raspberry consumption and blood pressure in hypertension — The five-person case series reports lower pressure over time, asymptomatic low readings in three and medication changes in two. It gives no orthostatic test, lightheadedness outcome, species assignment or frozen preparation.

oral raspberry challenge and blood pressure during allergy — Blood pressure remained normal during a challenge that produced respiratory allergy symptoms in one patient. This case has no orthostatic measurements or Parkinson cohort.

freeze-dried black raspberry slurry and crossover-sequence safety data — The registry records 0 of 5 participants with serious events and 0 of 5 with other events in each sequence. Each sequence received both treatments. The posted data provide no treatment-specific orthostatic estimate.

frozen raspberry beverage and resting blood pressure — Flow-mediated dilation improved without a clear central or peripheral BP effect. The healthy-men crossover used drinks made from frozen fruit and did not measure orthostasis.

freeze-dried red raspberry and blood pressure in hypertensive mice — Systolic pressure was 137 ± 4 mmHg with freeze-dried raspberry and 185 ± 4 mmHg with angiotensin II alone (p < .0001). This mouse model measured induced high blood pressure without an orthostatic endpoint.

freeze-dried raspberry and systolic blood pressure in hypertensive rats — Final systolic pressure was 20.8% lower than angiotensin II alone (p = .03). A potentially overlapping 2024 report found lower week-seven systolic pressure in raspberry-only and combined berry groups. No orthostatic symptom endpoint was measured.

raspberry snack and resting blood pressure in diabetes — Four-week raspberry supplementation showed a tendency toward lower resting systolic pressure. There was no standing blood pressure or lightheadedness outcome.
frozen raspberry and seated blood pressure — The time-by-treatment systolic interaction was p = .03 and treatment main effect p = .37. Neither standing blood pressure nor symptoms were assessed.

freeze-dried raspberry and blackberry and blood pressure in high-fat-fed mice — Systolic pressure was 98.9 ± 6.25 mmHg with raspberry alone (p < .0001) and 106.0 ± 9.10 with both berries (p = .002), versus 120.6 ± 6.79 with the high-fat, high-sucrose diet alone. Standing symptoms were unmeasured.

canola-containing diet and facial-expression domain in Parkinson disease — The published Part III motor aggregate included a facial-expression item. The item estimate and canola processing were unavailable. The randomized comparison was between whole diets.

cassia-containing formula and composite oral function in older adults — The aggregate oral score includes facial expressiveness but item changes were unavailable and the intervention combined 12 botanicals.

possible companion Parkinson-only manometry study — The 1998 proceedings and investigator bibliography verify the title and page. The original Parkinson-only body and any overlap with the mixed cohort remain open.

mashed potato in a Parkinson manometry study — Twelve Parkinson participants without dysphagia were tested with mashed potato and water. The reported pressure table pools water only. No potato-specific outcome or baked preparation.
mashed potato as a soft-food questionnaire example — The questionnaire includes mashed potato in a mixed soft-food category. The study supplies no potato bolus or Parkinson-specific food result.

potato paste swallowing ratings in healthy adults — Participants reported no clear difference in ease of swallowing across four pastes. The preparations and population differ from the frozen statement.

food-specific boluses during dual-task endoscopy — White bread caused more observed residue. Green jelly and dyed liquid had more spillage. The overall score differed inconclusively and the study used no potato.

boiled potato instrumental texture tests and classification by healthy older adults — Boiled potato passed fork cut and failed fork pressure, while healthy older adults placed it across several texture levels. Instrument results and perceived texture do not estimate clinical dysphagia severity.

meal-related cough or choking and bolus texture comparison by diagnosis — The expanded survey reports mealtime coughing or choking in 24% of 435 Parkinson and 49% of 82 PSP patients. The separate eight-person Parkinson imaging comparison used simulated textures. No baked potato, food-by-case attribution or food-level severity estimate.

soft food category in a Parkinson swallowing questionnaire — The soft-food response differed across groups while both medians were zero. Mashed potato was an example, and the direct swallow test used water.
water and wafer endoscopy in Parkinson disease — The study assessed water, thickened water and wafer, without a potato comparison.

clinical videofluoroscopy corpus with Parkinson-coded records — The public index identifies eight adults under Parkinson or PKD labels. Food-level transcripts require registration. Potato exposure remains unverified.

milk-free mashed potato in Parkinson endoscopic swallowing assessment — The 24-person study used mashed potato, water and a salted cracker. Table 4 gives four people with aspiration across the assessment and no food-level response or baked potato.

gummy chewing performance and nutrient intake in Parkinson disease — Ten participants with Parkinson scored 2 versus 6 among 24 comparison participants on the gummy chewing test. The diet questionnaire pools tubers and the paper reports nutrient estimates. It gives no baked-potato-specific result.

starch-thickened contrast and penetration in Parkinson disease — Pudding-viscosity contrast reduced penetration relative to thinner contrast and increased some residue measures. The study used no potato. The 2019 and 2020 reports share cohort details, and the dissertation likely overlaps.
foil-baked potato sensory variation across cultivars — A trained sensory panel found that varieties differ under the same foil-wrapped baking procedure.

choking by bolus consistency in a single Parkinson case — Clinical choking persisted with an unnamed solid after therapy, while liquid and pasty choking were absent at reassessment. No individual food or baked potato was identified.
modified oral food textures and enteral support in one Parkinson case — The case describes swallowing difficulty and a modified-food plan, without measured change or a baked potato exposure.

caregiver-reported dry and moistened baked potato in Parkinson disease — A caregiver reported choking with dry baked potato and no difficulty with moistened baked potato in one person. The account gives no clinical confirmation, standardized swallowing assessment, or comparison with foods other than baked potato.

biscuit and liquid boluses with endoscopic airway invasion results — Five cases underwent endoscopy. Figure 2 gives one penetration with a quarter biscuit, no aspiration with a half biscuit and two liquid conditions with penetration and aspiration. The 20 mL liquid bar total conflicts with cohort size. No potato was tested.

indirect — Fatal aspiration during eating with food recovered from airway in a woman with Parkinson disease and multifocal stroke. The meal ingredient was unreported, so this gives no estimate for baked potato.

boiled potato food code and diagnosis-level intake — The 2023 supplement names boiled potato and two 2026 analyses give potato intake by diagnosis. They use one cohort. No baked potato or choking outcome.

earlier Pará food consistency and choking questionnaire — Five of eight men with Parkinson disease reported choking. Four changed food consistency. No test food was named and overlap with the later 24-person endoscopy cohort is unknown.

named sandwich obstruction and Parkinson diagnosis — An official inspection documented severe choking during a peanut butter and jelly sandwich meal with bread identified, in a resident with Parkinson disease and dysphagia.

corrected food identity in a Parkinson choking event — The survey’s meal and witness evidence identifies honeydew where the hospital record described potato. It gives no comparative dysphagia measure.

observed baked potato consumption in a resident with Parkinson disease and dysphagia — The inspection documents actual baked potato consumption. A family member attributed difficulty during the meal to the chicken nugget coating and described a separate prior choking episode on liquid. No potato-specific swallowing symptom, instrumented outcome or comparison is recorded.

whole baked potato served in a dysphagia care record — The report documents serving a whole skin-on baked potato. It gives no Parkinson diagnosis for that resident and no potato ingestion or swallowing outcome.

baked-potato soup and chips offered to a person with Parkinson disease and dysphagia — The inspection identifies the soup on the tray ticket and records the resident beginning the meal. It does not establish soup or chip intake or a swallowing outcome from either item. The agency narrative is publicly mirrored and the original PDF did not open.

potato product on a menu and confirmed chicken obstruction — The general menu lists baked tater tots. The bolus removed from the resident with Parkinson disease was chicken, and the record gives no potato-linked outcome.

diet records with a derived Parkinson potato-consumption lower bound — At least 19 of 21 participants with Parkinson disease ate potatoes under the usual rounding of the pooled count. Preparation and swallowing response are unavailable.
distinct food in an autopsy with severe esophageal achalasia — The primary abstract identifies boiled rice and provides no comparison of swallowing by food or preparation.

combined nutrition intervention and dysphagia prevalence — In 54 Parkinson clinic patients, dysphagia prevalence fell from 66.7% to 21.7% under a multifaceted program. There was no concurrent control or potato comparison.

swallowing questionnaire in Parkinson disease with broad texture examples — Thirty-five of 200 scored above 11. Food examples are pooled within questions, and no baked potato comparison or attributable case was reported.

premeal aroma exposure with solid-food swallowing tests — One Parkinson patient swallowed madeleine, yogurt and water more quickly after combined nasal aroma exposure. The qualitative comparison was inconclusive and no potato was tested.

validation of swallowing questionnaire with named food examples — Meat and peanuts are examples of challenging foods, and compote is one medication-taking aid. The 19-participant study reports a swallowing subscale and no exposure-specific outcomes.
videofluoroscopy during electrical stimulation — The thesis and later journal article describe the same small cohort and unnamed paste, solid and liquid boluses.

yogurt and water contrast with bolus-specific aspiration — Figures report four patients with aspiration on barium-mixed yogurt and three on water. Denominators vary. Unnamed solids were omitted after no elicited swallow. There was no baked-potato comparison.
levodopa response during videofluoroscopy with liquid and solid boluses — The 22-person report names no foods. The paired contrast estimates medication response.

confirmed scalloped potato obstruction in a different population — Staff removed scalloped potato and the resident was admitted to intensive care with aspiration pneumonia. The decision lists Down syndrome and dementia, does not identify Parkinson disease, and does not specify the cooking method.

observed preparation of a composite potato meal — Caregivers prepared a mixed potato and vegetable purée and observed other meal practices. No isolated or baked potato swallowing response was measured.

clinical food textures in Parkinson and parkinsonism — Thirteen of 43 inpatients had food intake difficulty and received modified meals. The authors observed easier swallowing with semi-gelled textures than watery purees in severe cases. No named food, separate Parkinson count or quantitative swallowing outcome.

fatal choking in a case of parkinsonian syndrome — The fatal event followed a change from porridge and soft dishes to regular meals. The obstructing food and idiopathic Parkinson diagnosis are unverified.

jelly aspiration and positioning in one Parkinson case — An unnamed jelly produced penetration and aspiration at 45-degree cervical lordosis but neither at 30 degrees in the same patient. No baked potato, obstructive choking or across-food comparison.

choking during texture-modified meals with multiple comorbidities — Rice porridge, chopped food and thickened fluid were prescribed before decannulation. The later choking and aspiration events did not identify the obstructing material. Parkinson had been raised in a prior evaluation.

actual choking plus instrumental jelly aspiration in Parkinson — One patient with Parkinson and cervical osteophytes survived an obstructive choking event with unidentified food. Jelly aspiration and thickened water clearance were separate instrumental observations.

hospital food-choking series including 11 parkinsonism cases — Of 119 selected incident reports, 11 coded parkinsonism. Choking materials are pooled across all cases and give no ingredient identity or denominator for baked potato. The program synopsis is the same study.

senbei and manju considered feasible after postoperative VF — Clinicians judged the named foods permissible after rehabilitation in a single Parkinson patient with prior aspiration pneumonia. No food-level rates or baked-potato exposure.

rice cracker and other food textures in one case — Coughing or choking diminished after a switch from porridge with chopped foods to puréed meals. A senbei cracker in the therapy room elicited good mouth opening and chewing. The original abstracts describe one case and no baked-potato exposure.

food temperature and first swallow in unspecified parkinsonism — The four-person study reported a favorable result for hot food but supplied no food identities, absolute values or measured choking. The rice ball belongs to a cited secondary-parkinsonism case.

potato patty and perceived eating ease outside a verified Parkinson group — A potato oyaki patty ranked highly on perceived eating ease in a nursing-home recipe evaluation. A separate simmered tuber ranked higher, with species unspecified. There was no Parkinson subgroup, baked potato, or clinical swallowing outcome.

silent aspiration with water and rice porridge — In one Parkinson and lacunar stroke case, videofluoroscopy documented silent aspiration with both 3 mL water and rice porridge after vertebral fracture. No potato exposure or measured choking rate.

boiled potato oral processing in healthy volunteers — The experiment included 12 healthy participants and measured bolus texture and oral workload across five foods. It did not test baked potato, patients with Parkinson disease or swallowing difficulty severity.

whole-swallowing regular side dishes and choking in advanced Parkinson disease — The patient had choking with unnamed side dishes and low intake of a rice-ball staple. No potato exposure was identified and the clinical changes followed combined care.

crushed thickened cup ramen in Parkinson swallowing evaluation and training — One patient with stage III Parkinson and aspiration pneumonia underwent VF and conditional direct training with crushed thickened cup ramen. Intake improved under combined care. No potato preparation was identified.

soft-cooked egg and preferred snacks in a stage V Parkinson case — One patient received soft-cooked onsen egg, unnamed formula and later rice crackers, cookies and manju after clinical assessment. Aspiration was not attributed to a specific food and baked potato was not reported.
sweet potato mousse in unstratified care-facility reports — The menu included sweet-potato mousse. Care-facility feedback pooled foods and provided no Parkinson-specific outcome or baked potato test.

porridge retention and water aspiration in two Parkinson cases — Water alternation reduced esophageal porridge retention in one case. Water silently aspirated in the other, whose porridge retention improved with jelly alternation. Neither case assessed baked potato.
different potato preparation and bench outcome — The study measured texture of gelled, printed mashed potato powder without a clinical cohort, baked potato or swallowing symptoms.

tuber paste sensory evaluation with population unresolved — The title names a paste made with an unspecified tuber and a sensory evaluation. Species, diagnosis and results remain behind the individual abstract access barrier. It gives no estimate for baked potato in Parkinson disease.

meat-and-potato stew paste rheology and healthy-participant sensory work — A 2007 conference title and related 2008 university study concern a puréed stew. Eight healthy assessors rated a beef paste easier to swallow after 10% MCT addition. There is no separately served baked potato or Parkinson effect.
postoperative dysphagia and dry food guidance — The report documents ordinary and soft meal textures and repeat endoscopy. It gives no baked potato or confirmed obstruction.

inpatient choking and aspiration during subsequent tube feeding — The patient had a choking and aspiration event. The obstructing food was unidentified. Later enteral changes and mosapride accompanied fewer vomiting episodes.

qualitative dysphagia response during vinegar and levodopa coadministration — After total gastrectomy, one person with stage V Parkinson disease reportedly had less dysphagia when taking three fragrant vinegar capsules with levodopa. No dysphagia score, meal food or potato exposure.

confirmed foods in a hospital choking series including Parkinson disease — Five of 15 acute choking cases had Parkinson disease. Fourteen food identifications did not include potato, one was unknown, and food identity was not linked to diagnosis.

family observation during a baked potato and chili meal — The account describes brief coughing after a sneeze while eating baked potato and chili in a person with Parkinson disease and existing dysphagia. There is no verified aspiration, comparative meal or swallowing-severity measure.

indirect — One man with stage 5 Parkinson had cough and marked residue during a pork mousse trial; later videofluoroscopy found better handling of a different meat texture and alternating jelly cleared residue. Timing and rehabilitation differed. No baked potato was served.
levodopa response during swallowing across consistencies — Ten participants completed a modified-barium swallow in ON and OFF conditions. The report does not identify individual foods.

swallowing assessment with named foods in Parkinson disease — Five of seven participants had oral residue on the cracker test. No residue was seen for vanilla yogurt or water. Potato was not a test bolus.

contrast-mixed sugar solution, agar and cookie in a swallowing series — Small amounts of liquid entered the trachea in 3 of 10 clinically labeled participants, only on unthickened cup drinking. Per-bolus denominators and diagnostic status of the three are unavailable. The fixed protocol did not name potato.

observed choking during chopped buttered baked potato consumption outside documented Parkinson disease — The state surveyor observed coughing and choking after a resident had eaten about half the chopped baked potato. Repeated tags refer to the same event. The resident had recurrent difficulty on other meals, no documented Parkinson diagnosis and no instrumentally confirmed airway obstruction.

observed baked-potato flesh consumption in dysphagia without documented Parkinson disease — The inspector saw a person with dysphagia and prior aspiration eat about half a baked potato without its peel and with no difficulty during the mixed meal. No Parkinson diagnosis or food-specific comparison is documented.

within-person swallowing assessment across five liquid viscosities — Unsafe swallows were reported for 2, 1, 1, 0 and 1 of 17 Parkinson participants across increasing viscosity. Thicker liquids used xanthan gum. Potato starch was an allergy exclusion, and no potato was tested.

mashed potato in a healthy-volunteer manometry protocol — The record names 5 and 10 mL of mashed potato. It lists a healthy adult cohort, excludes current dysphagia and gives no verified Parkinson enrollment or results.
completed protocol for analysis of actual meals — The registry reports 22 enrolled and no posted results. Foods were not assigned and the protocol does not name baked potato.

combined fatal aspiration pneumonia or food choking — Among 46 deceased hospitalized Parkinson patients, 24 were assigned to the combined category. No standalone choking count, meal food or preparation is reported.

existing meal texture and tongue pressure — Forty-six Parkinson inpatients were grouped by existing meal textures. No baked potato intake or change in dysphagia severity after an assigned texture was measured.

texture adjustment with concurrent denture changes — An older Parkinson patient had quicker bolus formation after concurrent denture use and texture changes. The authors do not name any food or quantify dysphagia severity.

roasted sweet potato in a recreational program — Roasted sweet potato appeared in a seasonal menu and the program served adapted food to participants with dysphagia. No Parkinson subgroup or potato-specific outcome was reported.

thickened tea and mashed porridge during swallowing care — A stage III Parkinson case sometimes finished meals after multiple care changes. There was no baked potato or food-specific aspiration comparison.

soft bean jelly and multimodal swallowing therapy — A stage V Parkinson case regained partial oral intake using bean jelly during rehabilitation. The study did not test baked potato or isolate the jelly's effect.

yogurt and soft rice porridge during rehabilitation — A person with Parkinson resumed soft meals after major illness and multiple care interventions. No baked potato exposure or directional food comparison was reported.

mealtime choking case series with specific foods recovered — The case series identifies rice grains and egg in separate events in one patient. It provides no baked potato exposure or swallowing severity comparison.

indirect — Endoscopy in one stage 3 Parkinson case found small pharyngeal residue after cooked rice and no residue after rice porridge. This measured preparation contrast involved rice only and gives no direction for baked potato.
acute choking during an unmodified lunch — A Parkinson diagnosis and an unmodified lunch were recorded, while the responsible food was unnamed.

mashed potato obstruction in drug-induced parkinsonism — The coroner records mashed potato removed from the airway and a history of drug-induced parkinsonism. The acute obstruction differs from a comparative severity result for baked potato in idiopathic Parkinson disease.
named toast obstruction in a person with Parkinson disease — A coroner identifies toast in the airway in a fatal choking case. The report gives no comparative swallowing outcome.
potato and meat recovered in a fatal obstruction — Paramedics recovered both foods. The coroner gives no potato preparation, isolated obstruction attribution or Parkinson diagnosis.

cracker and thickened test liquids during Parkinson swallowing endoscopy — Aspiration with cracker was observed in 2 of 22 Parkinson patients and 0 of 32 other dysphagic patients. The cracker and test liquids do not establish swallowing severity with baked potato.
boiled mashed potato in healthy older adults — The study rated immediate swallowing difficulty across semisolid foods in healthy older adults.

post-meal choking and five-day diet history in Parkinson disease — Choking was reported in 22% of 105 Parkinson participants and 6% of 47 family controls. The abstract reports nutrient totals but gives no food- or preparation-specific outcome.

liquid barium aspiration and fixed water swallowing after exercise — Four of ten Parkinson participants aspirated liquid barium during assessment. A separate exercise comparison used a fixed 5 mL water stimulus and found shorter premotor time. No food comparison, and some case profiles match a 2004 report.

potato handling and swallowing accounts — One participant described help peeling potatoes, and women reported difficulty swallowing when hurrying. These accounts do not tie difficulty to potato preparation or exposure.

bedside cough by solid and liquid bolus in early Parkinson disease — Cough followed liquid in 40% and solid in 5% of 65 participants. The boluses were unnamed and the bedside screen supplied no baked-potato or instrumental aspiration result.

maximum water swallowing volume and esophageal transit in Warsaw — The 2003 report gives mean 6.23 mL versus over 20 mL in controls. An earlier related report used the same tests in a smaller group with unverified overlap. The available reports give no baked-potato result.

contrast jelly versus sugar water and immediate aspiration — Among 25 participants with Parkinson disease and dysphagia, 13 aspirated cup-administered sugar-water contrast. None of those 13 aspirated spoon-administered jelly contrast during the test. Texture and delivery differed. Baked potato, clinical choking and longer-term severity were outside the comparison.

reported potato intake in a Parkinson dietary survey — Table 1 gives 21.7 versus 20.9 g of unspecified potatoes in 80 Parkinson cases and 69 controls, with no significant difference. Preparation and swallowing outcome were unreported.
fatal choking autopsies and unavailable Parkinson food attribution — The publisher preview identifies the grape case as an infant. The food in the Parkinson case remains unverified.
solid-food intake and swallowing in a Parkinson cohort — Potato is a food coding example and no patient-level potato preparation or swallowing estimate was recovered.

applesauce, cracker, water and milk used in Parkinson swallowing assessments — Among 57 with Parkinson disease, 33 underwent FEES. The assessment pooled across foods and examinations, reporting 41/57 abnormal. It provides no result for baked potato or ingredient-specific choking.

thickened and unthickened contrast liquids, outcomes pooled across diagnoses — Two of 85 dysphagia patients had Parkinson disease. The primary report separates viscosity groups and does not identify Parkinson-specific or named solid food outcomes.

instrumental comparison of liquid and solid texture classes in Parkinson disease — The abstract reports tracheal aspiration in 46 percent of 24 patients and worse abnormalities with liquid boluses. The solid food ingredients and item-specific results remain unavailable.
aspiration pneumonia in two geriatric units — The abstract reports grouped pneumonia and clinical context. Patient-level food identity and the full report are unresolved.
baked or boiled potato options in a whole-diet comparison — The menu permits either preparation. No actual portion or comparison on the individual swallowing item was published.
food examples in a large Parkinson dysphagia questionnaire — The questionnaire includes example foods and pooled responses from 470 people with Parkinson disease, without a baked potato comparison.
human Parkinson endoscopy with named solid and liquid boluses — Biscuit increased swallow-trigger difficulty and residue, and thin milk was associated with aspiration. No potato exposure was tested.

autopsy-confirmed asphyxia in a Parkinson case series — Five aspiration pneumonia deaths and three asphyxia deaths were identified among 16 autopsies. The accessible primary abstract supplies no individual bolus or potato preparation.

video-recorded eating and swallowing observations — The related dissertation and report describe 24 Parkinson participants and distinguish swallowing from food handling. The accessible abstracts do not report menus or food-specific estimates.

named liquid and biscuit in serial Parkinson swallowing assessments — The protocol names lemon juice and cornstarch biscuit. The 2014 report gives ten improved, five unchanged, and nine worsened after combined management. The likely overlapping 2013 report has conflicting figure and summary values. The reports supply no ingredient-level effect.

biscuit mastication and pharyngeal residue during Parkinson videofluoroscopy — Fifty-six participants took a biscuit and two liquid textures. Biscuit images were used for mastication and residue. Airway outcomes were assessed with the thin liquid and do not establish baked potato choking.
clinical volume-viscosity test — The study assessed water and thickener among 19 screen-positive patients. There was no potato preparation.

cold water swallowing and dilute barium aspiration in a French cohort — The paper gives slower cold-water swallowing in early Parkinson and reports three aspiration events during barium imaging. The reported 5% overall uses a different denominator from the 31-person imaging subset. No baked potato or other solid was tested.

reported potato intake by swallowing symptom status — The 72 participants with swallowing disturbances reported 67 versus 50 g/day of potatoes among the 528 without disturbances. Fried potato intake was similar. The potato preparation and whether intake preceded the symptoms are unresolved.

bolus-specific endoscopic aspiration with water buttered wheat bread and wheat biscuit — The journal and dissertation describe one cohort. Dissertation tables identify PAS 6–8 in 30/119 on water, 3/119 on buttered bread and 3/117 on biscuit. All six solid-bolus ratings were silent aspiration and may overlap within participants. No potato was tested.

fixed contrast jelly and aspiration-pneumonia prediction — The 2018 and 2022 reports represent one cohort of 184 and assess swallowing a common contrast jelly. Neither reports a baked-potato comparison.

water, pudding, buttered bread and biscuit in a stimulation crossover — Table 3 has water aspiration in 1, 2 and 2 of 11 across three stimulation conditions and one biscuit aspiration with stimulation off. The fixed protocol used no potato.
standardized potato-salad lunch and dysphagia — Existing eating difficulties were associated with intake. The study did not test dysphagia change after baked potato.

named snacks and concurrent swallowing rehabilitation — Ice cream, cream puffs and sweet red-bean soup were examples of calorie additions during multimodal recovery. The study gives no baked potato exposure or isolated food result.
boiled potato as a diagnostic solid bolus — Swallow studies excluded neurological disease. Baked potato and Parkinson symptom change were outside the design.

roast potato obstruction with Parkinson status unreported — The case records an acute roast potato obstruction. The report does not identify Parkinson disease or compare swallowing difficulty by food.
potato starch in soup and acceptability — The intervention evaluated taste, texture and other acceptability measures. Baked potato and swallowing difficulty efficacy were not tested.

endoscopic swallowing outcomes during respiratory muscle training — The protocol used white bread, unnamed puree and dyed liquid. The primary comparisons are summed across bolus trials and do not isolate a potato effect.

aggregate potato and Parkinson counts in a choking series — Table 1 lists three Parkinson cases, three potato obstructions and one french-fry obstruction in separate totals. It gives no patient-level linkage or preparation for potato.
hospital incident narratives with named foods — The narratives include food identities, without a paired Parkinson and baked potato case or a comparative outcome.

potato obstruction in a clinical dysphagia interview — The narrative names potato and a participant with traumatic brain injury. The preparation and an effect among Parkinson participants are unverified.

named foods in a Parkinson videofluoroscopy protocol — Of 82 participants, supplementary Table S2 classifies the worst airway-entry outcome across the five bolus types as 49 subglottic aspirations, 16 supraglottic penetrations and 17 with no airway entry. It gives no bolus-specific counts or comparisons.
Japanese hospital food-obstruction study — The report describes 300 food obstructions. Case-level linkage between Parkinson diagnosis and a potato preparation could not be confirmed.

named rice and yogurt boluses in videofluoroscopy — The Parkinson cohort swallowed yogurt, rice porridge and boiled rice during testing. Airway invasion categories pool results across boluses, with no potato test or per-food estimate.

oven-baked potato served during observed Parkinson meal — One participant with Parkinson disease was served boiled potatoes at one meal and oven-baked wedges at another. The observer reported no potato-specific swallowing response, confirmed portion consumed or isolated contrast.
named fixed boluses in endoscopic swallowing tests — Applesauce and biscuit residue fell after mask training in 11 completers. The same boluses were used before and after, with no potato comparison.

named shortbread bolus and texture ratings — Two analyses of the same 31-person sample document the contrast-coated cookie bolus. Separate ratings show more difficulty with hard and dry foods than soft foods. The reports do not test baked potato.

named dry biscuit and vanilla pudding boluses — Penetration or aspiration occurred in 20 of 28 water tests, 15 of 33 vanilla pudding tests, and six of 27 dry biscuit tests. Rates are descriptive and exclusions differ by bolus. Baked potato was outside the study.

named pineapple and pudding boluses with swallow-level outcomes — The author data reproduce the pooled trial scores. Two of 11 concordantly coded pineapple-and-juice baseline swallows and two of 32 pudding swallows reached the aspiration score range. These are protocol observations with different food volumes and trial schedules. No potato was tested.

within-person swallowing test with named liquids — At 90 mL, 27 of 80 paired tests showed shallower airway invasion with carbonated mineral water, six worsened and 47 were unchanged. The comparison does not involve potato.

shortbread and pudding in a respiratory coordination experiment — Cued bolus holding changed some respiration-swallow timing outcomes. The 20-person study gave no instrumental airway invasion or baked-potato result.

airway-obstructing choking series including two Parkinson patients — The report describes 31 choking episodes among 18 psychiatric patients, two with Parkinson disease. It gives no case-linked food, preparation, or Parkinson-specific fatal outcome.

videofluoroscopy of dry barium-coated toast before and after medication — In 15 people with Parkinson disease, toast oral-phase and initial swallow durations increased after levodopa. The article defines aspiration as persistent entry into the laryngeal vestibule. It includes no potato or baked-potato-specific endpoint.

reported potato intake and clinical dysphagia assessment — Potato intake was reported weekly or monthly among 25 Parkinson participants. Preparation and a potato-by-swallowing-severity analysis are absent.

barium-coated cracker in a clinical swallowing series — Aspiration was reported in 10 of 25 Parkinson participants and 21 of 82 symptomatic controls across four contrast preparations. Choking counts differ between tables and discussion. The solid preparation was cracker, with no potato test.

IDDSI level 7 solid as an unnamed texture after combination therapy — The university abstract reports one DOSS-level improvement in three Parkinson participants with dysphagia. The exact solid and choking outcomes remain unverified. No baked-potato comparison.

bread and water in a clinical assessment with observed choking — Observed choking was reported in 13% of 47 Parkinson participants and 0% of 47 matched controls across the protocol. The result is pooled across bread and water and supplies no potato effect.

mashed and boiled potato in a mixed-diagnosis protocol — The protocol names mashed potato as a bedside test bolus and boiled potato on a modified tray. The results do not identify a Parkinson participant's potato exposure or response.
named solid and liquid boluses in a Parkinson cohort — The protocol names Maria biscuit and juice–barium mixtures. Results are pooled by dysphagia status.
dysphagia screening and grouped food intake in a Parkinson clinic — Sixteen of 55 participants screened positive for dysphagia. The reported diet measures give no individual baked potato comparison.

indirect — One man with Parkinson and dementia progressed from a chopped diet to bite-sized foods without reported aspiration during repeated nutrition visits and adjusted textures. No baked potato was documented or compared.

curry leaves listed in a multicomponent Parkinson diet with motor composite — The ingredient table does not confirm species, cooking or individual consumption, and the report gives no handwriting change or isolated curry leaf comparison.

methanolic basil leaf extract and rodent motor tests — Rotarod times were 31.0 and 32.7 seconds versus 12.7 seconds with haloperidol alone, and catalepsy scores were lower. Taxonomic naming and group sizes are internally unclear. No fresh culinary leaf or clinical Parkinson outcome was tested.

holy basil leaf extract and animal catalepsy — The higher-dose oral ethanolic holy basil extract was associated with lower catalepsy scores in mice under a reported comparison whose labels are unclear. Species, preparation, model and outcome differ from fresh culinary basil and human muscle rigidity.

injected sweet basil extract and rotarod/stair tasks — High-dose injected extract increased rotarod time from 57.3 to 144.6 seconds and shortened stair task time from 35.8 to 29.3 seconds. The text conflicts with tables at the lower level. There was no isolated clinical symptom measure.

separately numbered conference member with preparation or outcome limits — P-05.2-64 is a material comparison using processed basil seed mucilage. Its swelling and microscopy measures supply no fresh leaf exposure or Parkinson rigidity outcome.
fresh basil in both Parkinson trial diet menus — Both diets list fresh basil in different dishes. Motor outcomes cannot isolate the ingredient or give a rigidity estimate by individual basil intake.

mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score — Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes rigidity, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

intranasal peanut-oil comparator in postviral olfactory loss — The oil group improved 3.88 TDI points on average. The adjusted difference between vitamin A and the oil comparator was inconclusive, and no untreated arm or oral preparation was used.

Parkinson baseline turkey and general speech symptom — Very small positive correlation in duplicated plots reports no sound-level or intelligibility-specific measure and no baking or roasting preparation.
pooled poultry item and total Parkinson symptom score — The combined poultry comparison gives no identifiable roasted turkey exposure or speech intelligibility estimate.

levodopa challenge and Parkinson acoustic speech measures — A limited acoustic effect and poorer on-state voice measures associated with axial dyskinesia inform medication-state confounding. The study did not use a turkey meal or test its effect on intelligibility.

diet-pattern association and probable REM sleep behavior disorder — Questionnaire-defined probable RBD was measured in participants without Parkinson disease. A separate chard estimate and prospective dream-enactment counts were unavailable.
injected corn oil and motor behavior — The corn oil arm did not clearly improve motor proxy outcomes over saline. It gives no estimate for refined oral corn oil and human bradykinesia.

oral corn oil with injected toxin and time to combined motor signs — Combined phenotype appeared in 14.00 versus 20.21 days (p<.0001) in the two toxin groups. Oil-only animals did not exhibit the composite during observation. Animal replacement, oil grade, composite timing and species limit transfer to clinical bradykinesia severity.

corn oil changed in oral feed with stepping and locomotion measures — Corn oil went from 10 to 4 g/kg as safflower and soybean oil and DHA also changed. Four motor assays showed no clear diet effect. The mice and formulation do not estimate refined corn oil and human bradykinesia.

corn oil in mixed oral diets with timed motor measures — Corn oil was 30, 25 and 10 g/kg across three formulas. High-DHA mice did worse on the pole test and retained late open-field activity. The formula changed several ingredients and no oil grade was reported.

corn oil changed in a diet with a forelimb endpoint — The study did not isolate corn oil or its refining grade. The forelimb stepping result followed simultaneous changes to feed and exercise in mice.

corn oil gavage vehicle and pole timing in a lycopene mouse study — Pole turn and descent times measure model motor performance. Control groups are described inconsistently, and oil-only bradykinesia contrasts and refining grade are unverified.

cold-pressed pumpkin seed oil and broad neurobehavior after colchicine in rats — The primary preview verifies cold-pressed oil and lists open-field and elevated-plus-maze outcomes. The precise challenge route and an attention-specific result remain unverified.
oral nutmeg extract and sucrose intake in rotenone-exposed rats — Sucrose intake increased, a reward-related surrogate. The study does not measure Parkinson apathy or culinary nutmeg.

acute drooling after concentrated oral laurel decoction — One infant presented with drooling together with other acute symptoms after repeated concentrated decoction. No ground exposure or graded Parkinson drooling outcome.
blinded oral bay leaf extract trial in healthy adults — The records identify a controlled bay-leaf extract study. Its original outcomes, endpoint scope and patent overlap remain open.
ground bay leaf capsules in a type 2 diabetes trial — The metabolic trial tested ground bay leaf and excluded neurologic disease. Drooling was unmeasured.

acute drooling during a bay leaf foreign-body episode — The primary excerpt describes gagging, drooling and cough after lodging during a meal. A fragment was identified in contemporary reporting. No ground preparation, Parkinson diagnosis or drooling scale was reported.
human leaf extract tablet and salivary weight — Single intake increased salivary weight in the extract arm relative to baseline. Saliva output is a different outcome from drooling severity.

blueberry powder in juice and composite motor outcomes — An institutional announcement reports preliminary walking-variability observations without a trial ID or quantitative results. Facial expressiveness remains unreported.

mixed dietary patterns include optional raw or frozen blueberries; aggregate motor score — Menus allow blueberries but selection and consumption are unverified; UPDRS Part III total includes facial expression and no facial item or isolated blueberry estimate is reported.

clinical facial palsy with earlier combined herbal use — The case timeline records no facial improvement during prior Nigella and rosemary use. The formulation and separate response are unreported, and the diagnosis was a structural peripheral lesion.

isolated thymoquinone and peripheral facial nerve electrophysiology — An isolated constituent improved measured facial nerve conduction outcomes after traumatic injury in rabbits. No ground seed or Parkinson facial expressiveness was tested.

caraway seed extract and essential oil in mouse motor coordination testing — Neither injected preparation clearly changed rotarod retention compared with vehicle. The coordination task did not measure stride length or ground caraway ingestion.

isolated S-(+)-carvone and mouse locomotor activity — Injected carvone reduced spontaneous movement at early time points. Locomotor activity, plant constituent and study population differ from the ground-caraway stride claim.

aqueous curry leaf extract and toxin-model motor tests — Table 2 reports rotarod falls under a rigidity label. Bar-test immobility was shorter with the extract. Neither test quantifies clinical muscle rigidity.
curry leaf fractions and drug-induced catalepsy — The fractions prolonged haloperidol-related bar-test immobility. No muscle tone or cooked curry leaf comparison was measured.
methanol curry leaf extract and haloperidol bar-test immobility — The acute mouse experiment reported shorter bar-test immobility. Muscle tone and cooked leaf were untested.
curry leaves in a Parkinson diet menu with composite motor score — The menu lists curry leaves and UPDRS III includes rigidity. Leaf preparation and the individual rigidity score are unreported.

rye bread named in a Parkinson food questionnaire — Rye bread was separately listed in a 26-Parkinson and 26-control questionnaire. The study measured blood mycotoxins and intake associations, with no assigned bread or voice measurement.
rye kernel bread and mood and cognitive measures — A crossover assigned rye and white wheat breads and measured cognition and mood. No vocal loudness outcome or Parkinson cohort.

self-reported voice handicap in a Parkinson whole-diet comparison — Self-reported handicap scores favored the ketogenic arm in the reported changes. No rye bread intake or objective acoustic voice volume was identified.

mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score — Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes facial expression, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.
corn oil capsule placebo and planned Epworth scores in soldiers — The official protocol names corn oil and a planned daytime sleepiness scale. Results and linkage to the 2014 report remain open.
corn oil as an active treatment comparator with planned ESS; linked results retracted — The registry supplies protocol context. The linked journal outcomes are ineligible after retraction.

corn oil ethyl ester comparator and daytime sleepiness correlation in deployed soldiers — The abstract reports a relationship between omega-3 index change and sleepiness, without an effect attributable to dietary refined corn oil. The comparator is esterified and there is no Parkinson cohort.

corn oil as capsule placebo with a daytime sleepiness scale — The investigator's thesis gives arm-level Epworth scores with no clear difference at 4, 8 or 12 weeks. The comparison evaluated cannabidiol against the oil capsule and does not estimate refined corn oil's independent effect.

low — The Parkinson diet appendix lists pumpkin seed oil among several alternatives. Figure S2 reports total UPDRS III, not separate dyskinesia or Part IV effects. Oil grade, intake and ingredient contrast were not published.

low — Haloperidol model work used methanolic pumpkin seed extract and reports improvements in broad motor functions. It supplies no cold-pressed oil arm or separately verified levodopa-induced or other dyskinesia measure.

repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking — Vegetables were offered in conjunction with a reward. The sample was children, and neither adult symptoms nor the matched preparation were assessed. The registration gives n = 82, while the two arm counts in the poster add to 84.
cooked tomato sauce intervention with oxidative biomarkers — A prepared tomato meal increased lycopene in men with prostate cancer. Executive and rigidity outcomes are unavailable.

shared collection original source context — PO1.137 serves tomato sauce with both pasta conditions and measures appetite and breath hydrogen. The pasta contrast cannot estimate cooked tomato or the frozen neurological outcome.

shared collection original source context — Whole-food tomato meals, including cooked sauce, are cited for oxidation and lycopene outcomes. No separate executive function result in diagnosed Parkinson disease.

isolated lycopene in a rotenone rat model — Oral lycopene had favorable neurobehavioral results in toxin-exposed rats. The abstract lacks an executive outcome estimate and the exposure differs from cooked tomato.

isolated lycopene and water-maze performance in a rotenone mouse model — The authors report favorable water-maze and tissue outcomes with isolated lycopene. The outcome and exposure differ from the frozen executive-function claim.

Parkinson executive MoCA subsection after a whole-diet intervention — The ten-week Mediterranean diet comparison was favorable on the executive subsection in diagnosed Parkinson disease. It supplies no isolated cooked tomato treatment estimate.

multicomponent fruit and vegetable capsules and TESEN in healthy adults — Capsules including tomato gave favorable within-period TESEN results. The report supplies neither a direct crossover contrast with uncertainty nor an isolated cooked tomato or Parkinson-specific estimate.

boiled tomato powder in congee and cognitive processing in healthy older adults — Four-week auditory Cz P300 latency differed from control but eight-week comparisons did not. The study measured processing, memory and serum biomarkers in participants without Parkinson disease.

pooled tomato paste and executive test in healthy adults — The randomized crossover executive index contrast was +0.7 (95% CI −1.9 to 3.4, q = 0.669). The first-period and all seven Table S4 and S5 executive-index sensitivity intervals also crossed zero. Both serving methods were pooled and the cohort did not have Parkinson disease.

dried leaf capsules and questionnaire esophageal motility symptoms in diabetes — Any esophageal complaint changed from 3 to 5 of 21 under dill and stayed at 5 of 21 under placebo. Within-arm p was .317 for dill. No between-arm estimate, fresh herbs, Parkinson population or separate swallowing measure was available.

culinary dill and allergy-associated throat swelling — The case reported throat and tongue swelling after food cooked with dill and a positive fresh-dill skin test. Fresh-leaf consumption, a swallowing endpoint and Parkinson disease were unconfirmed.

pumpkin seed oil in a Parkinson diet and facial-expression item within a motor scale — The menu names pumpkin seed oil. The paper gives no individual intake, preparation, facial-expression item change or separate effect of oil.

coriander listed among seasonings of a mixed Parkinson vegetarian diet — Coriander plant part, fresh preparation and individual consumption were not reported; the study gives no apathy outcome or ingredient-specific effect.
living coriander plant visual and smell exposure with POMS in healthy adults — Participants did not eat cilantro; POMS mood and vigor do not establish a Parkinson apathy effect.
seed extract memory in scopolamine rats — Passive avoidance and water-maze results concern seed extract, a non-Parkinson model, and memory tasks.

carotenoid food recalls and macular pigment measurements — The participant records name several food sources and the authors report no detected association with optical pigment density. No assigned food preparation or relevant Parkinson symptom was measured.
whole Parkinson diet including unspecified zucchini — Aggregate motor changes do not establish grilled zucchini exposure or executive response.
seed extract motor outcomes in haloperidol rats — Motor changes followed methanolic seed extract. No grilled fruit or executive task was studied.

healthy volunteers; celery plant part unspecified; salivary flow during chewing — Increased salivary flow during chewing is not clinical drooling severity in Parkinson disease; exposure is not established as dried leaves.

lovage in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome — The menu lists lovage and the motor examination includes rigidity. The paper does not identify fresh leaf, isolate lovage or report change in the rigidity item.

comparative healthy-volunteer report with unverified chervil placebo — The original abstract reports self-rated cognition, and a later dissertation identifies chervil through author correspondence. Original ingredient identity, culinary preparation and standardized executive testing remain unverified.
garden chervil leaf and stem chemical analysis — Fresh-cut chervil leaves and stems were extracted for chemistry and cellular assays. Executive performance was not measured.
methanol extract of culinary chervil in enzyme and cell assays — The enzyme and docking experiments do not measure executive performance after eating chervil.

isolated capsaicin and MPTP mouse stepping abnormalities — The conference abstract describes abnormal steps and no significant aggregate gait change after MPTP. It gives no stride lengths or preparation match. A likely same-family thesis lacks a gait result.

topical capsaicin and heat with measured step-length retention — Next-day retention of a trained asymmetry was reduced after capsaicin-plus-heat pain. Baseline walking was comparable. The outcome was not clinical stride shortening, and the route was topical.

topical capsaicin and heat with human step-length learning and retention — Three groups acquired the gait task. Both pain groups retained less step-length asymmetry the next day. Healthy volunteers used a topical mixture rather than consuming smoked paprika.

topical capsaicin and heat with step-length learning in older and younger adults — Training and next-day retention of a visual step-length asymmetry were lower with topical capsaicin plus heat. Neurologic disease was excluded, and the measured outcome was not ordinary stride length.

rectal sesame oil in a multimodal regimen and facial motor item — Facial scores improved from baseline in an uncontrolled parkinsonism series. The preparation and route differ from toasted sesame oil consumption.
protein-rich meals and reported levodopa fluctuations — A chart study associated protein-rich meals with motor fluctuations in a subset. It did not estimate boiled shrimp or falls.
total dietary protein and reported falls — A cross-sectional comparison did not show a clear association with any or recurrent falls. It did not estimate boiled shrimp intake.
heat-processed soup with fresh lovage in healthy adults — The cooked soup contained fresh lovage as an input. Reflux and GI distress were reported without insomnia severity measurements.
individual Parkinson symptoms and diet scores — Diet scores were not significantly associated with insomnia and do not identify fresh lovage intake.

animal vehicle or flavored-milk preference outside the frozen preparation — PT080 and another member report injected corn oil as vehicle or control in a perimenopause model. The oil route, associated interventions and measures differ from oral corn oil.

oral corn oil comparator and measured walking and trotting stride — Randomized horse comparison recorded similar walking stride changes. The omega-3 arm had a larger descriptive trot-stride change, between-arm p=.08. Animal, diet and gait differences limit clinical transfer.

shared collection original source context — P233 is appended in the complete PMC HTML for this oral-key record and separately printed in the poster supplement. It compares corn and fish oil during shared exercise for strength and mechanistic outcomes. One study family.

shared collection original source context — Printed P233 reports an omega-3 versus corn-oil comparator during shared resistance training. Its strength findings are distinct from the frozen clinical outcomes. The other PMC key reproduces this member.

corn-oil control during exercise training — The final isometric interaction is p=.015 and the corn arm changed −1.4%. P233 uses −0.3%. Body strength during shared training does not measure any frozen Parkinson endpoint in these claims.

NUTRIMAL mixed oil control and exploratory gait speed — Neither postintervention gait-speed contrast resolves direction, and the control and protein-only drinks both contain high-oleic sunflower and corn oil. Gait speed does not identify stride length.

COPD blend includes corn oil and protocol measures gait speed — The supplement establishes the 50:50 blend while the abstract names four-metre gait testing. Accessible source material has no arm-specific gait estimates or stride data.

corn oil comparator and measured walking distances in claudication — Walking distances did not clearly change in the available abstract. Refined oil, stride length and Parkinson cohort are unverified.
shared Parkinson trial vehicle and aggregate mobility — The mobility score does not give stride length, and both CBD arms also used corn oil.
measured mouse stride with matched corn oil vehicle — Exposure group comparisons estimate PCB effects on matched oil backgrounds. The most shortened strides were in PCB-treated wild-type animals.

oral corn oil comparator and 400-m walking speed — Fish oil versus matched corn-oil gelcaps gave +0.010 m/s, 95% CI −0.025 to +0.044. Usual walking speed in mobility-impaired older adults does not estimate Parkinson stride length.

corn oil plus maltodextrin comparator and 4-m gait speed — The corn-oil regimen had +0.12 m/s within-arm gait speed change with a rehabilitation co-intervention. The small pilot did not estimate stride length or an isolated oil effect.

oral corn oil comparator and timed mobility — Timed Up and Go was slower at follow-up in the corn arm and faster in the fish arm. The task combines several components and no stride lengths were reported.

corn and soy oil comparator with measured walking performance in COPD — The mixed-oil arm also used maltodextrin. The abstract gives no stride estimate or positive functional outcome. The linked registry does not isolate corn oil, and the primary tables remain open.

repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking — Vegetables were offered in conjunction with a reward. The sample was children, and neither adult symptoms nor the matched preparation were assessed. The registration gives n = 82, while the two arm counts in the poster add to 84.

reported food categories and overeating — LBP2.005 includes carrot as a named candidate in Table 1. Neither group reported an overeating occurrence for carrot. Its thermal preparation and the frozen symptom were not assessed.

pasteurized carrot juice as a human comparator with an executive outcome — Trail Making B change in the seven-person carrot arm was inconclusive (p=.804). The study tested juice in healthy adults, without roasted carrot or a no-carrot control.

multicomponent capsule including carrot and executive testing — The capsules contained carrot among numerous dehydrated fruit and vegetable ingredients. TESEN within-period changes were favorable. Roasting, the carrot quantity, and outcomes in diagnosed Parkinson disease are unresolved.
purple carrot extract and memory in reserpine rats — Novel object recognition is a model memory test. The abstract does not measure human executive function or roasted carrot.

ALS three-arm diet and exercise pilot with preliminary combined-arm swallowing burden — The preliminary result describes the combined intervention. An estimate isolating the diet-only contrast remains open.

whole Mediterranean diet and planned chewing or swallowing measure after STN DBS — The protocol encourages olive oil as a principal dietary fat. It labels a secondary outcome as chewing/swallowing but cites discrepant MDS-UPDRS numbering. It provides no isolated oil grade or result.

topical olive oil, betaine and xylitol versus usual care in crossover dry-mouth cohort — The crossover measures swallowing attributable to dryness and reports a benefit on the overall dry-mouth score. The swallowing item was not among the significant comparisons.

experimental local pharyngeal infusion and time between voluntary swallows — The original abstract reports longer voluntary swallowing intervals during olive oil pharyngeal stimulation than with water stimulation. Grade, an ordinary eating exposure, and a clinical dysphagia estimate remain unverified.

historical dysphagia lecture on peptic esophageal ulcer with mixed treatment advice — The lecture attributes a mixed atropine and olive oil regimen to earlier clinicians treating peptic esophageal ulcer. It reports no isolated olive oil outcome.

chewable olive oil, betaine and xylitol versus sorbitol in xerostomia crossover — The article describes better swallowing in its conclusion and reports only an aggregate questionnaire change in its results.

swallowed extra-virgin olive oil and lycopene spray versus water, dryness-related swallowing VAS — A water-controlled trial measured swallowing complaints after an extra-virgin olive oil and lycopene oral spray. The reported item comparison was inconclusive. The higher initial symptoms on active and the combined product limit interpretation of the larger raw decline.

companion English report of first reported 2014 uncontrolled topical radiation cohort — Dryness-related difficulty swallowing improved in uncontrolled pre/post data. The matching 2014 and 2016 reports describe one likely cohort. Multiple topical ingredients and radiation context prevent dietary olive-oil attribution.

independent earlier referred population and combined diagnostic code — Table 1 lists seven Parkinson disease or parkinsonism cases among 51 older patients with sepsis and dysphagia. The 2013–2014 referral sample differs from the 2022–2023 admissions cohort. No ingredient-specific comparison.

matched topical olive and parsley oil products in primary Sjogren syndrome — The swallowing VAS comparison was inconclusive (p=.57), with a numerically larger raw improvement in the control. Several active ingredients and oral-care route limit transfer.

original animal physiology abstract with locally infused extra-virgin olive oil — Extra-virgin oil elicited swallowing in an anesthetized rat preparation where ordinary olive oil did not. The experiment assesses a local reflex, with no clinical dysphagia estimate.

postoperative oral olive oil and cola with measured dysphagia grades after stenting — Swallowing grades improved after stenting plus bundled care. Neither the oil's own effect nor dietary extra-virgin oil in Parkinson disease can be estimated.

oral organic extra-virgin olive oil and weekly dysphagia ratings in a cancer case — The case measures a swallowing symptom while the patient used EVOO. Concurrent treatment and recovery prevent an isolated effect estimate.

direct Parkinson comorbidity context without assigned exposure — Table 4 identifies higher odds of incident recorded dysphagia in hospitalised people with Parkinson disease. PP0011 reports the same cohort and result. No ingredient allocation, preparation or symptom severity contrast is measured.

usual olive oil frequency and concurrent swallowing assessment in a Parkinson cohort — Daily unspecified-grade olive oil and dysphagia are both reported. The analyzed contrast is by weight group and does not yield an oil-specific swallowing comparison.

reported olive oil intake by swallowing symptom status — Reported intake averaged 37 versus 29 mL/day in Parkinson participants with and without swallowing disturbances, respectively. The oil grade was unspecified and this comparison measured intake alongside existing symptoms.

fennel capsule and daytime dysfunction component — Among 50 postmenopausal women, mean PSQI daytime dysfunction changed from 0.36 to 0.25 with anethole-standardized fennel capsules and 0.28 to 0.16 with placebo (week 12 p = .439). The daytime wakefulness item was not reported separately. Exposure was a capsule and not toasted seed.

low — The 2019 trial collected aggregate PSQI components following intranasal whole pumpkin in sesame oil. The standard PSQI has a bad-dream item, while this study reported neither a separate item result nor observed dream enactment. Parkinson was excluded.

fresh cilantro leaf oral allergy challenge — A patient developed oral itching and a systemic allergic reaction during a fresh cilantro leaf challenge. Dysphagia and Parkinson disease were not reported.

mixed meal containing coriander and exercise-associated dysphagia — Dysphagia developed after a mixed meal followed by running. Skin testing implicated fresh coriander and tomato. The food exposure and exercise cannot isolate cilantro in Parkinson disease.

parsley flavonoid preparation and exertional fatigue model — Concentrated flavonoid preparations improved fatigue-related physiological measures and gastrocnemius morphology in an excessive-fatigue mouse model. The source did not test fresh leaf or Parkinson fatigue.

source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits — S1.97 proposes parsley as a possible dietary source of related Rubisco peptides while modelling spinach-derived rubiscolin. No parsley isolate, dose or Parkinson outcome is measured.

veterinary reference context only, without a tested Parkinson comparison — The Petroselinum crispum entry describes furanocoumarins and primary photosensitization. The broader common-name cross-reference includes other genera. No frozen culinary or Parkinson symptom result appears.

parsley among optional mixed-juice ingredients — The original protocol lists parsley among optional mixed-juice ingredients. It does not verify participant-level fresh preparation or intake. Edited testimonials report outcomes for the combined program without a separate fatigue severity comparison for this ingredient.
mixed fresh/heated parsley human feeding — Two one-week randomized feeding periods with or without culinary parsley measured apigenin and antioxidant endpoints. Fresh parsley fatigue was unmeasured.

reported parsley preparations and pooled fatigue frequency — Parsley appears in two use citations and fatigue appears in a separate aggregate figure. Neither exposure preparation status nor within-person fatigue changes were reported.

topical sunflower oil and salivary outcomes in medication-induced dry mouth — A crossover measured stimulated and unstimulated salivary flow and reported subjective dryness benefits within groups with oil. The oil versus water dryness comparison was p=.067. The route, oil and symptoms differ.

sesame-based topical rinse and reports of reduced saliva — At eight weeks, a 40-person randomized trial reported no between-group difference in subjective saliva reduction or mouth dryness. The oil blend was spat out and no Parkinson drooling was measured.

specified clinical Parkinson drooling and salivary-flow outcomes — The case-control study found lower unstimulated saliva flow and higher symptom prevalence for drooling and dry mouth. There was no oil exposure; flow alone cannot assign clinical drooling direction.
watermelon and acute oropharyngeal reactions in an allergy-selected group — Six of 29 watermelon-sensitive patients had symptoms after ingestion. No speech or Parkinson outcome was measured.

sunflower food frequency and composite Parkinson symptom burden — The poster reports +2 total PRO-PD points per intake frequency category (95% CI −10 to 13, p=.787). The cross-sectional exposure did not specify an oil grade. It gives no individual bladder symptoms estimate.
acute poisoning; multi-ingredient powder; dysarthria eligibility only — Dysarthria was an entry sign, not a treatment outcome; no Parkinson or ground caraway-only speech comparison.
ground sumac powder capsules with captopril in hypertension — Blood pressure decreased relative to placebo plus captopril. The report gives no orthostatic symptom or Parkinson outcome.
sumac capsules in adults with hyperlipidemia — Small reported reductions in systolic and diastolic pressure provide non-Parkinson cardiovascular context. No orthostatic symptoms were measured.

combined sumac and pomegranate in nonspecific acute dizziness — Both arms had fewer reports of dizziness. Table 4 contains inconsistent percentages and denominators. There is no distinct orthostatic outcome, isolated sumac effect or Parkinson population.
grapeseed oil carrier in a topical eucalyptus animal experiment — The topical mix delayed response to heat. No isolated carrier or oral-oil pain contrast.
topical grapeseed oil mixture in Gua Sha and pain — A randomized comparison favored bundled Gua Sha with lotion on a Parkinson pain scale. It did not estimate the effect of eating the oil.

reported blood-pressure drop after a hazelnut-containing food — A blood-pressure drop was reported in the second acute allergy case. There was no standing challenge, assessment of orthostatic lightheadedness, or verified hazelnut oil ingestion.

shared hazelnut flake vehicle in human orthostatic challenge — In ten healthy men, presyncope occurred after 18 ± 7 and 17 ± 6 minutes in the astragalus and placebo periods, with no significant difference. Both drinks contained hazelnut flakes. There was no hazelnut-free or oil comparison.

pooled hypotension outcome in pediatric food-allergy cohort with hazelnut challenges — Four children of 88 had hypotension in a pooled cohort covering several foods. The report does not attribute these cases to hazelnuts or measure postural lightheadedness, oil intake or Parkinson disease.

injected black mustard seed extract and mouse tail suspension — At the highest extract dose mean immobility was 109.16 seconds versus 233.00 with saline. The experiment used an injected ethanolic extract and did not measure clinical depression.
topical mixed botanical patches and PHQ-9 in subthreshold depression — The controlled comparisons favor mixed topical formulas. Neither arm isolates orally consumed mustard seed.

white mustard seed oil and mouse stress-related behavior — Behavioral effects favored mustard seed oil in mouse stress models. The study also examined isolated allyl isothiocyanate. Clinical depressive symptoms after ground seed were untested.

caraway included in a Parkinson odor discrimination panel — Caraway was one of five odor samples in a panel with 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity. No individual caraway accuracy, toasted exposure or change after consumption was measured.

reported habitual spice use and identification of caraway among 12 odors — Healthy adults reported spice use and identified odors including caraway. The abstract gives no isolated caraway effect, individual clinical result or toasted-ingredient comparison.

caraway essential oil presented as one odor stimulus in a cross-sectional study — The cross-sectional study uses caraway oil to measure odor perception. It offers no food intervention or clinical comparison.

dried caraway recognition in Parkinson disease — The primary workbook gives 0 of 34 correct in Parkinson disease versus 5 of 53 in controls. The article reports no clear caraway group difference. The dried odor was sniffed.

Parkinson dietary assessment and six-metre course length outcome — The measure labeled stride length averaged 0.48 m in Parkinson cases and 0.56 m in controls (p=.001). Dietary assessment gives no tomato-stride comparison, and methods do not distinguish the stride calculation from step length.

repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking — Vegetables were offered in conjunction with a reward. The sample was children, and neither adult symptoms nor the matched preparation were assessed. The registration gives n = 82, while the two arm counts in the poster add to 84.

isolated oral lycopene and unnamed motor tasks in rotenone rats — The publisher figures show lower day-30 time and score with isolated lycopene. The available figure axes do not identify a stride test or the behavioral protocol.

isolated oral lycopene and beam crossing in MPTP mice — Beam crossing took about 8.1 s in model controls and 6.2, 4.8 and 5.1 s at three lycopene doses. The task is balance and coordination. No step-length or tomato-food estimate was reported.

Tomatoes listed in a provided mixed vegetarian menu with composite motor scores in Parkinson disease — Six patients received diet alone and ten also had bowel cleansing. Table 3 names tomatoes, without preparation, dose or individual intake. Figure 4 one-year composite UPDRS III improved within groups (P=.033 and .005); neither a stride measure nor a tomato-specific contrast is reported.

dietary lycopene and usual-pace gait speed in a community cohort — The adjusted estimate per 10 mg/day dietary lycopene was +0.0043 m/s/year gait-speed change (SE .0010, p<.01). The study gives no Parkinson subgroup, stride outcome or tomato cooking comparison.

carotenoid Raman peaks and instrumented step length during Parkinson rehabilitation — Both baseline carotenoid-associated peaks correlated −.49 with maximum step length (p=.01 each), adjusted for age and disease duration. The biomarker is not a lycopene or dietary tomato measurement. Treadmill rehabilitation was the intervention.

Parkinson Mediterranean diet trial protocol with instrumented stride — The PRIME protocol explicitly measures same-foot and height-normalized stride, and records individual dietary intake. The intervention assigns whole diets and physical activity. It supplies no cooked-tomato arm or posted result.

isolated oral lycopene and open-field and pole outcomes in an MPTP model — Isolated lycopene improved multiple exploratory motor measures, including pole turn and arrival time. The full study gives no animal footprint or stride endpoint.
adult suspected allergy after a sumac-containing meal — A possible adult acute allergy event after a mixed meal had no hallucination outcome.

possible allergic reaction in a pediatric sumac-containing meal case — The case reports gastrointestinal and allergic symptoms after a mixed meal. There was no Parkinson visual hallucination assessment.
lovage root methanol extract and acetylcholinesterase — The enzyme experiment used root extract, with no attention testing.

lovage extract and spatial performance in neuroinflammation rats — The abstract reports improved spatial learning and memory in the inflammatory rat model. The tested organ is unavailable and attention was not measured.
lovage extract and treadmill in neuroinflammation rats — The abstract reports effects with running alone and running plus extract. It gives no fresh-leaf attention estimate.

micrographia in a case with a combined dietary change — The primary abstract reports apparent resolution of micrographia after adding foods rich in fisetin and hexacosanol. The case report body, exact strawberry preparation and individual food contribution remain unverified.

strawberries suggested within a bundled dietary intervention — Strawberries were an optional recommended food. The pilot tracked apples and fiber, with no strawberry preparation or consumption measure. The motor assessment excluded handwriting.

strawberry leaf extract and movement in a mouse model — Rotarod and pole-turn measures favored the higher extract diet in rotenone mice. The intervention used leaves rather than fruit and gives no human handwriting result.

measured comparison or exposure context with a different preparation, outcome or population — The PPMI analysis verifies prodromal REM sleep behavior diagnoses and questionnaire scores in a biomarker study. Caraway and food-dependent dream enactment results are absent.
isolated caraway constituent and pentobarbital sleep in mice — S-(+)-carvone prolonged drug-induced sleep. REM behavior, dream enactment and toasted caraway ingestion were untested.
fennel nanosuspension and mouse sciatic functional recovery — The study measured hind-limb strength and nerve recovery in peripheral injury, without a ground seed or handwriting contrast.

Crude fennel seeds in food in mice with sciatic nerve injury; motor and sensory recovery — Neither Parkinson disease nor handwriting was tested. The abstract has inconsistent significance wording, and original full preparation methods remain unavailable.

Mixed Parkinson vegetarian menu includes fennel seed; individual seed intake and handwriting not reported — Seed grinding and intake were not verified, and total motor scores do not identify a handwriting response to fennel.

Fennel seed methanolic extract in feed in mice with sciatic nerve injury; hind-paw grip — The preparation is an extract, the grip test concerns hind paws, and the model is peripheral injury; none tests ground seed and Parkinson handwriting.
low — Mandrake was confirmed among chard and spinach leaves. An aggregate hyperactivity or hallucination outcome does not estimate the effect of cooked chard on visual hallucinations in Parkinson’s.
