sumac fruit drink during exercise in healthy volunteers — Pain during an exercise program was measured without instrumented stride assessment.
sumac fruit fractions in stressed muscle cells and zebrafish embryos — The muscle progenitor and embryo experiments did not measure limb gait or stride.

ground cayenne served in a controlled breakfast without target clinical measurements — The same-accession thesis names cayenne powder and compares metabolic outcomes in healthy adults. Fixed meal order conflicts with registered random allocation. Dyskinesia was unmeasured.

levodopa dyskinesia and a TRPV1 antagonist combination in rats — URB597 plus capsazepine reduced graded abnormal movements. The protocol did not administer capsaicin or cayenne. Isolated capsaicin in the related Lee report measured different hyperactivity outcomes.

capsaicin as a receptor probe in a dyskinesia mouse model — Capsaicin blocked the reduction in dyskinetic movements associated with a separate experimental agent. The study did not test ground cayenne consumption.

optional spinach intake and objective postpartum attention — Spinach entries were documented in both intervention groups and the MANT accuracy interaction was significant. The intervention varied a bundle of foods without a cooking or spinach-specific contrast.

low — Mouse pretreatment with spinach ethanol extract or separate linoleic acid improved working and aversive memory measures in a trimethyltin model. The article gives no cooked-spinach comparison or dedicated Parkinson attention result.

thawed spinach and direct attention tests in healthy people — Power of attention and continuity of attention comparisons were inconclusive (p=.70 and .84). A cooked preparation and Parkinson’s were not verified.

red spinach extract and Stroop outcomes in resistance-trained men — The crossover found no clear Stroop difference. The product was an extract and is distinct from cooked common spinach in Parkinson disease.

historical oral lovage root use for pain and a separate leaf tea use — Two interview reports describe root decoction for joint pain and two leaf tea for inflammation. No dried-leaf pain response, comparator, or Parkinson diagnosis is reported.
isolated pulverized lovage root and mechanical nociception in rats — The root arm reduced mechanical nociception versus vehicle. Species matches, while organ and clinical pain context differ.
dried lovage leaves in in vitro enzyme comparisons — Dried leaf extracts altered inflammatory enzyme inhibition after simulated digestion. Neither animals nor patients had pain assessed.

pooled legume or bean intake and whole-diet daytime sleepiness scores — Table 2 reports daytime sleepiness against whole diet scores. Table S4 evaluates pooled bean or legume intake against aggregate symptom burden and does not identify species or preparation.

mixed evening meal with lentils and next-morning Epworth sleepiness — The 20-participant comparison found no clear Epworth difference (p=.45). Ingredients and calories changed together, and canned lentil and Parkinson effects were unmeasured.

brewed spearmint crossover and subjective smell in nasal polyposis — High and low rosmarinic acid teas showed no diary smell difference. The comparison used two active teas in a non-Parkinson population.

mint scent in a bundled olfactory training protocol — The protocol uses a mint label and conventional menthol stimulus among four odorants. The population has olfactory dysfunction and subjective cognitive decline. There is no independent mint arm, established culinary spearmint species or brewed preparation.

spearmint test odor in Parkinson and drug induced parkinsonism — The original reports less accurate spearmint odor recognition in 78 Parkinson participants versus 31 with drug-induced parkinsonism. The groups differed by age. The ingredient served as a test odor, with no brewed ingestion or treatment contrast.

fresh and convectively dried red cabbage extracts and fibril-exposed cells — Extracts reduced alpha-synuclein-fibril-associated cytotoxicity in SH-SY5Y cells under some drying and exposure conditions. The study tested no cooked food intake or rigidity outcome.
oral red cabbage anthocyanin preparations and behavior in aging mice — The paper reports no motor effect, but the available abstract does not identify a rigidity measure.
asparagus in a tube complication — The case trail concerns a feeding tube complication. The accessible material gives no drooling estimate for steamed asparagus.

asparagus oral liquid with mecobalamin and reported unstimulated saliva — A later systematic review extracts a positive salivary-flow comparison in 28 burning-mouth patients with high risk of bias. The original body is unavailable, and drooling, steamed food and Parkinson effects are unverified.

clove oil odor detection during an oxytocin crossover — Clove oil was a detection probe in a schizophrenia study of oxytocin. The abstract reports no clear clove threshold change. The later journal report has no clove threshold. Neither route nor endpoint matches the frozen culinary comparison.

standardized clove oil with rice bran oil and self reported cognitive failures — Cognitive Failures Questionnaire scores moved from 39 to 27 in the higher-dose arm (within p≤.005). The randomized design has two active doses and no placebo. Participants did not have Parkinson and the study does not isolate ground clove or objectively measured executive change.

clove scent within four odorants and Trail Making cognition assessment — Journal protocol verifies intended Trail Making assessments and bundled odors, including eugenol for clove in conventional training. No isolated clove intake or clinical Parkinson results are reported.

clove odor kit and Trail Making Test B in an HIV protocol — The recruiting study lists a conventional odor kit that includes clove and a cognitive task measuring executive performance. Results are not posted. The intervention bundles odors and has no identified ingested ground-clove or Parkinson arm.

isolated inhaled eugenol and healthy-volunteer executive inhibition — Twenty-five healthy volunteers performed manual Stroop tasks. Eugenol versus air was not associated with a detected change in reaction times. The study did not test culinary clove or Parkinson executive function.

clove as one of six odorants in a diabetes cognition training trial — The original abstract reports MoCA change +1.9 versus +0.4 (p=.001) and executive-domain gains with the training package. Exact executive estimates remain open. Clove is one inhaled stimulus and the participants had diabetes with mild cognitive impairment.
eugenol in multi-odorant training and composite cognition — General cognition favored training. The study did not isolate ingested clove or executive function.
acute food overdose and subjective dry mouth — The patient reported xerostomia after accidental excess ingestion. Drooling and saliva flow were not measured.

acute loss of speaking ability after kernel anaphylaxis with prior topical oil use — A child was unable to speak after chewing and spitting out a macadamia kernel. The prior oil exposure was topical. The report does not measure speech intelligibility or establish an oral oil effect in Parkinson disease.

oral macadamia oil and postmeal sleepiness in healthy adults — The 2025 study family reports less acute postmeal sleepiness and fatigue with macadamia oil. The companion figures report a trend for sleepiness at 30 minutes in the larger experiment. Prior-night sleep timing and daytime ratings do not measure REM dream enactment. The oil pressing method is unknown.
spearmint extract and sensor hits or reaction time — These outcomes are indirect motor measures. There was no clinical hand dexterity scale or Parkinson population.
mint leaves named in a Parkinson diet with hand tasks in its motor scale — Species and preparation were unspecified. No isolated mint exposure or item-level dexterity estimate was reported.
oral summer savory oil and rotarod balance after lead — Improved retention on a rotating rod does not count clinical falls.

aqueous oral Sichuan pepper preparation in MPTP mouse model — Example 1 reports shorter pole-task times at three decoction levels. Exposure began before model induction. This offers a species-specific motor proxy with no toasted culinary exposure or clinical bradykinesia comparison.
related pepper species and animal movement-speed proxy — Distilled Japanese pepper given intranasally shortened pole descent in mice. It did not test culinary Sichuan pepper in humans.

optional walnut oil and planned depression scale in a non-Parkinson trial — The program offered walnut oil as a dietary option. The protocol prespecified a geriatric depression scale. Public results material supplies neither the depression comparison nor participant-specific intake, processing grade or oil allocation.

mixed-nut Mediterranean diet and onset of depression in cardiovascular-risk adults — PREDIMED 2013 incident depression adjusted HR was 0.78 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.10), with a diabetes subgroup estimate of 0.59 (0.36 to 0.98). The trial supplied whole mixed nuts and a diet pattern; prevention of diagnosis is distinct from symptom severity.

whole-walnut bread and depression-dejection subscale in healthy students — Mean POMS Depression-Dejection scores were 9.7 with walnuts and 12.1 with control (n=49, p=.103). Sex subgroups and overall depression comparison were inconclusive; male total mood is a separate endpoint. Whole ground nuts in bread differ from cold-pressed oil.

walnut-oil milkshake and fear extinction in young adults — The author abstract reports faster extinction of learned fear. The secondary acute Total Mood Disturbance difference was -4.99 (95% CI -10.75 to +0.07). The recovered supplement has no POMS component scores, and the original body, clinical symptom measure and oil processing remain open.

avocado and soybean unsaponifiables in a probable aspiration case — An older adult with severe reflux and hiatal hernia developed lipoid pneumonia during long-term oral use. The case does not isolate avocado oil or measure clinical swallowing difficulty in Parkinson disease.

Confirmed frozen dill product contamination notice without patient data — The recall is for a microbiological contaminant and supplies no patient exposures or symptoms. It cannot establish hallucinations, their frequency, or an effect of fresh foliage.

Dill fruit survey and literature-based toxicity attribution — The individual fruit row does not report hallucinations. The grouping of toxic plants in prose cannot establish a hallucination case or incidence attributable to fresh dill.

dried Perilla leaves processed into aqueous extract and used in an ocular accommodation trial — Binocular near-point distances changed from 7.96 to 7.27 cm versus 9.00 to 9.67 with placebo. The article inconsistently reports sample size and has no Parkinson fatigue measure. NCT02641470 identifies another plant study.

perilla leaf flavonoid extract and exercise endurance in adolescents — The abstract reports longer exhaustion time in male track athletes. It provides no clinical fatigue score, Parkinson population or culinary dried-leaf exposure.

mixed oral formula with unresolved perilla and prospective fatigue items — Registry says 10 g/day and includes perilla. The linked protocol says 30 g/day and omits perilla from Table 1. Termination and absent results leave fatigue effects and actual formulation unresolved.
cocoa in rice beverage — The pilot tested fatigability and left its effect uncertain. It supplies no speech outcome estimate.
mixed vegetables and device adverse event — The case describes a bezoar with a jejunal tube. Parkinson symptom severity was reported stable.
pooled leek and spinach intake in a Parkinson cohort — The single weekly leafy-green category cannot identify roasted leek or estimate effects on clinical rigidity.

separately numbered conference member with preparation or outcome limits — P-05.2-64 evaluates swelling of crosslinked basil-seed mucilage in buffers. The material experiment supplies no dried basil leaf consumption, transit or stool outcome.
culinary seasonings in a constipation case — Multiple dietary and other interventions leave the contribution of the individual seasoning unresolved.
dried basil powder trial and adverse-event scope — Adverse effects do not give a constipation score or bowel-frequency estimate.

hairy basil seed and stool outcomes — Thirty adults in a one-group study reported more frequent and softer stool after seven days of soaked hairy basil seed. Gastrointestinal adverse effects were reported. This was seed from a differently identified herb, with no Parkinson comparison.

direct Parkinson population and questionnaire scope only — Gastrointestinal questionnaires were completed by 76 participants with Parkinson disease. Only one of eight showed definite delayed emptying in the tested subset. PAC-SYM is listed but no constipation measure is stratified by this frozen exposure.

bedside walnut-oil comparator and bathroom-related sleep interruption — Bathroom awakenings mean 2.42 with walnut vs 2.18 with active blend (p=.046). No inert arm, oral ingestion, identified cold-pressed grade, Parkinson cohort or urgency score.

common bean pod extract and rat catalepsy — Catalepsy means were lower with methanol pod extract than with haloperidol alone. Pod cultivar and cooking were unverified. Catalepsy is a pharmacological motor proxy and human rigidity was untested.

mixed garden produce distribution — The garden reported distribution of green beans, kale, chard and watermelon within a mixed harvest. The evaluation concerns program delivery without an ingredient-specific intake or clinical symptom measurement.

common bean pod and seed levodopa concentrations — Validated mass spectrometry found 0.020 to 2.34 micrograms per gram dry weight across uncooked pod and seed samples. The study did not measure clinical rigidity or prepare cooked snap beans.

green beans in a Parkinson menu and aggregate motor scores — Green beans were offered within a mixed intervention. Aggregate motor change was inconclusive. Neither green bean consumption nor a separate rigidity estimate was reported in the primary article or supplement.
dried summer savory infusion and awake rat activity — Distance surrogate fell by day seven. Neither sleep nor clinical insomnia was measured.
diet pattern and composite outcome — Protein timing and motor activities were tested. Raw pear and daily off time were not isolated.
source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits — S7.519 includes pear in fruit-tree grafting work, with no pear feeding or levodopa off-time measure.

low-protein dietary regimen and matching off-time outcome — An 18-person crossover found shorter OFF time with low-protein products. The separate seven-day study reused six participants and listed equal unspecified fruit portions across diets. Neither supplies a raw pear contrast.

oral peanut oil placebo and planned falls in a sarcopenia trial family — TEMPUS-FUGIT specifies a 1 g peanut-oil placebo and planned falls surveillance. Published ENHANce feasibility results and accessible publisher supplement cover mobility and sarcopenia measures without a verified arm-specific falls estimate. Parkinson disease was excluded and refining was unreported.
source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits — The arsenic model compares a chelator in peanut oil with a saline carrier. Peanut agglutinin is a separate laboratory reagent.

peanut-oil carrier and vehicle controls in a related rat experiment — The published methods list vehicle-injected controls. The comparison addresses corticosterone-related biochemical outcomes and does not estimate oral peanut oil or Parkinson fall frequency. Cohort overlap with the meeting abstract remains open.

intraperitoneal peanut oil as the carrier for corticosterone in rats — The verified poster measures hippocampal choline uptake and acetylcholine release. The oil is a non-oral vehicle, with no separately measured oil result for Parkinson fall frequency.

peanut butter and lower-limb function in older adults at risk of falls — Five-times sit-to-stand improved by an adjusted 1.23 s with peanut butter. The gait-speed result was inconclusive. The study gives no verified prospective fall-frequency result and did not use isolated oil.
cayenne frequency and combined mood and apathy domain — The exploratory analysis did not provide a cayenne-specific coefficient on the mood and apathy domain or standalone apathy.

oral dried dill aerial-part and black rice extract and open-field center entries — After ischemia, the low dose on day 7 and middle dose on day 14 increased center entries compared with stroke vehicle. Total crossings showed no clear change, and no distinct anxiety severity scale, single herb arm or Parkinson population was studied.

boiled dill seed and postpartum anxiety — The childbirth trial reported fewer severe anxiety ratings at six hours with boiled dill seed versus oxytocin. The seed preparation, comparator and postpartum population differ from the frozen dried leaf and Parkinson claim.

maternal oral dill extract and offspring elevated-plus-maze behavior — Figure 4 shows more open-arm entries and time after extract in nicotine-exposed mice. Pairwise symbol definitions, n and plant part remain access-limited. Supplementary F and p values have apparent inconsistencies.

oral sowa extract and open-arm exploration during alcohol withdrawal — Open-arm entry proportion increased under extract versus withdrawal alone at 24 hours. Rotarod performance also improved. The extract, plant part and rodent withdrawal population differ from the hypothesis.
dill extract beverage and registered anxiety scale outside Parkinson disease — Thai DASS-21 is the primary outcome. The official completed registry gives no arm results or clear leaf preparation.

injected Perilla constituents and conditioned defensive behavior — Original abstract reports dose-specific direction in defensive freezing and unchanged spontaneous movement at active doses. It measures a rodent fear proxy after isolated compound injection. The earlier forced-swim experiment and later review are separate reports.

intranasal perilla leaf essential oil and anxiety-like behavior in mice — Open-field and elevated-maze exploration increased in stressed mice after essential oil. Nasal delivery, the stress model and behavior measures differ from fresh leaves and clinical anxiety.

seed oil and open-field behavior in a rotenone mouse model — The highest seed oil diet was associated with more center entries and less grooming. Mouse locomotion and anxiety-like behavior cannot establish clinical anxiety after fresh leaves.

perilla-containing formula and anxiety in major depression — The waitlist-controlled abstract reports improvement on anxiety outcomes without separate numerical estimates. Perilla was one component and participants had major depression.
hydroalcoholic celery leaf extract and animal nociception — Evoked writhing decreased and thermal responses changed. No fresh-leaf meal or Parkinson pain severity measure.

celery leaf decoction in uncontrolled gout care — The abstract reports two cases and a score of 5 to 3. The original body specifies one patient and 5 to 2. Boiled preparation, concurrent advice and no control limit causal attribution.

celery leaf and stalk decoction in two uncontrolled gout cases — Both recorded pain scores moved from 5 to 2. The collection dates and intended regimen do not establish follow-up timing. Differences in setting and overlapping outcomes with a later report leave independence unresolved.

transdermal capsaicin and spontaneous healthy eye blinking — Five healthy volunteers had no statistically clear change in spontaneous blink rate. Blinking and focal blepharospasm do not measure overall Parkinson facial expressiveness.

dizziness mentioned after oral cumin essential oil in an uncontrolled IBS series — The original mentions dizziness without count, posture, associated blood pressure or control. The abstract and Results give inconsistent enrollment counts. Concentrated essential oil and uncharacterized dizziness do not establish a ground cumin effect on Parkinson standing lightheadedness.

Parkinson survey recording cumin use with aggregate nonmotor measures — Cumin intake was recorded and exploratory nonmotor comparisons were inconclusive after correction. No preparation or cumin-specific orthostatic lightheadedness estimate is reported.

cumin essential-oil softgels and resting blood pressure in metabolic syndrome — Diastolic pressure was lower at follow-up and systolic comparisons were inconclusive. The study did not measure standing change or lightheadedness.

ground cumin seed infusion with diet and resting blood pressure — Resting systolic pressure fell in both groups, with a larger reduction for the infusion. Standing blood pressure and orthostatic lightheadedness were not measured.
isolated eugenol and evoked detrusor contractions — Eugenol suppressed phasic and sustained rat bladder contraction ex vivo. The result addresses neither urinary urgency frequency nor ingested clove.

PD grouped beans and composite motor burden; no black-bean or postural-instability estimate — Grouped bean question and total symptom outcome do not measure the effect of boiled black common beans on postural instability.
uncooked common bean composition; no clinical outcome — Analytical levodopa concentrations in uncooked varieties cannot establish a clinical effect or its direction after boiling black beans.
trained sensory panel for roasted button mushroom — Panelists rated mushroom product aroma and flavour. The design gives no longitudinal effect on participants' smell.
cooked button mushroom volatile composition — Volatiles and an electronic nose characterize the food stimulus. No consumer smell test was performed.
exact mushroom species fraction in a Parkinson model — Beam-walking results used an isolated protein fraction in mice. No olfactory test was reported in the abstract.

Trained human panel evaluated rice bran oil during eating — Reported differences concern flavour and perceived aroma of the test oil, without a diagnosed olfactory impairment or pre-post olfactory performance measure.

Named rice bran oil odor control and measured sensory ratings — The rice oil had lower perceived intensity than the active cypress stimulus in healthy adults. Relative stimulus intensity is distinct from change in Parkinson olfactory impairment.

oral coriander aerial-part ethanol extract and movement tests in mice — The 2014 dissertation and three patent disclosures report the same experiment. The extract reduced normalized pole descent time from 178.44% to 102.58% of control and increased normalized rotarod retention from 29.68% to 84.84%. Lee's later experiment used different exposure arms within the same research program.

aqueous freeze-dried cilantro leaf and stalk extract in developmental toxicant model — Toxin plus extract offspring covered 20.47 m versus 14.35 m with toxin alone. Spontaneous open-field distance is not measured walking velocity. Exposure was maternal.

coriander in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome — The menu lists coriander without specifying the plant part and the motor examination includes gait. The paper does not establish dried cilantro exposure or report walking speed.

coriander fruit extract and rotarod performance in MPTP mice — There was no clear early rotarod benefit. A longer time to fall was reported on day 20. The tested plant part was fruit and the result does not measure clinical walking speed.

cilantro leaf extract and motor tests in two mouse models — In MPTP mice, grip strength rose from 2.31 ± 0.05 N to 2.65 ± 0.08 N and 2.75 ± 0.06 N with oral leaf extract. The preview names rotarod and pole tests without a verified effect estimate for those outcomes. Dried culinary leaf and clinical walking speed remain untested.

topical cold-pressed pumpkin seed oil in a combination and a speech-containing oral mucositis composite — The combination improved the aggregate PROMS score versus benzydamine. PROMS includes speaking difficulty and speech restriction from mouth sores. The study reports no individual item changes, listener speech intelligibility or toasted oil exposure.

pumpkin seed oil on a Parkinson diet menu and motor-scale speech item — The published score combined motor items. The trial did not identify toasted oil intake or report a separate speech or intelligibility result.

crushed nigella seed capsules and timed human attention tasks — Timed letter cancellation and Trail Making favored nigella. Cancellation accuracy was inconclusive. The authors did not report toasting and participants did not have Parkinson disease.

oral ground fruit powder and Beck Depression Inventory in non-Parkinson randomized trial — Table 4 reports mean BDI-II changes −10.41 ± 11.08 with powder and −9.74 ± 8.50 with placebo (p=.78). Both received calorie restriction. IRCT20131228015968N6 and the later appetite paper are from the same trial family.

injected ethanolic Rhus coriaria extract in mice — Tail-suspension immobility fell while open-field locomotion showed no significant change. The study used an injected extract in a non-Parkinson model.

onion-containing mixed extract and catalepsy in mice — Bar catalepsy reductions versus MPTP alone did not meet the reported significance criterion. The blend was processed and does not isolate raw onion or clinical rigidity.

veterinary reference context only, without a tested Parkinson comparison — The poisoning entry reports onion among foods hazardous to dogs and cats. It supplies no measured oral onion effect on Parkinson rigidity.

onion odor and motor progression classification — Recognizing onion odor had an inconclusive association with rapid versus slow motor progression (OR 1.56, p = .477). Neither raw onion intake nor individual rigidity change was assessed.

onion odor and examiner-rated rigidity — The cross-sectional odds of identifying onion odor were lower at higher rigidity scores with q = .119. Participants smelled the stimulus and no raw onion intake effect was estimated.

lentils among Parkinson menu options and motor examination total — The plant menu group had a lower four-week motor total. The comparison does not isolate lentils or preparation, and facial expression was not reported separately.

shared Parkinson vegetarian menu with lentils and motor composite — The two small groups improved on total UPDRS III. The study gives no lentil preparation, isolated intake or facial expression item contrast.

lentils among prebiotic menu options and composite motor score — A four-week menu and lactulose intervention produced an inconclusive motor total change. Published data do not isolate lentil preparation or intake and omit individual facial expression changes.

paprika xanthophyll supplementation and executive tasks — Open UMIN000055963 crossover with 21 analyzed. Trail Making B and two Stroop interactions gave p=.877, .495 and .581. Extract and ground paprika differ, and participants did not have Parkinson disease.

red bell pepper extract and before–after Trail Making B — Before-exercise Trail Making B moved from 50.1 to 45.2 seconds (p=.039) and after-exercise from 42.2 to 41.7 (p=.061). All 31 participants received extract with repeated testing and exercise. UMIN and article are the same cohort.

paprika xanthophyll with eye exercise and executive outcomes — The registry describes a controlled crossover in healthy participants. Clinical Parkinson executive impairment and ground paprika exposure are not specified.
heat-processed soup with fresh lovage in healthy adults — Feasibility and pooled gastrointestinal adverse events were reported, without a fatigue severity estimate.
individual Parkinson symptoms and diet scores — Diet scores were associated with fatigue at the pattern level, without a preparation-specific lovage estimate.

soybean oil diet and rodent open-field freezing — Open-field stopping time was 135.0 seconds on soybean oil versus 72.76 on equal-fat perilla under rotenone. This includes anxiety-like immobility and gives no human gait-freezing episode estimate.

pea protein breakfast and exploratory cognition reporting — The registry schedules cognitive assessments before breakfast and at 90 and 180 minutes. The 37-person likely companion publishes intake only. A separate 32-person study uses NCT03154606 and cannot supply the registered executive results.

pea protein comparator and prospective executive tasks — The registered 119-person healthy adult comparison uses about 40 g per day of pea protein as the comparator and specifies executive accuracy, Stroop and flanker outcomes. Results are unposted. No intervention arm uses cooked whole peas or enrolls people with Parkinson disease.
isolated lectin and rat working memory — Y-maze spontaneous alternation declined in the combined toxin and lectin arm. The lectin-only arm had no clear change. The study measured rat behavior.

A parsley allergy patient reported tolerance of dried preparation — Fresh and cooked exposure produced allergic symptoms. The dried tolerance was reported as clinical history. The abstract gives no formal graded oral swallow assessment or Parkinson cohort.

A garlic-and-parsley dish appears in a dysphagia home-menu design — The published result is recipe development with workshops, without confirmed dried parsley consumption in a clinical subgroup or measured change in swallowing difficulty.

Parsley-containing thick puree measured before and after oral processing — Five healthy volunteers prepared boluses that were spat out. Noodle purée viscosity decreased 61.07%, with no isolated parsley exposure or swallow severity measure.

A parsley-containing recipe in a clinical dysphagia meal programme — Appendix A includes garlic and parsley in both versions. Only aggregate acceptability and production or texture outcomes were reported.
working memory in non-Parkinson aged rats receiving lyophilized mushroom — Working memory improved at 0.5% dietary supplementation. The other concentrations did not demonstrate that improvement.

randomized capsule exposure to dried white button mushroom in healthy older adults — Reported no significant cognitive treatment effect across the randomized comparison. Dried capsules and healthy participants leave the roasted Parkinson exposure unresolved.

button mushroom supplementation in an amyloid model — The study reported spatial-memory improvement in a transgenic mouse model of amyloid disease. It supplies no preparation-specific Parkinson executive outcome.
pooled mushroom intake and executive measures — Positive cross-sectional associations could reflect confounding or reverse causality. Species, roasting, and Parkinson status were unavailable.

randomized white button and oyster mixture in non-Parkinson adults — Both arms improved immediate memory. Control-only delayed list recall improvement and null attention tasks are indirect cognitive findings. No roasted exposure was assigned.

randomized whole UV-treated cremini exposure and cognitive testing — RBANS domains showed no significant time-by-group effects. Cremini shares the species but the trial used another market type, no roasting assignment, and no Parkinson cohort.
exact mushroom species fraction in a Parkinson model — Beam-walking results used an isolated protein fraction in mice. No executive task was reported in the abstract.

other mushroom species and direct executive task — Oyster mushroom trial reported a reaction-time interaction, with placebo slowing and unchanged accuracy. Button mushroom and Parkinson were outside the trial.

hot-water pomegranate extract and drowsiness scores in sleep-deprived rats — The primary abstract reports amelioration in a sleep-deprivation model. Numerical score estimates are unavailable. The result does not establish daytime sleepiness after raw fruit in Parkinson disease.

multi-ingredient polyphenol blend and registered daytime sleepiness — Sleepiness is registered in healthy adults. The primary pharmacokinetic report gives no separate score. The blend includes many plant extracts, with no isolated pomegranate comparison.

four-botanical blend including pomegranate peel and self-reported alertness — Day-21 predose alertness favored the blend in a follow-up versus placebo (p=.03), while the group-by-session interaction was p=.07. The blend, healthy cohort and proxy measure preclude a conclusion about raw arils and Parkinson daytime sleepiness.

nanoemulsified pomegranate seed oil and planned Parkinson daytime sleepiness — NMSS and a Parkinson sleep scale were planned. No results were verified. The intervention is a nanoformulated oil capsule.

oral pomegranate juice and global sleep quality during opioid treatment — Global PSQI improved in the methadone subgroup. No separate daytime dysfunction estimate or sleepiness adverse-event count was verified. The cohort and exposure differ from the claim.

pomegranate rind extract and a sleep-change subscale in premenstrual syndrome — The post-intervention sleep score was 8.40 versus 9.63, p=.146. The paper did not measure dedicated daytime sleepiness, raw arils or Parkinson disease.

sequential pomegranate acai combination and self-reported alertness — The healthy cohort received the Peach Mango product first and Pomegranate Acai later. Alertness was planned. No result is posted and an isolated aril contrast is absent.
reported tofu intake and diagnosis — The adjusted association with Parkinson diagnosis was inconclusive (OR .86, 95% CI .65 to 1.15). The abstract gives no baked preparation or drooling endpoint.

okara-enriched tofu and acute salivary secretion during chewing — Enriched tofu elicited higher acute secretion in the author abstract. Baking and Parkinson drooling were not assessed. Saliva production and external loss are distinct outcomes.

corn-oil comparator and time until fatigue during analgesic withdrawal — At the first visit off active diclofenac, time until fatigue changed by −0.76 hours in the corn arm (p=.19) and −0.19 hours in the fish arm (p=.64), each within arm. The eight-week table also gives inconclusive within-arm changes. Oil refining and Parkinson fatigue severity were not measured.

animal vehicle or flavored-milk preference outside the frozen preparation — PT080 and another member report injected corn oil as vehicle or control in a perimenopause model. The oil route, associated interventions and measures differ from oral corn oil.

corn-oil high-fat rodent comparison — Muscle molecular markers differ across high-fat oils. The active comparator and molecular outcome do not estimate an isolated refined corn oil and Parkinson endpoint effect.

separately numbered conference member with preparation or outcome limits — P-07.1-14 evaluates liver markers after malathion against a control group given corn oil. It does not compare refined corn oil or measure fatigue.

shared collection original source context — Carney 2009 combines sertraline with corn oil; other original or protocol records use different lipid mixtures and symptom scales. The review cannot isolate the oil or a Parkinson endpoint.
shared collection original source context — P210 compares EPA/DHA-enriched high-fat chow against corn-oil high-fat chow for muscle transcriptome and proteins. No separate frozen patient outcome.

corn oil as high-fat diet control and partial marine-lipid substitution — Corn oil was one base formulation, with and without different marine PUFA fractions. Adiposity and lipids were measured. The possibly overlapping article concerns the same broad research and a refined corn oil symptom effect is unresolved.

shared collection original source context — P233 is appended in the complete PMC HTML for this oral-key record and separately printed in the poster supplement. It compares corn and fish oil during shared exercise for strength and mechanistic outcomes. One study family.

shared collection original source context — Printed P233 reports an omega-3 versus corn-oil comparator during shared resistance training. Its strength findings are distinct from the frozen clinical outcomes. The other PMC key reproduces this member.

corn-oil control during exercise training — The final isometric interaction is p=.015 and the corn arm changed −1.4%. P233 uses −0.3%. Body strength during shared training does not measure any frozen Parkinson endpoint in these claims.

oral corn oil comparator and VAS fatigue — A six-month Sjögren trial reports no clear group difference in fatigue or 24-hour sleep/rest time when comparing corn oil and evening-primrose gamma-linolenic acid. The public abstract omits grade and arm-level fatigue estimates.
corn oil vs omega-3 and fatigue in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis — FSS contrasts p=.97 at six months and p=.57 across 24 months. Group means and oil grade unavailable.

separate gastrointestinal conference member and ingredient context — A tumor experiment incorporates corn oil in control or combined diets involving EPA and aspirin. The study does not assign the frozen preparation and clinical endpoint.

oral corn oil comparator and prespecified fatigue ratings — A Japanese registry identifies a completed healthy-adult study measuring fatigue around mental work and on awakening. The record has no arm-level results or refining grade.
corn versus fish oil and exercise fatigue — Twenty healthy adults; official result reports no group difference without numbers. Separate from the UMIN mental-work fatigue study.

blend containing marjoram and PSQI in rheumatoid arthritis — Massage trial reports global sleep changes across groups and no separate REM dream enactment. Mixed essential oils, skin exposure and rheumatoid arthritis differ from the claim.

marjoram massage and bruxism trial or conference abstract — Registry specifies complaints and bruxism measures. The conference abstract reports jaw ultrasound results. No fresh culinary exposure or dream-enactment measure.
blend containing marjoram, inhalation and topical bruxism trial — Trial specifies jaw ultrasound with pain and stress symptoms. It does not measure dream enactment and has no posted results.
essential oil massage and detector-derived sleep measures — Wake or dream duration showed no clear group difference. The study did not measure dream enactment or eating fresh marjoram.

methanolic basil leaf extract and rodent motor tests — Rotarod times were 31.0 and 32.7 seconds versus 12.7 seconds with haloperidol alone, and catalepsy scores were lower. Taxonomic naming and group sizes are internally unclear. No fresh culinary leaf or clinical Parkinson outcome was tested.

injected sweet basil extract and rotarod/stair tasks — High-dose injected extract increased rotarod time from 57.3 to 144.6 seconds and shortened stair task time from 35.8 to 29.3 seconds. The text conflicts with tables at the lower level. There was no isolated clinical symptom measure.

fresh basil in both clinical Parkinson diet menus — Both diet groups offered fresh basil in different dishes. The study gives no basil-dose contrast or separate postural instability effect by exposure.

mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score — Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes postural stability, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

oral sweet basil essential oil and coordination in mice — The highest oral oil group showed worse rotarod coordination, while the intermediate group did not show a clear motor deficit. The study used concentrated oil in mice without a Parkinson model and did not measure postural instability after eating fresh basil.
rectal sesame oil in a multimodal regimen and speech item — The parkinsonism series reported a favorable within-person speech score. It supplies no speech estimate after consuming toasted sesame oil.

sesame oil swishing and speech difficulty ratings in oral submucous fibrosis — The original table has inconsistent arm totals and gives no reliable between-arm speech estimate. The study does not verify consumption, toasted preparation, Parkinson disease or listener intelligibility.

caraway essential oil odor; adults without neurodegenerative disease; no writing outcome — Odor ratings and separately analyzed language scores cannot determine handwriting size after toasted caraway.

People with persistent smell problems describe lentil odor — Uncontrolled post-COVID self-report, not Parkinson disease; lentils are objects of altered odor perception and no ingestion effect, objective smell score or boiled preparation is established.

Prospective dietary pattern includes legumes and analyzes B-SIT hyposmia — The cohort excluded diagnosed Parkinson disease; the reported null result compares overall Mediterranean-style diet adherence, not lentils or their preparation. Smell impairment was dichotomized against a reference distribution rather than tested as a lentil-specific change.

PD broccoli and ground white mustard tea; single self-reported handwriting series — One unchanged handwriting rating under a mixed uncontrolled exposure does not assess toasted mustard seed or isolate its effect on hand dexterity.
sesame oil used as a diagnostic smell stimulus — The adapted diagnostic test used a sesame oil scent to measure existing impairment. It did not test an ingestion effect.

sesame oil odor in a community smell assay — The oil substituted for coffee as a test odor. The study provides a measure of sensory recognition without assigned ingestion or preparation-specific effect.

diagnostic sesame-oil odor in Parkinson and multiple system atrophy — Correct identification was 44.4% in Parkinson disease and 100% in seven multiple system atrophy comparators (p=.010). This does not measure a change from consuming oil.

intranasal sesame oil with respiratory and sleep outcomes — The original Methods and tables do not provide a measured change in olfactory function. The healthy study uses nasal exposure and no oral sesame comparison.
sesame-labeled stimulus in Parkinson olfactory screening — The sesame stimulus had AUC 0.655 during discovery. An odor diagnostic contrast does not establish effect of oral cold-pressed oil.

probiotic drops with reported soybean vehicle and stimulated saliva — Stimulated flow rose in both periodontal trial arms. The original abstract does not identify the oil. Soybean vehicle is secondary attribution, refining is unverified, and drooling is distinct from stimulated flow.

human soybean-oil oral contact and measured emulsion properties — The study identifies the soybean oil in a mixture that participants swished and spat out. Incomplete recovery prevented estimation of salivary flow. Drooling severity in Parkinson disease was outside the study.

registered one-week dark chocolate crossover with aggregate Parkinson symptom outcomes — A separate one-week protocol plans UPDRS and PDQ-39 along with several other measures. Status is Unknown and no outcomes are posted. Speech-item reporting and listener intelligibility remain unverified.

plain dark chocolate versus cacao-free white chocolate and aggregate Parkinson motor score — The single-dose crossover tested 200 g of 80.1% cocoa dark chocolate without other supplements in 26 patients. The one-hour composite UPDRS III between-treatment effect was −0.54 points (95% CI −1.50 to 0.42). The original body gives no separate speech result or listener intelligibility test.

flavonoid-rich cocoa in a rice beverage and fatigue in Parkinson disease — The pilot measured fatigue and fatigability after high- versus low-flavonoid cocoa beverages. The study gives no plain dark chocolate contrast or speech intelligibility estimate.
fish odor in a Parkinson smell-identification test — The smell test used fish odor as one item and reported a group composite. It neither identifies cod nor measures change after eating baked fish.

pooled fish intake and objective olfactory impairment in older adults — Top versus bottom fish intake quartile associated with lower prevalent olfactory impairment, OR 0.65 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.96), but five-year incident OR was 1.23 (0.75 to 2.02). The food category does not isolate cod or baking and the cohort results are for community-dwelling older adults.

oral avocado-oil comparator and Visual Analog Mood Scale tranquility in healthy adults — Mean tranquility was 297.3 to 301.3 in the mint-flavored avocado oil arm and 303.0 to 302.4 with CBD, baseline-adjusted p=.85. This short-term proxy gives no verified refined grade, oil-free comparison or Parkinson anxiety result.

oral cold-pressed avocado oil and plus-maze measures in obese mice — Plus-maze open-arm time and entries did not clearly differ across groups. The oil was cold-pressed, and the experiment did not measure clinical anxiety.

avocado oil mayonnaise in a broader ketogenic case description — The uncontrolled Down syndrome and Alzheimer case included avocado-oil mayonnaise. Improvement in anxiety was qualitative. Neither a refined oil comparison nor Parkinson disease was present.

ketogenic diet and measured Parkinson anxiety with unisolated oil exposure — The seven-person continuation reports mean PAS change −6.29 (p=.0313). A participant mentions coconut or avocado oil. The reported exposure, change, control and preparation do not allow an oil-specific effect.

oral avocado oil during pregnancy and lactation and rat anxiety-like behavior — Oil and pulp groups showed shorter open-arm time and adult offspring in the oil group moved less. Refining, a Parkinson population and clinical anxiety were unverified.

avocado oil within an oral placebo blend and measured anxiety in fibromyalgia — HADS anxiety means were 9.40 and 9.60 before and after the mixed placebo. The between-arm estimate was −1.56 (95% CI −4.43 to 1.32). The trial has no isolated refined avocado oil or Parkinson anxiety contrast.
cardamom listed in multicomponent Parkinson diet and composite UPDRS III — The composite improved and includes postural stability. The authors did not report that item separately or isolate cardamom.

Parkinson case with depression in treatment timeline — Authors reported improved depression during follow-up after combined formula treatment and rehabilitation. No scale or isolated culinary exposure was available.

red and green pepper extracts and stress-model behavior — Red and green pepper extracts changed immobility during forced swimming. The red and green species differed in open-field effects. No Parkinson clinical outcome was measured.

Sichuan pepper polyphenol extract with internally inconsistent mouse immobility reporting — The original Figure 2 bars for extract are above negative control, in agreement with Results and opposite to the Discussion's reading. Methods describe time until resting, and the graph gives only a generic time label. This result and the unaltered voluntary activity give no reliable direction for clinical depression from toasted pepper.

mixed topical Sichuan pepper preparation and combined anxiety depression item — The recruiting pelvic-pain trial includes ground Sichuan pepper in a mixed plaster and EQ-5D as a secondary quality-of-life measure. It has no separate pepper arm, confirmed toasting, Parkinson cohort or posted results.

placebo-controlled mood proxies with oral Nepalese pepper extract in healthy adults — In 82 healthy adults, the acute contentment interaction had no clear between-arm contrast at any individual assessment. No clear chronic mood or anxiety difference was reported over 56 days. The lipid extract is a separate species preparation, with no clinical depression scale or Parkinson cohort.

Sichuan pepper fruit essential oil and stress-model behavior — Forced-swim immobility changed at all doses, with low-dose null findings for sucrose preference and tail suspension. The experiment used mice and essential oil.
filtered marjoram tea and motor examination in Parkinson — The motor examination is reported in aggregate. No measure of letter size was presented.
baked rye preparation and other human outcomes — The rye formulation was baked and measured mood and cognition. Freezing episodes and Parkinson’s were outside the design.

gluten withdrawal report in one celiac parkinsonism case with partial original access — The original preview establishes walking difficulty, postural instability and baseline UPDRS II 8 and III 19. It stops ahead of the outcome table. The title and subsequent review describe improvement, without a verified freezing or rye bread outcome.

paprika xanthophyll in a student exercise and mouth-rinse comparison — Trail Making B improved within conditions with exercise and mouth rinse with or without paprika. The abstract gives no direct isolated contrast.

paprika xanthophyll in a seven-condition nighttime crossover — Only the three-component condition produced a reported pre-post Trail Making improvement. No paprika-alone or addition contrast was reported.

repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking — Vegetables were offered in conjunction with a reward. The sample was children, and neither adult symptoms nor the matched preparation were assessed. The registration gives n = 82, while the two arm counts in the poster add to 84.

oral red bell pepper extract and executive tasks in older adults — Trail Making B times improved in the before-exercise comparison across visits (p = .039) with an inconclusive postexercise comparison (p = .061). The 31 participants all received the extract and no Parkinson cohort was included.

oral paprika xanthophyll and executive outcomes in a healthy crossover — Same UMIN000055963 crossover. Trail Making B improved by 1.1 seconds during extract and by 1.0 second during control, with interaction p=.877. Within-supplement changes cannot establish a comparative effect. Grilled pepper and Parkinson were outside the design.

registered parallel paprika extract and cognitive testing in healthy adults — Official registry lists 40 enrolled, completion and unpublished outcomes. It lists cognitive tests and a supplement comparison, without a grilled food exposure.

placebo-controlled paprika extract and executive tasks in students — The crossover plans Trail Making B and Stroop outcomes with extraocular exercise and oral capsules. Results remain unpublished and the study has no Parkinson cohort.

green kiwi juice and rotarod in mice — Post-dose rotarod times were slightly lower and marked p < .05 versus saline despite the paper's absence-of-muscle-relaxation conclusion. The population and preparation differ.

kiwi-containing extract combination and motor coordination — The oral three-fruit extract improved hanging-wire performance in a haloperidol model. A kiwi-only arm, raw fruit and clinical postural assessments were absent.

kiwi as an ingredient and composite Parkinson motor results — The diet included kiwi and UPDRS III measured postural stability within a composite. The paper gives no preparation, isolated exposure or item-level estimate.

hardy kiwi juice and beam walking in a Parkinson model — The investigator follow-up gives group sizes and a p < .01 motor comparison. Beam walking in MPTP mice and previously frozen hardy kiwi juice differ from clinical postural instability and raw fruit.

rosmarinic-acid-containing perilla extract and urinary frequency — The patent reports fewer nighttime voids and inconclusive daytime and volume comparisons. The intervention was perilla extract and urgency was unmeasured.

daily whole walnuts and Epworth Sleepiness Scale — Healthy young adults showed −1.37 points relative to baseline after 8 weeks (95% CI −2.21 to −0.52, p=.002). Control period had no clear baseline change. Whole nut and open-label non-Parkinson exposure.

walnut oil within a placebo blend and reports of somnolence in fibromyalgia — The placebo containing walnut, avocado and MCT oil had three somnolence event reports versus five with cannabinoids. The endpoint and combined comparator leave cold-pressed walnut oil and Parkinson daytime sleepiness unresolved.

sweet almond oil massage and total postoperative delirium scores — After open-heart surgery, the sweet almond oil massage arm had mean total NEECHAM scores of 26.70 on day 1 and 27.62 on day 3, versus 26.20 and 27.18 in routine care, with across-three-arm p=.39, .66, .06 at the three assessments. A separately scored attention item was unavailable. Topical massage, acute postoperative delirium, and chronic Parkinson attention impairment differ.

sweet almond powder with rock candy and Alzheimer attention-domain scores — In Alzheimer disease, sweet almond powder plus rock candy changed mean MoCA attention scores from 5.26 to 5.20 versus 4.86 to 4.83 in routine care (p=.776 for the between-group change in the attention domain). The intervention combined whole-nut powder and candy and did not test oil or Parkinson disease.

sweet almond syrup and parent-rated inattention in pediatric ADHD — Inattention scores moved 11.57 to 6.20 versus 8.05 to 8.10 under placebo. Raw Tukey contrasts were p=.003 at baseline and p=.011 at week 12. The printed table does not clearly show a baseline-adjusted estimate. All children took methylphenidate and the syrup is a separate formulation from cold-pressed almond oil.

topical almond massage and delirium composite in acute cardiac care — A randomized post-infarction trial reported an overall three-arm NEECHAM composite time-by-group p<.001 after lavender massage, unscented sweet almond oil massage, or routine care. The published result does not isolate an almond-specific attention domain, and this was a topical intervention in acute cardiac care.

retrospective registration for isolated pharmaceutical and aggregate motor scores — The described compound and outcome fields do not identify fresh celery leaves or a separate freezing-of-gait frequency measurement.
whole celery extract and beam walking in mice — Beam crossing improved. The study did not count freezing episodes or use fresh leaves.
celery named in a Parkinson diet with a gait-inclusive motor scale — No isolated celery arm, leaf identification or separate freezing of gait outcome.

oral grapeseed oil cookie and registered gait speed — Gait speed was specified for a secondary correlation. No gait or fall estimate was reported in the publications checked. Participants were healthy adults.
oral grapeseed oil cookie and registered walking speed — Walking speed is listed in a planned secondary correlation. There is no posted result or fall-count measure and no Parkinson cohort.

grape seed extract and gait or rotarod in Parkinson-model rats — The hydroalcoholic extract increased stride length (p < .05) and rotarod time (p < .01). The study did not record clinical falls or feed grapeseed oil.

dietary cold-pressed oil and measured sucrose intake and sociability — Oil in feed increased sucrose consumption in both sexes and sociability in males only. The unlesioned rat endpoints do not establish ground nigella seed effects on Parkinson apathy.

Nigella oil and social approach after experimental antibiotic exposure — Nigella oil groups had higher sociability indices than the antibiotic-only group. Clinical apathy and the ground-seed preparation were untested.

Multi-food Parkinson diet contains cooked green peas and reports an individual with prior postural hypotension and ongoing falls — Low-fat menus include peas in several cooked multi-ingredient recipes; individual consumption and event timing are unknown, falls are not counted, and midodrine was increased. No isolated pea or fall-frequency estimate.

low — Seven healthy students received orange oil and eugenol odors. Orange produced greater P3 amplitude and odor quality did not affect ERP latencies. The oddball paradigm gives no clinical impairment or oral ground-berry estimate.

low — In 25 healthy volunteers, eugenol air-block comparisons showed no detectable effect on manual Stroop reaction time or interaction with congruency. This is a human null for isolated odor exposure and a laboratory task, with no Parkinson population or fruit ingestion.

low — Six participants received linalool and eugenol as odor stimuli. Attention instructions changed odor-evoked electrical signals. The intervention contrast provides no estimate of clinical attention impairment after ground allspice ingestion.

rat CNS activity and fresh allspice leaf extracts — Rat behavioral screening after injection included nonspecific CNS suppression. No explicit attention task or oral ground-berry comparison was reported.

sunflower food frequency and composite Parkinson symptom burden — The poster reports +2 total PRO-PD points per intake frequency category (95% CI −10 to 13, p=.787). The cross-sectional exposure did not specify an oil grade. It gives no individual olfaction estimate.

sunflower oil original source context — Study groups shared injected tamoxifen in sunflower oil. Gait and nonmotor tests include a buried-food olfaction task and operant sensation seeking, with no separate dietary oil comparison.

freeze-dried cranberry powder and baseline PHQ-9 screening in healthy older adults — The protocol scheduled PHQ-9, and the Connell thesis and paper confirm baseline PHQ-9 screening in COMBAT participants. The cognitive, metabolite and baseline analyses do not give a post-treatment depression comparison by arm. Same trial family as ISRCTN76069316.

cranberry extract in a mixed snack and depression scores during simulated altitude — POMS depression was higher in both high-altitude conditions than low altitude, with no detected difference between same-altitude mixture and placebo. HADS depression had no detected condition, time or interaction. A preliminary abstract based on the low-altitude contrast is from the same cohort. Cranberry was one of multiple ingredients and the adults did not have Parkinson disease.

cranberry juice crossover with a planned global mood score — The trial planned overall Profile of Mood States disturbance. It supplies no depression-subscale result or assignment to dried cranberries.

The POMS depression-dejection contrast was adverse at week 4, with later point estimates in the opposite direction and intervals spanning zero. HADS depression overall and at week 12 was inconclusive. Trial participants were healthy young adults taking 236 mL cranberry juice daily. The time-specific scale finding does not settle the effect of dried cranberry on depression in Parkinson disease.

source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits — A nursing-home poster reviews cranberry and oral anticoagulant coexposure. It does not compare frozen cranberries for Parkinson symptom changes.

cranberry juice and older adult self-rated general mood — In the randomized six-week 50-person pilot, the author abstract reports inconclusive between-group tests for perceived mood and energy changes without item effect estimates. Juice and self-rated general mood are distinct from dried cranberry and depression severity in Parkinson disease.

berry polyphenol extracts in a rat metabolic model — The biochemical table marks triglyceride differences in several extract arms. Preparation and model differ, and there is no symptom outcome. The cranberry denominators and route wording do not fully reconcile.

freeze-dried commercial cranberry juice applied to a cell-free MAO-A assay — The article reports inhibition with discordant IC50 values and units. The enzyme source is unspecified. No participant exposure or depression outcome was tested. A separate human adipose experiment by overlapping authors used pomegranate.

cranberry anthocyanin extract and mouse immobility proxies — Figure 2 shows no detected change relative to vehicle in tail-suspension or forced-swimming immobility at either extract dose. The animal measures and concentrated extract do not estimate a dried cranberry effect on clinical depression.
diet pattern and composite outcome — Protein timing and motor activities were tested. Raw apricot and daily off time were not isolated.
low-protein dietary regimen and matching off-time outcome — Randomized crossover reported shorter off time with low-protein products. Raw apricot was not isolated.

apricot kernel extract and haloperidol model catalepsy rather than fruit or OFF time — Saleem and colleagues prepared a methanolic extract from authenticated fresh apricot kernels. In haloperidol-exposed rats, the highest tested extract group showed shorter bar-test catalepsy latency than disease controls (Figure 1, p < .001), with additional findings in beam and open-field tasks. This examines seed-kernel extract and evoked animal motor impairment. It supplies no human OF...

habanero extract and acute swallowing timing — Thirteen participants completed the Parkinson crossover. Four videofluoroscopy timing measures showed no clear difference after extract versus placebo. Ground cayenne and symptom severity were outside the comparison.

placebo-controlled oral capsaicin film in mixed chronic dysphagia — In 42 gastrostomy-fed patients including people with Parkinson, oral capsaicin film reduced pooled immediate swallowing reflex latency. Sustained latency change was inconclusive. The abstract supplies no Parkinson subgroup estimate or ground cayenne exposure.
aerosolized extract in an uncontrolled dysphagia series — The 16-patient series reports clinical use and associations without a Parkinson subgroup response or controlled severity estimate.
capsaicin drink or chilled capsaicin probe and water swallow signs — The abstract reports pooled signs without a Parkinson subgroup or separate probe temperature effect.

aerosolized capsaicin and endoscopic swallowing in mixed neurogenic dysphagia — Interim diagnosis footnotes conflict. Final pooled counts establish a cough response in all four Parkinson-labeled aerosol participants and bound swallowing responses at two to four of four versus zero to one of five. Exact swallowing counts and severity remain unavailable.

capsaicin jelly and green tea swallows in a mixed cohort — Nine participants included five with Parkinson. Pooled swallow latency and duration fell five minutes after jelly. No Parkinson subgroup data or ground cayenne. Same authors report follow-up in 2002, with participant overlap unknown.

capsaicin jelly and instrumental timing in Parkinson — Fifteen with Parkinson and no overt aspiration took contrast jelly with and without capsaicin. Mean pharyngeal delay and passage times were shorter with capsaicin, with no significance tests given. The preparation and short-term endpoint differ from the claim.

related ground red chili and non-Parkinson gargle — A filtered ground red chili gargle increased mean saliva-swallow counts from baseline at 20 minutes in ten healthy adults. Cultivar, between-condition effect and clinical Parkinson outcomes were unverified.

related ground red chili and non-Parkinson physiology — Twelve healthy adults chewed fewer times and had altered manometry with commercial ground red chili in mochi. Cayenne cultivar and Parkinson dysphagia severity were untested.

capsaicin and swallowing-related breathing with cohort and results unavailable — Miura and colleagues presented a study on capsaicin, swallowing apnea duration, and breathing pattern. The title provides no preparation, population or result. No publicly readable counterpart was identified. It leaves ground cayenne and Parkinson swallowing severity unresolved.

qualitative dysphagia response during vinegar and levodopa coadministration — The single postoperative case involves a different coadministered ingredient and gives no swallowing severity score. It did not examine cayenne.

oral capsaicin jelly and six-month dysphagia follow-up — The 15 participants had Parkinson or cerebrovascular disease; 12 completed. Four reported improvement, three had reduced laryngeal penetration, group videofluoroscopy change was inconclusive, and two developed pneumonia. No placebo, Parkinson subgroup result or ground cayenne.

nonpungent CH-19 Sweet capsinoid seasoning on a VF jelly — The 17-person mixed dysphagia report describes changes in instrumental timing and movement. There was no Parkinson subgroup or group clinical swallowing result for ground cayenne. Earlier five-person progress report is the same project.
inhaled diagnostic stimulus — The registered and published analyses characterize cough physiology. No culinary or swallowing treatment contrast.
inhaled diagnostic stimulus — Posted outcomes describe cough sensitivity and separate swallowing testing by disease group. No ground cayenne treatment contrast.

aerosolized capsaicin used to measure reflex cough — The one-arm study used capsaicin during testing before and after cough training. Reflex cough peak flow did not clearly change. It gives no ground cayenne or swallowing difficulty estimate.

acute pharyngeal catheter challenge with CH-19 Sweet capsiate — In 12 older patients with aspiration pneumonia, mean reflex latency was 16.3 s with water and 6.1 s at 100 nM capsiate. Extract, catheter route and cohort differ from the frozen claim, and no Parkinson subgroup was reported.

red-pepper-seasoned cabbage and swallowing reflex latency — Within-group latency shortened in older adults without dysphagia. The study had no unexposed control and removed the red pepper slices and pickling liquid before serving.
topical aural capsaicin and mixed dysphagia — Pooled swallowing outcomes favored the intervention on some measures. Parkinson subgroup contained three participants with no separate effect.

swallowing endoscopy after nebulized capsaicin in a stroke case — After a week, secretion ratings improved and silent aspiration for IDDSI Level 1 liquid remained unchanged. Later measurements followed combined therapy and used different test consistencies. This is an uncontrolled post-stroke inhalation case.
aerosolized cayenne and cough — A mixed cohort included three participants with Parkinson disease. The study measured cough and supplied no Parkinson-specific swallowing estimate.
capsaicin wafer and swallow timing — No clear swallowing timing improvement in the small wafer comparison.

capsaicin as part of a Parkinson cough training program — The intervention combines cough practice, feedback and aerosol stimulus. It gives no isolated capsaicin or swallowing difficulty treatment estimate.
capsaicin solution and mixed dysphagia population — The active arm showed a within-arm change. The abstract does not give a between-group or Parkinson-specific estimate.
oral liquid extract and cough provocation in healthy adults — Transient cough suppression occurred in 23 of 25. The project gives no Parkinson swallowing difficulty measure.

The original 2018 and 2019 reports and 2020 abstract share the research line. Acute capsaicin elicited reflex swallowing, while later air-evoked swallows decreased after prolonged direct laryngeal contact. The 85 refers to the later article total. Oral culinary exposure and clinical Parkinson severity were not studied.

The independent S270 poster reports swallows evoked by isolated capsaicin in mineral oil compared with mineral oil alone. Anesthetized non-Parkinson rats were assessed on reflex initiation. The poster supplies no analyzed denominator and no clinical difficulty outcome.

In separate healthy-volunteer experiments, short preconditioning with a cayenne-distinct red pepper sauce suspension favored cued swallow precision and continuous exposure did not show the same improvement. The experiments used multiple outcome denominators and assessed physiology rather than symptoms.

The 21-person healthy crossover tests active versus sham cortical stimulation. Both periods receive the same oral capsaicinoids. The volume-per-swallow difference supplies no independent capsaicinoid estimate or Parkinson dysphagia result.

corn oil comparator in a randomized human primary-insomnia trial — Among 30 analyzed, the ISI endpoint contrast was minus 1.9 points for CBD versus corn oil (95% CI minus 5.0 to 1.1). An objective sleep efficiency contrast favored CBD. Both arms used corn oil. The main and cognitive reports are one cohort. The registry dose and duration differ and refining is unreported.

animal vehicle or flavored-milk preference outside the frozen preparation — PT080 and another member report injected corn oil as vehicle or control in a perimenopause model. The oil route, associated interventions and measures differ from oral corn oil.

planned PSQI and ESS in a deployed-soldier corn-oil capsule comparison — The registered three months and corn-oil capsules differ from the possible published match at 60 days with corn-oil ethyl esters. Secondary review numbers mix denominators and leave timing uncertain. Full primary estimates and exact trial linkage remain open.

planned adolescent sleep measures with a mixed oil placebo containing corn oil — The protocol names a 64-participant sleep substudy. Neither the official registry nor the accessible thesis yields verified arm-specific sleep outcomes. Four oils, unspecified corn processing and a non-Parkinson population limit correspondence.

conflicting corn versus soybean label in a postmenopausal sleep trial — The registered placebo fat is unspecified. A meeting listing says corn oil, while the original thesis and two published reports identify soybean oil. SHAPE does not supply a verified corn-oil exposure or a Parkinson insomnia comparison.

same pharmaceutical grade corn-oil vehicle for both study groups — The primary drug report gives an actigraphy treatment difference and no clear pairwise subjective waking-often result. Both arms received the same pharmaceutical-grade oil. The comparison does not vary corn oil and does not involve Parkinson insomnia.

registered PSQI in randomized corn-oil exercise comparator trial — The registry registers the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Ethics code S61809 confirms the Dalle article belongs to the trial, but the complete primary paper and original seven-page supplement omit the PSQI outcome and registry has no posted results.

sponsor reported sleep scale in a separate phase 2b corn oil comparator trial — The sponsor reports 355.4 versus 364.2 at endpoint for corn-oil placebo versus 1 mg drug (p=.24). The sleep-specific n and error-term definition are unavailable. No structured registry results, no Parkinson cohort and no oil-specific comparison.

sleep quality registered for an energy-matched corn canola and fructose control — Older adults undergoing bed rest received a composite oil-and-fructose control or ketone monoester. Sleep quality and sleep disturbance were listed, with no registry results or separate oil assignment.

registered corn-oil comparator with linked sleep results retracted — The registry lists PSQI and ESS and shows no structured results. The linked reported results were retracted after data and analysis discrepancies. Registry narrative and repeats of the retracted publication supply no directional result.

oral corn-oil comparator and broad NPI nighttime behavior item in Alzheimer disease — Six-month nighttime behavior p=.69. Corn-oil means 4.9 to 3.7 among item-positive subsets of 33 and 19. Changing denominators and a broad nighttime item leave an insomnia outcome unresolved. No refining grade or no-oil arm.

equal corn-oil carrier in an overnight crossover and objective sleep measures — In 26 healthy completers, corn-only versus drug-in-corn sleep latency was 13.4 versus 9.8 minutes and wake after sleep onset 46.2 versus 47.10 minutes. Both were inconclusive. PSQI was a screening measure. No oil-free phase, refined grade or Parkinson insomnia diagnosis.
corn oil as capsule placebo in a REM sleep behavior trial — The primary measures covered REM sleep behavior rather than insomnia. No independent corn oil contrast was available.

corn oil capsules as comparator in a 12-week sleep quality trial — Endpoint measured efficiency was 96.0% with DHA/EPA versus 93.7% with corn oil, p=.018. Subjective sleep initiation and maintenance had p=.351. The result is a fish-oil comparison in generally healthy adults and does not identify a corn oil effect, refining, or Parkinson insomnia.

topical corn-oil-containing comparator and global sleep quality after herpes zoster — Comparison-arm mean PSQI 7.83 to 6.25 versus 7.88 to 4.35 in the active arm. Adjusted treatment-comparison difference -1.95 with 95% CI -3.18 to -0.72. Multiple co-ingredients and topical exposure prevent a dietary or independent refined-oil inference.

eggs on a Parkinson example menu and clinical walking speed — The study measured 0.93 versus 1.06 m/s in Parkinson participants and controls. The illustrative menu had eggs as an option with no egg-specific exposure or speed comparison.

observational tea analysis or prediabetes egg program — Three members identify the EGGSPDITe egg intervention program in prediabetes, including protocol and remote-delivery snapshots. They do not report a relevant egg effect on the frozen symptom.
egg frequency and perceived slow movement in Parkinson baseline data — Near-zero inverse sign for general slowness. The report gives no timed walking, poaching or pairwise uncertainty.

poached egg in food-frequency measures and physical performance in older adults — The physical performance battery included an 8-foot walk with no clear group effect on the composite. The study did not assign individual preparations or report a Parkinson effect.
boiled eggs with a labeled phosphatidylcholine challenge — The egg challenge concerns gut microbial and blood metabolites. The outcome and preparation are separate from the frozen claim.
egg within varied nonseafood dietary proteins — Egg is a bundled exposure in the nonseafood dietary pattern. The trial reports lipids instead of falls or gait, and does not isolate poached egg.

shared collection original source context — Genuine egg exposures appear in food intake surveys and the varied nonseafood arm of PO2.144. The student surveys overlap, and no isolated poached or Parkinson outcome is reported.

shared collection original source context — Recorded exposures include eggs in dietary groups, prospective food introduction and pooled nutritional food samples. These reports do not supply a poached egg or clinical Parkinson outcome estimate.

egg intake frequency predictor of low protein intake — The adjusted model treats egg frequency as one predictor of estimated low protein intake. Egg preparation and Parkinson falls and walking speed were not studied. The conference presentation and full article share the same data.
reported chicken and egg label use — The survey identifies consumer attention to product labels. It does not measure consumption at a controlled preparation or fatigue, falls or gait.

carotenoid food recalls and macular pigment measurements — The participant records name several food sources and the authors report no detected association with optical pigment density. No assigned food preparation or relevant Parkinson symptom was measured.

shared collection original source context — C4 studies fertilized egg-yolk extract relative to cheese powder for muscle protein synthesis. The preparation and outcome do not match poached egg and Parkinson falls or walking.

processed egg yolk and tissue synthesis — Twenty older adults received the yolk fraction or cheese powder. The published 18% synthesis difference concerns tissue metabolism and is not a poached-egg fall or walking outcome.

eggs in a Parkinson diet intervention and composite motor score — The intervention menu lists eggs and the motor scale includes gait. The study gives no egg preparation, actual exposure, or outcome specific to walking slowness.

weekly egg intake and gait tests reported by osteosarcopenia status — The author abstract associates weekly egg intake with osteosarcopenia and describes gait by musculoskeletal diagnosis. The available text gives no egg-to-gait estimate or cooking detail. The full article remains gated.

commercial mint oil and post-cesarean flatulence pain — The abstract favors oral Supermint for procedure-related pain and gives inconsistent participant totals. Species, fresh spearmint and Parkinson pain were unverified.

commercial mint drops and pediatric colonoscopy pain — The primary paper gives a lower procedure pain score with the product versus no drops. The paper calls the product peppermint, and the study lot species remains unconfirmed.

commercial mint drops and post-cholecystectomy pain — Early pain contrasts were inconclusive, and the abstract and figure describe differing later directions. The concentrated product is not verified as fresh spearmint.

spearmint among suggested culinary herbs — The original protocol lists spearmint among suggested culinary herbs. It does not verify participant-level fresh preparation or intake. Edited testimonials report outcomes for the combined program without a separate pain severity comparison for this ingredient.

mixed extracts including spearmint and IBS abdominal pain — The small placebo comparison reported lower abdominal pain severity p=.016 with the three-extract mixture. Standard treatment also depended on bowel subtype. Fresh spearmint and Parkinson pain were not separately tested.

spearmint oil contact allergy and erosive oral lichen planus — The retrospective study found 14 cases of erosive oral lichen planus among 19 clinically relevant patch test positives. No fresh leaf or Parkinson pain comparison.

brewed spearmint and osteoarthritis pain — The high-rosmarinic-acid tea arm reported reduced knee pain from baseline without a significant between-arm contrast. Fresh leaves and Parkinson pain were outside the study.

mint oil capsule with inconsistent botanical identity and epigastric pain — The mint group reported no epigastric pain during washout. The trial enrolled adults with tuberculosis and does not supply a fresh spearmint pain effect.

whole-diet comparison and a qualitative OFF-time report — One participant described prolonged OFF time after a high-fat meal during the ketogenic period. The trial does not isolate refined coconut oil or report a separate daily OFF-time treatment contrast.

coconut oil as an example in self-reported Parkinson OFF coping strategies — The Fox Insight survey included 2,110 respondents with OFF periods and 1,416 free-text coping responses. Coconut oil is one example in the six-response supplements category. No oil-specific count, processing grade, comparator or measured change in daily OFF time is reported.
fractionated oil and ordinal daily off-time ratings — The standard-diet group had higher off-time scores, including at baseline. This whole-diet comparison does not isolate refined coconut oil.

confirmed saffron odor in a post-traumatic rotating regimen — The 2024 companion Methods identify saffron in month three, together with other odors. The 2021 report evaluates the full program, with no separate saffron contrast or oral Parkinson exposure.

hyposmic non-PD cohort; orange and saffron extracts in salt; taste outcome — Flavor mixture was tested for taste perception, not treatment-related olfactory severity; no stand-alone ground saffron effect or PD comparison.
