pumpkin seed oil versus raw seed and resting blood pressure — The primary 2018 abstract reports no clear blood-pressure change in the oil arm. No orthostatic outcome was reported and the linked dissertation remains inaccessible.

oral pumpkin seed oil and resting pressure in postmenopausal women — The abstract reports lower brachial and central systolic pressure after oil and no clear heart-rate variability or stiffness change. Standing pressure and lightheadedness were not measured.

pumpkin oil-enriched diet and seated blood pressure measurement in hyperlipidemia — The registry specifies seated pressure after rest. The published abstract omits arm-specific values, and the verified four-page supplement reports fatty-acid laboratory results only. Main clinical tables, processing grade and standing symptoms remain unverified.

oral pumpkin seed oil and resting diastolic pressure in postmenopausal women — Mean diastolic pressure fell from 81.10 to 75.67 mmHg in the oil arm. The 12-week arm contrast was inconclusive and neither standing pressure nor lightheadedness was assessed.

branded pumpkin seed oil capsule and measured seated pressure versus placebo — Seated systolic change was −1.2 versus +1.0 mmHg (p = 0.496); diastolic change was −0.1 versus −0.8 (p = 0.813). No pressure after standing or scale for triggered lightheadedness. The complete capsule formula and pressing grade are unverified.

oral pumpkin seed oil and dizziness reporting with active drug comparison — Zero of 39 oil participants and two of 34 tamsulosin participants reported dizziness. The active-drug comparison gives no measured orthostatic symptom or cold-press grade.
refined olive oil and dementia composite score — Dementia severity ratings improved within both oil groups. No apathy-specific estimate or Parkinson participants.
multicomponent Parkinson diet and baseline apathy — Published material includes a baseline Starkstein Apathy Scale and no isolated refined-olive-oil or follow-up apathy contrast.

olive oil in a composite dietary score among older coronary patients — The outcome is reported by Mediterranean dietary score and diabetes status. No grade, oil-specific estimate or Parkinson symptom result was reported.

Mediterranean diet adherence and apathy outside Parkinson disease — Table 4 adjusted OR 2.76, 95% CI 0.83 to 9.21, p=.099 for diet nonadherence and apathy during quarantine. The prose describes an association. There is no oil-specific contrast.

Parkinson cohort diet scores and individual apathy assessment — Recovered institutional Table 4 covers 162 participants and MDS-UPDRS I item 1.5. Lifestyle-adjusted MIND, DII and HDI p=.612, .687 and .369. The models use entire dietary patterns and supply no separate oil-grade result.

Parkinson dietary patterns, olive oil questionnaire and patient-rated motivation — The two diet scores show lower difficulty on the motivation or initiative item at p<.001 each. The supplements list olive oil questions but report question-level estimates only against the aggregate PRO-PD measure. The food processing grade and separate oil-to-apathy estimate are absent.

apathy during sublingual cannabinoid treatment with olive oil carrier — Apathy decreased in one uncontrolled Alzheimer cohort. Same cohort as the 2022 preprint. Formulation uses unspecified olive oil as carrier and there is no carrier-only arm.

low — The report used dyskinesia in a five-case peripheral neuropathy syndrome in men with diabetes. Product form and motor phenomenology remain unverified. It did not measure Parkinson or levodopa-induced dyskinesia after toasted groats.
retrospective pharmaceutical registration and generic motor outcomes — The registry lists UPDRS but no independent stride-length endpoint or fresh celery leaf intervention.
whole celery extract and gait task performance in mice — Grid foot faults decreased and beam crossing improved at some doses. No stride length was measured.
celery named in a Parkinson diet with a gait-inclusive motor scale — The composite motor score improved. The study gives no confirmed fresh leaf exposure or stride length value.

pomegranate peel extract and sucrose consumption in stressed mice — The primary report highlights a greater sucrose response with flax and imipramine, while pomegranate peel changed selected biomarkers. Sucrose intake is a reward-related measure, without clinical apathy or raw fruit.

nanoemulsified pomegranate seed oil and planned Parkinson mood and apathy domain — The planned NMSS covers loss of interest. No item-level result or trial outcome publication was verified. The intervention is a nanoformulated oil capsule.

multi-ingredient pomegranate-acai product and registered motivation — The single-arm healthy adult registration lists self-reported motivation. There are no posted results or isolated aril comparison.

Dill extract and involuntary contractions of isolated visceral smooth muscle — A methanol extract of dried aerial parts inhibited experimentally induced and spontaneous intestinal smooth muscle contractions. This ex vivo result provides no neurological dystonia evidence.

Oral sowa extract and experimental motor behavior — The animal withdrawal study used motor coordination and locomotor measures without a neurological dystonia endpoint or culinary foliage verification.

acute and repeated cognitive function with black cardamom extract — Both reports use the same registration family and measure timed cognitive-task outcomes. They provide no sleepiness scale and use aqueous black cardamom rather than ground green seed.
cardamom crude extract and pentobarbital-induced sleep in mice — The extract lengthened drug-induced sleep. The study did not measure waking sleepiness in Parkinson’s.

topical mustard constituent and elicited swallow reflex in rats — Topical allyl isothiocyanate triggered reflex swallows and local TRPA1 antagonism reduced them. Reflex counts and direct chemical application do not measure food swallowing safety.

topical mustard constituent after experimental rat pharyngolaryngeal injury — The injury comparison prolonged allyl isothiocyanate-evoked swallow latency without changing swallow count. The design did not test culinary mustard in Parkinson disease.

mustard sauce and allergic swallowing symptoms — The primary abstract verifies three systemic allergic reactions. A later case table attributes acute dysphagia to two patients. Parkinson disease and a ground-mustard comparison were absent.
saffron capsules and composite Parkinson motor score — The eight-week motor total comparison was inconclusive, F=.53 and p=.424. The accessible report supplies no separate facial-expression item 3.2.
saffron plus chamomile and composite outcomes — Registered combination and constituent comparisons. No posted results.
isolated constituent and composite motor score — Within-group composite motor improvement. No ingredient-level or symptom-specific treatment estimate was available.
strain-defined fermented milk — The trial measured bowel function, anxiety and composite nonmotor symptoms for a distinct preparation.

publisher abstract of kefir-grain isolate and fermentation tests — Three kefir-grain isolates differ from drinking plain kefir. The later Figure 3 reuses enzyme measurements for two isolates. The tests do not measure falls or fatigue.
commercial kefir in myeloma and planned patient fatigue measures — Official protocol names fatigue. No primary result or exact product grade was verified.

kefir during cancer treatment and aggregate physical symptoms — The fourth-cycle physical symptom outcome favors the kefir arm. Tiredness is one physical item and is not given separately. Product flavor and contribution of extra contact remain unclear.
commercial kefir and registered PROMIS Global Health — A planned fatigue item in a broader outcome supplies no result. Observational protocol without a parallel untreated comparison group.
kefir bolus and instrumented swallowing test — The study compared swallowing under different food and liquid textures and measured no fatigue.

separately numbered conference member with preparation or outcome limits — P-07.2-08 assays bacterial isolates from kefir, amasi and mahewu. It gives no plain kefir intake or patient fatigue endpoint.

ordinary commercial beverage composition without participant outcomes — The study tests three packages each of three kefir products and six other products in laboratory composition and enzyme assays. It does not measure symptoms or blood pressure after kefir consumption.

original isolate comparison with documented reuse — KF1 and ABK enzyme results are reused from the 2021 grain study. The paper separately compares strains in laboratory fermentation. No participant consumed plain kefir, and there are no fall or fatigue outcomes.

formulated kefir and treadmill exhaustion in healthy participants — The crossover likely corresponds to registry NCT04293666 based on design, sample and exact strains. Registry says freeze dried and paper says spray dried. Endurance was 11.76 versus 9.08 minutes with p=.0048 in Results and p=.0004 in abstract. No patient fatigue comparison.

kefir after exercise and patient-reported fatigue in cancer survivors — The 24-person article abstract reports 39.3% fatigue improvement. The likely related 19-person dissertation reports an interaction p=.002. Product flavor, full article contrast and Parkinson treatment remain unverified.
kefir, milk and water and acute postexercise fatigue — Postexercise fatigue improved with kefir and water before retesting. The author abstract does not show a clear kefir superiority estimate.
kefir powder and planned fatigue visual analog rating — Physical fatigue is secondary in the 75-person powder protocol. Results are unpublished in the official record.

hazelnut oil mixed into chocolate and measured secretion — Panelists licked and expectorated two same-sugar fat matrices. Replacing some cocoa butter with hazelnut oil gave no statistically clear difference in saliva per gram of sample. The experiment did not measure drooling or specify oil grade or Parkinson status.

compound hazelnut-oil gargle and ex vivo tongue wetting — Higher liquid retention refers to formulated wetting in excised tissue. The preparation was mixed and its oil grade unspecified. It measures no saliva production or drooling.

macadamia oil comparator and sleep-related impairment — There was no clear treatment-by-time effect on PROMIS sleep-related impairment (p = .6878). Neither oil-free exposure nor diagnosed insomnia was tested.

oral macadamia oil and acute daytime ratings with pretreatment sleep information — Two healthy-student experiments found lower acute sleepiness and fatigue with a macadamia oil meal. The study family collected selected past sleep information and did not assess treatment-period insomnia or establish cold pressing.
carrot juice and functional gait comparison — Usual gait speed in the carrot arm changed inconclusively (p=.350). Stride length, steamed carrot and a Parkinson cohort were absent.
oral purple carrot extract in Parkinson model rats — Catalepsy and oral movements improved. No stride-length test or steamed carrot comparison was given.

green beans in a Parkinson menu and aggregate motor scores — The Parkinson pilot offered green beans as one of many options. Aggregate motor change was inconclusive and individual facial-expression scores, steaming and participant-specific green bean intake were unreported.

oral sweet basil extracts and beam motor coordination in an ischemia model — The 2009 poster and 2011 journal abstract share researchers and endpoint but differ in reported occlusion duration. Overlap unresolved. The accessible outcomes give no stride estimate or fresh-food exposure.

oral sweet basil leaf extract after cerebral ischemia in mice — Author abstract reports improved motor coordination and a neurological severity score after post-ischemia treatment. Detailed results, fresh herb intake and measured stride remain open.

mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score — Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes gait examination, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

injected Capsicum fruit extract in a barbiturate challenge — Some extract and fraction groups showed a longer loss-of-righting interval. Natural sleep and clinical insomnia were outside this mouse assay.

extract and a sleep diary in healthy athletes — An early within-group sleep-quality change appeared in the combined NMN and xanthophyll arm. The xanthophyll-only changes were inconclusive. Ground paprika and clinical Parkinson insomnia were not tested.

hot sauce and mustard mixture and sleep in healthy men — The six-person experiment reported worsened sleep-stage and wake measures after the seasoned meal. Separate spice-specific and Parkinson effects were unmeasured.
paprika oleoresin in a matched cannabinol crossover — The randomized comparison varied cannabinol. The paprika colorant was listed among excipients. There is no separate ground-paprika sleep effect.

clove smell identification item and Parkinson freezing phenotype — The clove odor recognition contrast between freezers and non-freezers was inconclusive (p=.212). The study did not measure change in freezing after ingesting clove.

self-reported coconut oil use and overall PD symptom progression — The observational total score does not isolate refined oil or listener intelligibility; baseline and progression models differ and uncorrected multiple testing limits inference.
self-reported coconut oil frequency and total Parkinson symptom score — The cross-sectional composite association gives no refined-oil classification or listener-rated intelligibility outcome.

virgin coconut oil within mixed ketogenic plan and composite motor score — The plan specifies virgin oil in recipes but not refined oil or confirmed individual intake; reported UPDRS motor totals do not isolate intelligibility.

ketogenic diet and Parkinson patient-reported voice handicap — Reported VHI-10 means favor the ketogenic group after three months. The intervention does not assign a named coconut oil and the voice handicap instrument does not measure intelligibility.

ketogenic diet and companion report of talking; oil exposure unverified — Participant 013's companion described better talking without listener-rated intelligibility or individual coconut-oil intake; participant 019 separately mentioned regular coconut or avocado oil.

pineapple frequency and pooled urinary incontinence impact — One of eight mild and one of 12 severe impact participants reported pineapple weekly. Raw preparation, separate urgency counts and clinical Parkinson diagnosis were unmeasured.

pineapple fruit and juice as reported bladder symptom triggers — Pineapple and juice were rated as worsening bladder symptoms in a painful-bladder cohort. No assigned intake, raw preparation or separate Parkinson urgency episode counts.

pineapple or juice before pelvic pain and bladder symptom flares — Case-crossover odds were inconclusive overall and in participants reporting a possible dietary trigger. The dietary item pooled fruit and juice and the endpoint was a flare, without a Parkinson urgency estimate.

pineapple juice sensitivity in veterans — The symptom survey recorded pineapple juice sensitivity in 42 interstitial cystitis participants and two in each comparator. It did not measure raw pineapple or Parkinson urgency.

bromelain-containing mixture in bacterial and ex vivo bladder models — The mixture altered some bacterial and inflammatory measures. It provided no voiding or urgency outcome, no raw pineapple and no Parkinson participants.

grouped high-acid foods and urgency urinary incontinence — Adjusted OR 1.29 (95% CI 1.03–1.62) for grouped high-acid foods. Pineapple membership and separate estimate unverified. The endpoint includes leakage.
canola vehicle and acute throat symptoms during olive challenge — Acute symptoms followed a blend containing extra-virgin olive oil. No canola-specific voice estimate or designated processing grade.
canola menu and speech domains in Parkinson disease — Part II and III include speech, but no separately reported speech item, sound-pressure data or processing-specific canola contrast was available.

instrumented mouse stride length with equal soybean oil in two blends — The Angelman-model gait experiment measured longer strides on standard feed and shorter strides toward control with a safflower blend. Both experimental diets contained the same soybean oil amount, and the model had no Parkinson shortened-stride phenotype.

dietary soybean oil substitution and ordinal stepping and coordination in rats — After spinal cord injury, scores on an ordinal measure of stepping and coordination were lower in soybean-oil-fed animals than in menhaden-oil-fed animals. No stride distances or soybean-oil preparation grade were reported.

equal soybean oil and mouse treadmill stride variability — Curcumin changed stride variability while the diet oil amount was matched. The study did not isolate soybean oil or measure shortened clinical stride.

soybean-oil laboratory chow and quantified treadmill gait timing — The study found no clear differences in propulsion, swing or braking time between soy-fat chow and a coconut oil/DHA/ARA developmental feed. No stride distance, oil processing grade, or Parkinson context was reported.

Cuminum fruit water extract by gavage in MPTP mice; rotarod and activity endpoints — Motor activity tasks are not levodopa-induced dyskinesia; the extract, species model and preparation do not establish a toasted cumin effect in humans.

Parkinson diet trial includes pan-heated cumin in soup; diet-level motor complication score — Heating in a mixed soup is not verified toasting; individual intake and a cumin-specific dyskinesia result are unavailable.

UK Parkinson survey recorded cumin use in previous month; preparation and dyskinesia outcome unreported — Individual cumin use is reported but toasting, dose and dyskinesia severity are not assessed as a cumin contrast.

oral extract of dried tarragon leaves and forced-swim immobility — Both extract arms under restraint had lower immobility than restraint alone, with similar total maze arm entries. This comparison concerns a concentrated extract and stress behavior rather than a clinical depressive symptom.

oral tarragon tincture and rat forced-swim behavior — The paper reports no activity for the remaining preparations including tarragon in its forced-swim test, without raw tarragon estimates. The preparation and outcome differ from dried herb and Parkinson depressive symptoms.

tarragon extract in feed and behavior after mouse social defeat — Social interaction and grooming improved in the behavioral model. Sucrose preference did not differ clearly. The results do not measure depressive symptoms in people with Parkinson disease.

injected tarragon extract and behavioral immobility in mice — Extract reduced immobility in forced swim and at one tail-suspension dose. These are rodent proxies and do not test clinical depression or dried culinary tarragon.
refined olive oil and 1-back task activation — The activation interaction was inconclusive. Imaging does not establish a clinical attention effect.

MIND meals with extra-virgin olive oil and planned flanker testing — The registered outcome covers attention, but the intervention is a whole meal pattern and the oil is extra-virgin, with no posted results.

olive oil shared in placebo and active arms with original attention measures — The 12-person comparator arm showed slower psychomotor vigilance and faster task switching at follow-up. Both arms contained olive oil and no verified refining grade was specified.

olive-oil comparator and sustained attention battery — The full article reports fish-arm sustained-attention change. The table gives no corresponding olive-arm means, no oil-free control, and no verified oil grade.

olive-oil comparator with letter cancellation and reaction times — The older-adult trial reports inconclusive secondary cognitive differences between fish and olive oil, with small descriptive changes in the olive arm. No standalone refined-oil estimate.

olive comparator and complex reaction time in trained athletes — A fish-versus-olive contrast produced a group interaction. The original reports anomalous units and baseline spread. No verified refined grade, oil-free arm or Parkinson cohort.

usual cooking olive oil and attention scores in a cross-sectional cohort — Higher adjusted attention scores were reported overall, with a larger association among women with HIV. The questionnaire did not separate oil grades.
olive oil as a shared vehicle in an attention trial — The group-by-time complex attention interaction was p=.049 for the pearl formulation comparison. Both preparations were dipped in olive oil.

refined-plus-pomace intake and adjusted attention change — The fully adjusted estimate for common olive oil was −0.006 z-score units per 10 g/day (95% CI −0.047 to 0.035). Refined-only intake was not modeled separately in the published comparison.
refined oil taste and exploratory EEG — Six healthy adults tasted oils and underwent EEG. No functional attention score was measured.
summer savory oil and rat rotarod motor coordination — Balance after lead exposure gives no dystonia measure.

common-sage extract chemistry and antiproliferative experiment — The author abstract confirms sage-derived extracts and chemical and cancer cell endpoints. P33 references this same report. It provides no culinary dose or Parkinson symptom comparison.

isolated ellagic acid gavage and measured stride in rats — Stride improved in a small lesion model after purified acid. A 2016 report shares the investigators and possibly the same cohort, so it is not counted as independent. Ground sage, dose correspondence and human stride remain untested.
sage leaf extract and paw-print index after sciatic injury — Footprint index improved after extract. No stride length was measured.

safflower oil capsules and bowel tolerability — Some volunteer participants reported bloating. No tally of constipation, bowel rate or stool consistency during the active period. The comparison did not establish oil refining.

safflower oil comparator and constipation adverse event in Glut1 deficiency — Constipation was reported in 1 of 42 on safflower oil and 1 of 43 on triheptanoin during blinded exposure. This is an adverse-event count rather than a constipation severity comparison against no oil.

safflower-containing comparator and registered bowel diaries — Protocol measures stool frequency and consistency in a synbiotic comparison. High-oleic safflower is one placebo ingredient. No posted outcomes.
safflower oil frequency and composite PRO-PD — The adjusted composite difference was +6.8 points per frequency step (95% CI −6.8 to +20.5). No separate constipation or grade comparison is available.

high-oleic safflower and canola in defined diet and stool characteristics — The blend with different fiber produced firmer stools and greater output per unit fiber. The formula varied several ingredients and did not measure Parkinson constipation.

inhaled marjoram oil and resting blood pressure — In nine seated healthy adults, mean arterial pressure decreased versus plain air at the last two minutes. A separate supine comparison used baseline. Standing symptoms and oral fresh marjoram were outside the experiment.
marjoram extract and aortic ring relaxation — Vascular tissue relaxation is not an orthostatic symptom measurement.
filtered marjoram tea and composite nonmotor scale in Parkinson — The report gives no separate estimate for standing lightheadedness. It tested a dried-leaf tea.
inhaled marjoram oil and mean arterial pressure — Rested between-group pressure change was inconclusive. No standing symptoms or food exposure.
clinical allspice allergy case with limited access — The primary citation reports severe allergy. Preparation, swallowing data, and the full case history could not be verified.

anise in a Parkinson honey mixture and broad sleep disturbance in an unlinked survey — The survey's sleep-disturbance category is not an exposure-linked dream-enactment count; ground preparation and individual intake remain unverified.

older-men exercise comparison with a candidate cold-pressed pumpkin component in the control blend — The manuscript confirms the blend and brand. A matching 2015 NIH label names cold-pressed pumpkin seed oil. The specific lot is unverified. The trial measures strength and walking under exercise without handwriting or Parkinson outcomes.

vegetarian Parkinson intervention naming pumpkin seed oil and a motor composite — Appendix A lists the oil among other foods, and supplement Figure S2 reports UPDRS III totals. The pressing process, individually consumed oil and handwriting outcomes are unreported.
filtered marjoram tea and composite nonmotor scale in Parkinson — The reported NMSS total cannot identify a change in visual hallucination frequency.

tested oral marjoram extract and behavioral observation in rats — The Methods specify female rats and a dried aerial-parts extract. General observation and acute mortality do not measure hallucinations. No Parkinson or fresh-leaf exposure.

historical report of attempted use without verified hallucination outcome — An ethnobotanical article mentions alleged use with the intent to induce hallucinations. The description does not authenticate a marjoram species, clinical event, visual modality or preparation.

fresh basil and a separate vial of unspecified culinary basil in a Parkinson diet pilot — The ingredient form in the vial and participant use cannot be confirmed. The Part I composite supplies no dried-basil result on apathy severity.

basil listed with other spices in a Parkinson hospital diet — The report gives a baseline Part I total and clinical motor follow-up. Basil preparation, individual consumption and apathy severity results are unavailable.

inhaled basil oil and stress-model mouse immobility — Inhaled oil reduced forced-swim immobility vs untreated stressed mice. The behavioral measure and route cannot isolate dried-basil intake or clinical apathy.

rotating versus stable mouse odors including tarragon — At 60 minutes the rotating odor group preferred a new odor by time and visits, while stable mixture and empty-cage groups lacked clear preference. The assay used limonene and carvone. Tarragon was one enrichment odor.

tarragon versus thyme odor pair in mice — Author spreadsheets give mean pair 7 acquisition/reversal errors of 7.40/7.47 in 15 Alzheimer-model mice and 7.83/15.22 in 18 controls. Both scents were present, paired exposure was olfactory, and genotype and task order limit interpretation.

odor rotation including tarragon and mouse olfactory deficit — Discrimination index after reopened naris was lower than intact controls without enrichment, with no clear difference from intact controls in the enriched group. Rotating odors and food ingestion are distinct.

odor rotation including tarragon and mouse odor recognition — Enriched mice retained odor recognition through 240 minutes while controls showed it only at 30 minutes. Both conditions lacked clear recognition at 480 minutes. No tarragon arm or dietary exposure.

odor rotation including tarragon and impaired mouse odor discrimination — Double knockouts discriminated two esters after enrichment p < .001, with p = .72 in empty-container animals. The study did not isolate tarragon odor or measure eating dried herb.

occasional stiffness after whole macadamia kernels in dogs — Stiffness was among the less frequent field signs after kernel ingestion. The experimental dogs had marked weakness, and Parkinson rigidity and orally administered cold-pressed oil were not tested.

macadamia oil and cerebellar tissue markers in rats — Author abstract describes changes in biochemical markers and cerebellar pathology after chemical injury. Oil grade, motor outcomes and Parkinson rigidity are not established.

thyme-containing topical oil blend and registered facial anxiety — The protocol registers a facial expression scale for anxiety in an intensive-care population, with no posted results, fresh thyme intake or Parkinson reduced expressiveness endpoint.
thyme-containing mixed diet; aggregate motor examination score — The Part III total includes facial expression, but the paper gives no separate facial item or fresh thyme effect.

mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score — Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes speech, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

low — Two uncontrolled blepharospasm cases reported symptom or treatment-frequency changes with topical frankincense. Almond oil was one of three possible diluents with no patient-level assignment. No isolated oral almond oil, processing grade or Parkinson-related dystonia measure was verified.

fresh whole blackberries and measured baseline gait speed in older adults — The mean baseline eight-foot gait speed subscore was 2.6 ± 1.3 out of four in 28 older adults. Plain fresh blackberries were eaten in a separate plate-waste exercise. Attrition of 82% prevented a before-and-after estimate. The registry, thesis and program reports are one study family.

blackberry diet and plank walking in aged rats — The small-plank task improved after blackberry feeding. The experiment assessed motor coordination in aged rats and gives no human walking speed or raw fruit contrast.
ground sumac as an aroma stimulus — Ground sumac is the tested smell stimulus. The study did not evaluate impairment after consumption.
sumac volatile profile across fruit preparations — Volatile analysis describes products and food preparations without clinical smell testing.
aroma compounds across Sicilian sumac preparations — Headspace chemistry compared sumac sources and processing without exposing Parkinson participants.

sumac descriptor familiarity in an olfactory test adaptation — Kamrava and colleagues surveyed familiarity with candidate odor descriptors for the Iranian Sniffin’ Sticks identification test. Table 1 gives sumac a 57% familiarity rating in the 200-person survey, below the study’s selection threshold. It was excluded from the final identification odors. No participant consumed sumac as a test exposure, and the result does not measure a change in smell.

COVID-19 trial of commercial sumac plus pomegranate juice — Men reported less combined smell-and-taste dysfunction within the intervention arm, but the post-treatment comparison was null in both sexes. Sumac was combined with pomegranate and olfaction was not measured separately.

healthy adult sensory crossover of culinary brown sumac — Aroma liking did not clearly differ between butternut squash soup with versus without brown sumac. The trial excluded factors affecting sensory perception and did not test participants for olfactory impairment.

oral ground botanical as a strained infusion and general tolerability — The trial asked about tolerability on day 11 and reports no event that substantially affected the protocol. It gives no fatigue scale or arm-specific adverse-event counts.

reduced responsiveness and lethargy after oral infusions — Poison-center cases describe acute infant hyporeactivity or lethargy after oral laurel preparations, which differs from chronic Parkinson fatigue.

healthy adult randomized safety study of standardized leaf extract — The abstract reports zero adverse events in 12 extract recipients and 10 placebo recipients after four weeks. It gives no fatigue-specific measure and used an extract in healthy adults.
inhaled leaf and an attention task susceptible to vigilance decline — Low-exposure inhalation preserved task vigilance. A fatigue severity outcome was not measured.

fatigue during probable injury associated with leaf infusion — Fatigue accompanied probable herb-induced liver injury after prolonged crushed-leaf infusion exposure. The report describes no standardized fatigue result or Parkinson population.

canola vehicle and stepping tests in a Parkinson model — The 6-OHDA experiment assessed stepping and bridge performance with canola as the vehicle. It did not estimate independent oil effects or track freezing episodes.

canola menu and freezing-of-gait domains in Parkinson disease — The Parkinson trial scored the Parts II and III domains containing freezing items. It reports no item-specific change, frequency or independent canola contrast.

canola comparator and six-minute walk in older adults — The ketone-ester comparison reports inconclusive post-treatment walking distance and composite lower-extremity function. The cohort excluded active neurologic conditions, with no freezing episodes logged and no isolated oil effect.

canola comparator and instrumented walking outcomes in older adults — Walking speed and step-length differences between arms were inconclusive. The study enrolled healthy elders and did not log freezing events.
canola comparator and timed mobility in adults — Timed up and go improved in all arms and differed inconclusively between arms. The test did not report freezing frequency.

rectal sesame oil in a multimodal regimen and gait item — Gait scores improved from baseline in the uncontrolled series. Neither walking speed nor an isolated cold-pressed sesame oil effect was reported.

injected sesame oil comparator in a planned mobility assessment — The registered critical-care study uses intramuscular oil as the testosterone comparator and plans Timed Up and Go. No posted outcome or oral cold-pressed oil.

same Parkinson rectal sesame-oil cohort across two publications — The congress item republishes the 15-person rectal formulation comparison. Combined botanical and sesame oil exposures and MDS-UPDRS components provide no separate walking estimate.

oral sesame seeds and Timed Up and Go in knee osteoarthritis — Timed Up and Go improved in each group, with post-treatment difference p=.002. The abstract gives no group-specific times. Exposure was seed with standard care.

topical sesame oil and eight-meter walk in knee osteoarthritis — Noninferiority to diclofenac was reported for walk time. The abstract lacks the walk means, interval and margin. Topical treatment of knee osteoarthritis leaves effects of cold-pressed dietary oil on Parkinson gait open.

mustard listed on a multi-item Parkinson intervention menu — The published motor composite includes postural stability. Appendix A names mustard without preparation. No separate postural-stability estimate or effect of the mustard was reported.
anethole and rotarod fall latency in toxin-exposed rats — The PLoS report describes longer rotarod fall latency and longer stride. Fall frequency in ordinary activity and ground seed were unmeasured.

low — Aqueous seed extract lowered arterial pressure and heart rate in rats. A likely precursor explicitly used daily oral extract in salt-fed rats. The reports give no measured orthostatic symptoms, everyday falls, or ground-seed clinical exposure.

aniseed ether placebo excipient and a secondary falls outcome — Vitamin D doses were assigned against placebo in kidney disease. Falls are registered at six months, with no posted results or isolated ground anise exposure.

ground anise mixture and open adverse-event ascertainment — The acute-COVID trial reports general symptoms including throat itching or thirst in the anise group. No prespecified fall endpoint or fall-frequency result.

topical sweet almond oil massage and knee joint stiffness — In 60 women with knee osteoarthritis receiving physical therapy, joint stiffness improved within the topical almond-oil massage group (reported change interval −1.04 to −0.36), but between-group stiffness differences were nonsignificant (p=.707). Joint stiffness, topical massage, and Parkinson muscle rigidity are different.

topical sweet almond oil placebo and knee joint stiffness — The topical sweet almond placebo arm had WOMAC joint stiffness means 6.30, 6.50, 5.10, 4.90 at baseline, immediate postintervention, one week and three weeks versus 6.40, 6.93, 5.53, 5.26 in routine care. Reported three-arm p=.924/.001/.22/.195 with post hoc emphasis on tarragon comparisons. It does not test oral cold-pressed oil or Parkinson muscle rigidity.

banana-flavored grain reward in a macaque drug comparison — Four rhesus monkeys received a banana-flavored reinforcer. The later papers confirm flavored grain pellets. Drug assignment, uncertain fruit content and reinforcement outcomes leave eating raw banana for the named Parkinson symptom open.

plain levodopa granules mixed directly with banana — At one hour, 40.0% of starting levodopa remained in the banana-water mixture and 47.0% in the banana-milk mixture. This is chemical compatibility without a dyskinesia outcome.

pediatric case and levodopa compatibility assay — The poster describes dark vomiting in a child with dystonia and drug loss after direct mixing with banana and milk. No Parkinson dyskinesia result was measured.
banana and milk mixture with dissolved levodopa tablet — The manufacturer reported a decline in measurable levodopa in a bench mixture. There was no patient exposure or dyskinesia assessment.
fresh banana juice and levodopa exposure in rats — Drug exposure was lower with fresh juice in a three-rat group. The rat study gives no dyskinesia result.

suspected interaction and secondary report of dyskinesia worsening — A secondary summary of the same case describes worsening dyskinesia during wearing off, opposite to the frozen claim. The primary text, banana preparation and severity measurements remain unavailable.
banana with levodopa and dark vomiting — The letter describes a patient observation and separate fruit and levodopa mixture darkening. No dyskinesia or drug exposure estimate is given.

Waking sleepiness occurred in 17/50 after coded active tea and 13/50 after coded placebo, with 16/50 after labeled active tea in the same group. The paired test was inconclusive and transition cells were unavailable. The infusion was stronger than customary and the item measured occurrence at waking. A separate uncontrolled group had 5/11 acute reports after morning tea.

Four Parkinson cases reported unchanged unexpected daytime sleep under inhaled or topical essential-oil treatment. Three began at zero. The route differs and the series supplies no controlled beverage estimate.
Dresden lunch measured ON-state cold potato salad intake; infusion lunch study (PMID34509136) lacked potato isolation or OFF hours; Arak and case-control questionnaires omit daily OFF time.

The 2006 crossover of 18 reports reduced daily OFF with multiple low-protein replacements. The 2007 methods identify all six participants as drawn from that trial. In Figure 1 their daily OFF was 3.5 versus 5 hours, p=.01, while dyskinetic ON lasted 6 versus 4.5 hours, p=.04. The regimen varied multiple foods and did not test roasted potato.

Both self-selected diet groups could eat potatoes. Tables 5 and 6 give ordinal waking-day OFF distributions with baseline imbalance and an inconclusive four-week comparison, p=.054. There is no preparation-specific potato assignment or pairwise estimate.

isolated DHA and forceplate-detected dyskinesia — Dyskinesia was detected in three of nine assessed DHA recipients and six of fifteen assessed placebo recipients. The posted counts have incomplete follow-up and give no severity effect for baked trout.

All seven participants displayed consistent dyskinesia during low daytime protein under fixed levodopa doses. Related full-text figures show one patient with higher dyskinesia on low protein and worse disability on high protein. Same-team participant overlap remains unresolved. This is a whole-diet pattern with no baked trout assignment.

Figure 1 reports longer daily dyskinetic ON with low-protein products, 6 versus 4.5 hours, p=.04, alongside shorter daily OFF. Six participants were selected from the earlier 18-person report. Time with dyskinesia is different from severity and the products did not test baked trout.

adult beverage survey with black tea, kefir and coffee — The study reports beverage use by sex. The methods and table contain different participant totals, and there is no matched gait, falls or fatigue endpoint.

oral black tea extract and spontaneous locomotion and circling in 6-OHDA rats — Primary Fig. 1 shows about 190 rotations per 30 minutes after lesion alone versus 143 and 102 with 1.5% oral extract started post- and pre-lesion. Secondary preparation sources suggest a daily water brew and ad libitum access. The experiment does not provide a walking-speed contrast.

unspecified tea exposure and time to Hoehn and Yahr stage 3 — Tel Aviv retrospective study of 278 PD patients found an inconclusive association with stage progression. A companion article explicitly repeats the same cohort for its onset analysis. Neither establishes black tea or walking speed.

caffeine dose escalation with Timed Up and Go and patient-rated mobility — Timed Up and Go baseline was 10.39 seconds (SD 3.04). The main text gives no follow-up number. PDQ-39 mobility improved 2.8 points among those tolerating 400 mg/day of caffeine in the single-group trial.

isolated theaflavin and narrow-beam crossing in an MPTP mouse model — Oral 10 mg/kg theaflavin shortened beam crossing and reduced slips at p < .05. The figure declares six per group while methods state twelve were assigned and all had behavioral tests. The task measures balance and coordination in mice and the preparation was isolated theaflavin.

randomized caffeine and UPDRS III gait in Parkinson disease — The week-six examiner-rated gait contrast was −0.28 points (95% interval −1.16 to 0.59). The study used caffeine capsules and provides no timed gait speed or brewed tea estimate.

grouped black and oolong tea and clinical gait assessment in older adults — Adjusted Table 3 gait B=.01, SE=.006, p=.02. The paper gives a different p-value in prose. The fixed-distance task used qualitative gait scores with a grouped exposure and no Parkinson subgroup.

randomized caffeine capsules and walking-related composite items in Parkinson patients — No individual MDS-UPDRS Part II components differed clearly after six months. There was no reported timed-walk value or black-tea arm.

caffeinated tea and progression to Hoehn and Yahr stage three — Ever versus never caffeinated tea HR 0.93 (95% CI 0.51–1.71, p=.82). Exposure and outcome lacked black tea and walking-speed specificity.

laboratory green and fermented tea extracts and reported animal behavior — Supplement Fig. S1 shows 100 mg/kg/day orally per extract. Primary Fig. 4A shows about 300 seconds for fully fermented black tea versus 55 seconds for model alone, with all tea arms sharing one significance letter. The motion-test protocol and gait-speed fit remain unresolved.

regular black tea in distinct Parkinson populations with composite follow-up — Two exploratory LRRK2 samples reported lower log MDS-UPDRS II levels with black tea while two idiopathic samples were inconclusive. No walk or gait item coefficient, tested brew or tea-by-time slope was reported.

black tea intake and MDS-UPDRS motor examination in Lithuanian dietary cohort — Black tea 26.67 versus 13.33 mL/day in cases versus controls (p=.008). The motor regression is for the dietary score, and symptom-specific black tea comparisons were not reported.

oral ethanol black tea extract and catalepsy and locomotion in haloperidol mice — Day 12 bar time decreased from 237.14 s to 76.4 and 64.28 s with 4 and 8 mg/kg. Ten-minute beam breaks increased from 107.83 to 191.42 and 247.28. The extract and test differ from brewed tea and clinical walking speed.

The crossover reports earlier walking and tapping responses to levodopa under isolated caffeine and a greater walking response. The abstract does not define the walking measure or provide a separate speed result.
Abstract 41 groups coffee and black tea for sleep-duration categories in community adults. The gait-device experiment is a distinct abstract and supplies no tea contrast.
Black tea appears in stimulant guidance for nonsustained atrial arrhythmias. Parkinson disease appears separately in orthostatic hypotension. No walking comparison is reported.
Abstract 281 reports tea exposure in relation to diabetes incidence, with black, green and oolong as subgroups. No Parkinson walking measurement or brewing specification.

Sixty-one people randomized to isolated caffeine or placebo. UPDRS III rest tremor differed by -0.32 (95% CI -0.73 to 0.10) and -0.28 (-0.83 to 0.27) at weeks three and six. Both timepoints use the same trial. Tea chemistry confirms caffeine in the beverage with substantially smaller amounts per reported serving.

A caffeine dose escalation without an external comparator gives a within-group rest score reduction of 1.18 points at two weeks. Tremor worsening and physiological tremor occurred among discontinuation reasons. Twenty-five participants described, with substantial attrition.

Six percent of survey respondents with Parkinson perceived worse tremor with coffee. The same publication reports no clear increase after acute caffeine and does not give a separate compatible rest estimate. Group linkage and timing are unresolved, so no additional family count was assigned.

Brewed black tea averaged about 39 mg caffeine per 200 mL in cup-sized bags and 24 mg for loose leaf under those conditions, compared with 200 or 400 mg daily isolated caffeine in the clinical trial. Measured constituent bridge, with no symptom observations.
Some LRRK2 groups had favorable MDS-UPDRS II composite comparisons. The idiopathic comparison was inconclusive and a separate rest-tremor estimate was unavailable.

The levodopa dyskinesia subgroup reported longer involuntary movements under oral caffeine. The author abstract gives no subgroup count or separate rest-tremor result. Duration of dyskinesia and the mixed medication context do not give a black-tea rest-tremor direction.

coconut-derived triglycerides and motor complication composite — Within-period MDS-UPDRS IV improved in the earlier report. The microbiome replay found inconclusive adjusted associations with total Part IV. Neither analysis gives a separate dyskinesia or virgin coconut oil estimate.
self-reported coconut oil frequency and total Parkinson symptom score — The cross-sectional composite association specifies no oil grade and no independent dyskinesia estimate.

oral virgin coconut oil and levodopa-related behavior in adult rats — The oil reduced some abnormalities during levodopa co-treatment. The model tested drug toxicity and the public abstract did not report dyskinesia severity or abnormal involuntary movement scores.
fractionated oil and mixed diet with dyskinesia ratings — Daily dyskinesia ratings showed no clear group difference. The comparison changed the whole diet.
oatmeal frequency and reported Parkinson balance — Near-zero inverse plotted sign. Rolled-oats preparation and pair-specific uncertainty remain unavailable.

oat bran and chickpea products with planned balance assessment — The trial plans single-leg stance and related outcomes but excludes diagnosed neurodegenerative disease. The protocol supplies no balance result, rolled-oats arm or Parkinson comparison.

bioprocessed oat bran/chickpea intervention and planned single-leg stance — Data collection finished with analysis ongoing. No published balance result, rolled oats alone or Parkinson population.

preparation, endpoint or population context from an authenticated source — The saffron table cites an Alzheimer's donepezil comparison with global cognition outcomes. It provides no isolated executive function measure with dried saffron in Parkinson disease.

saffron-containing three-extract formula and executive switching — After 12 weeks in older adults with mild cognitive impairment, reported switching difference was +1.42 points (95% CI -0.15 to 2.99) and contrast +1.56 (-0.09 to 3.20), with one-tailed p=.038 and .032. original study or review context for the exposure and endpoint — Saffron extract data concern spatial memory in a rat model. Separate physical activity work supplies other cognition outcomes.
powder tablet and general cognitive status — The global cognitive score favored saffron. Executive function was not isolated in the accessible report.

dried aqueous saffron extract and specifically measured executive-related subtests — No significant randomized between-group working-memory or CPT reaction-time change. Formulation, adult Parkinson transfer, unblinded comparator and attrition limit scope.

Standardized oral extract derived from the stigma contains documented crocin isomers and safranal. Primary ISI change interaction p=.017 versus matched oral placebo. Parkinson disease was excluded. Self-report, attrition and supplier funding limit transfer.

A separate registration and cohort. The abstract reports favorable secondary ISQ totals and classifications; arm estimates and analysis denominators remain unverified. The registry and paper are one family.

Three insomnia adverse events in each group. Depression was the efficacy outcome. The extract is from flower petals, fluoxetine is an active comparator and overlap with the other Tehran petal study is unverified.

Preprint Table 3 reports an inconclusive global PSQI interaction (p=.2) and latency interaction (p=.7). Two secondary components favor extract in ITT and do not resolve per protocol. Registry and preprint belong to one trial.
PROMIS sleep disturbance contrast 0.38 points (95% CI −2.40 to 3.16). A separate sleep-related impairment result favors extract. Neither is an isolated insomnia severity estimate.
Abstract reports that both arms improved on ISI. It provides no between-arm ISI difference. Route and mixed botanicals prevent assigning the result to oral ground saffron.
The prospective extract study identifies ISI as secondary. Recruiting record has no posted results and does not study culinary powder or a Parkinson cohort.

The primary abstract reports prolonged pentobarbital-induced sleep for safranal and the highest aqueous extract level, with no apparent hypnotic signal for crocin. Model and injection route cannot establish spontaneous insomnia or culinary symptoms.
The middle extract dose increases drug-induced loss of righting reflex in mice, p<.05. Other doses have no significance mark. The original supplies no ground-saffron Parkinson insomnia outcome.

Some ethanol-challenged passive-avoidance outcomes improved. Normal and scopolamine conditions did not. Oral extract and memory responses do not estimate culinary saffron and clinical executive function.

isolated raspberry ketone and behavioral outcomes in stressed mice — Forced swim, tail suspension, locomotion and sucrose preference measured depression-related and activity proxies after oral isolated ketone. No whole frozen Rubus fruit or separate anxiety endpoint. This is distinct from the retracted 2022 work.

raspberry juice powder and raised maze behavior after nicotine cessation — Applicant reports lower closed-arm time with juice powder in mice. The exposure and behavior differ from frozen raspberries and clinical Parkinson anxiety.

red raspberry powder and mood in older adults with overweight or obesity — The completed registry schedules Profile of Mood States at baseline, two and six hours and posts no results. The 2023 investigator report gives no separate tension or anxiety estimate. A possible related serum assay supplies no mood values or independently confirmed participant linkage. The tested exposure is freeze-dried raspberry powder in a non-Parkinson cohort.

dried mixed berries and state anxiety in healthy older adults — After 12 weeks the state-anxiety change favored the dried berry mixture versus cocoa in an exploratory Dunn comparison (reported z = -1.88, p = .031, conventionally about .060 two-sided). Within the berry arm p = .185. Raspberry was 16.7% of the dried mixture. The comparison cannot isolate frozen raspberry, and the analyzed volunteers did not have Parkinson disease.
original study or review context for the exposure and endpoint — Raspberry polysaccharides altered gut metabolites in an animal comparison without a frozen raspberry and anxiety result.

mixed thawed berry smoothie and negative affect — PANAS negative affect did not show a clear intervention effect. The drink contained four fruits including raspberry and the trial did not measure clinical anxiety.

freeze-dried raspberry and mouse anxiety-related behavior — Twenty-four weeks of red or yellow raspberry did not change open-field grooming or defecation clearly. This was an Alzheimer model and the exposure was freeze-dried.

clinical case or dietary history without a matched ingredient comparison — A severe arrhythmia case reports a dual-ingredient supplement containing raspberry ketones. It gives neither whole raspberries nor an isolated effect.

raspberry juice powder and categorical anxiety in two smokers — Applicants report less anxiety during cessation counseling without concurrent matched control, arm-level numeric scores or Parkinson cohort. Later family publications reuse the same disclosure.

Randomized four-arm adolescent conference abstract (DOI10.26911/mid.icph.2018.01.24) reports banana-only arm anxiety regression coefficient -7.84 (p<.001); raw preparation and full methods remain unavailable.
Small randomized healthy-adult trial (DOI10.12691/jfnr-10-12-2, n=20) found no significant between-group tension-anxiety change after Cavendish bananas.

Ambon-banana inpatient study (ijphrd.v11i7.10253) had unclear allocation, varied medications, and baseline imbalance; post-breast-surgery trial (PMID40331125) printed a t statistic conflicting with means, SDs, and group sizes.

Uncontrolled PD personalized nutrition (PMID30278074) offered optional banana-flavored liquid without isolating fruit; case (PMID35802918) and rat juice study (PMID16327247) note levodopa interaction without anxiety scores.
The prebiotic food list includes banana without a separate anxiety outcome or exposure comparison.

uncontrolled gastroresistant ground red pepper and abdominal pain diary in IBS — In ten adults with IBS, five weeks of 2.5 g/day pepper was followed by a reduction from 3.08 to 1.71 points (p<.05 within participants). There was no concurrent comparison, and the study did not verify ground cayenne or Parkinson pain.
topical capsaicin and localized neuropathic pain — One person reported pain relief after a patch. Route differs and the case lacked a control.

oral red pepper powder and epigastric pain in functional dyspepsia — In functional dyspepsia, week-five epigastric pain was 1.15 versus 2.32 after 2.5 g/day encapsulated ground red pepper or placebo. Two active participants stopped for pain. The paper and earlier letter describe one cohort. Cayenne cultivar and Parkinson pain were unverified.

oral ground red chili and urgency thresholds in healthy adults — Three days of 5 g/day ground Capsicum frutescens in capsules lowered first, moderate and severe rectal urgency thresholds relative to placebo. The pressure range elicited no pain threshold, and there was no Parkinson population.

meal with ground red chili and acute abdominal pain in IBS-D — Both 2 g oral chili conditions increased peak abdominal pain versus the standard meal (p<.05). A project manuscript records pain in 5/20 without chili, 11/20 with chili in food and 13/20 with chili capsules. The commercial chili cultivar and Parkinson pain effect remain unverified.

colon-release whole ground red pepper and daily abdominal pain in IBS — The full Results report no significant between-group diary pain contrast. Active-arm late pain improved compared with its own baseline, six active patients discontinued for onset pain and eight patients reduced dose. The abstract conclusion and the personal overall effectiveness rating are distinct from the diary contrast.

repeated red chili powder capsules and separate abdominal pain, burning and first rectal sensation endpoints in IBS-D — The 16-person crossover found lower meal-provoked abdominal burning and higher pressure at first rectal sensation. Maximum abdominal pain was inconclusive (p=.799 at week six, Figure 2B). Earlier ten-person reports appear to overlap and are counted once with the 2014 report.

topical capsaicin and experimentally provoked localized hand pain — Study participants in the pain group averaged 3.5/10 before the training task. No participants in the NoPain group reported pain. Skin provocation cannot estimate Parkinson pain after consuming ground cayenne.

commercial ground red chili and separate acute pain and burning outcomes — In a double-blind randomized crossover, 15 healthy adults and 15 people with nonerosive reflux disease consumed commercial ground Capsicum frutescens or placebo in capsules. The reflux group’s postprandial abdominal burning scores were 2.2 ± 2.5 versus 0.3 ± 0.8 (p < .05). Abdominal pain was collected separately and was inconclusive, as were both pain and burning comparisons in the healthy volunteer...

oral formulated red chili extract and abdominal pain reports — Results section 3.5 records four early abdominal pain reports in the higher-dose group. The discussion conflicts with this count. The report supplies no pain intensity, verified cayenne cultivar or Parkinson cohort.
Acute chest pain and inferior infarction after cayenne capsules. Trigger attribution and preparation remain uncertain. No Parkinson pain estimate.
Author abstract reports myocardial infarction during product use. Do not count the possible repeat conference presentation as a further person.

Both original cases report chest pain and distinct tachyarrhythmias while taking a cayenne-containing capsule. Case timing, attribution and formulation cannot resolve the ground-cayenne Parkinson pain claim.

dried parsley placebo and headache pain in a feverfew crossover — Pain worsened on feverfew withdrawal and improved on the reverse transition. No comparison isolates parsley from feverfew withdrawal. The underlying condition was migraine, and the primary timepoint table is unavailable.

source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits — S1.97 proposes parsley as a possible dietary source of related Rubisco peptides while modelling spinach-derived rubiscolin. No parsley isolate, dose or Parkinson outcome is measured.

veterinary reference context only, without a tested Parkinson comparison — The Petroselinum crispum entry describes furanocoumarins and primary photosensitization. The broader common-name cross-reference includes other genera. No frozen culinary or Parkinson symptom result appears.

parsley among optional mixed-juice ingredients — The original protocol lists parsley among optional mixed-juice ingredients. It does not verify participant-level dried preparation or intake. Edited testimonials report outcomes for the combined program without a separate pain severity comparison for this ingredient.
traditional parsley infusion for headache — Participants reported Petroselinum crispum infusion for headache. The published row does not specify drying or measure pain response.

mixed parsley sauce meal and abdominal pain — Median abdominal pain increased from one to three on a 10-point scale after a large mixed meal (p=.03). The authors attributed the changes primarily to the fat load. No dried parsley contrast or Parkinson pain measure was reported.

fresh parsley, rat gastric injury and author's pain report — Fresh leaf reduced rat gastric injury. An author separately described less gastric burning and pain after fresh parsley without a control or quantified outcome. No Parkinson pain or dried parsley was studied.

The registered controlled pilot followed 10 PD participants and 10 household controls completing a four-week multi-food and lactulose intervention. Both groups received the intervention. Green beans were optional. The study did not measure participant bean consumption or fatigue severity.

Original clinic-garden implementation abstract. Output measures describe produce, volunteers and program interactions. Exposure from a distribution list does not measure individual green bean consumption. No fatigue result was reported.

Fox Insight (DOI10.34024/rnc.2025.v33.20260) linked daily pooled fresh fruit with a binary non-daily/missing bowel category without isolating oranges; PD probiotic trial (PMC7774928) used orange flavor in both arms and hospital records (PMID38756536) counted mixed Citrus aurantium decoctions.

Sequential pasteurized OJ was null (PMID30638420), levan-OJ gave juice to both arms (PMID22852055), surgical OJ vs coffee lacked untreated control with registry mismatch (80 vs 476), and Chagas (n=12) and trifoliate-orange (n=25) lacked controls.

Functional constipation review reports favorable comparisons for a multi-herb mixture. Chenpi in the preparation is dried and may include more than one source species. No component attribution or separate raw-orange contrast.
Orange extract served as a brief odor challenge. Stool measurements compare genotype and age independently of the odor test. No randomized orange ingestion.
Apigenin source list names parsley alongside other foods. Cancer models and extracted compounds do not test pain severity after dried parsley.

Fatigue component incidence was lower with total vegetable intake (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.78–0.88), not estimated for separately measured cooked green beans in the original body. Exact supplemental tables and the Parkinson comparison remain open.
Stool frequency favored the probiotic preparation. Both test mixtures were similar in taste and the probiotic was orange-flavored. There is no stand-alone fruit exposure comparison.

Randomized Parkinson trial of unspecified saffron capsules (DOI10.1016/j.hermed.2024.100968, n=52) found null MDS-UPDRS Part III total (p=.424) with no separate rigidity item; NCT05696665 has no posted results.

Injected safranal (PMID38683404), crocin (PMID29204935), and crocetinate (PMID39850110) shortened rodent catalepsy latency; non-oral isolated constituents and animal catalepsy do not establish clinical passive rigidity after ground saffron.
cumin extract in Wistar rodent anxiety tasks — Open-arm measures were reported after extract. The report is inconsistent about the extraction medium and does not involve people or toasted seed.

multi-ingredient cumin formula and anthropometric measures — LBP4.128 reports anthropometric outcomes from a multi-ingredient cumin-containing formula. It does not isolate culinary cumin, its preparation or the frozen symptom.

Parkinson survey recording cumin use with aggregate nonmotor measures — Cumin intake was recorded and exploratory nonmotor comparisons were inconclusive after correction. No preparation or cumin-specific anxiety estimate is reported.

Randomized crossover of 19 men with type 2 diabetes given ground Cinnamomum cassia in water or capsules vs control meal found inconclusive breakfast-smell pleasantness (all p>=0.80) and measured no clinical olfactory impairment or Parkinson outcome.

Open-label 16-week RCT of six inhaled odors including cinnamon improved overall olfaction in diabetes-related cognitive impairment without oral ground cinnamon intake, standalone cinnamon attribution, or Parkinson subgroup.
Completed respiratory trial of seven oral essential oils including cinnamon essential oil posts no results and lacks ground bark, isolated cinnamon contrast, or validated Parkinson olfaction scale.
Cinnamon-odor recognition is 25/54 in controls, 16/54 in iRBD and 17/54 in Parkinson disease with omnibus p=.154. No causal ingestion comparison or symptom change.

Bunium and black pepper extracts were assigned jointly. The memory experiment does not measure anxiety or assign culinary Cuminum cyminum.

high-dose nutmeg misuse and uncontrolled depressive symptoms — The self-reported temporal relation of recurrent dysphoria and psychosis to deliberate misuse prompted a substance-induced mood diagnosis. Prior bipolar diagnosis, toxicity and uncertain cooking limit transfer.

multi-ingredient food including nutmeg and perimenopausal mood — The crossover lists mood measured by HADS as a secondary outcome and no posted results. Nutmeg is one of many ingredients. No Parkinson cohort or separate grated nutmeg intervention is specified.

oral nutmeg seed extract and rodent depression-like behavior — Lower forced-swim immobility was reported, opposite the claim direction on this surrogate. Grated nutmeg and human Parkinson depression remain unmeasured.

separately numbered conference member with preparation or outcome limits — P-03.2-20 applies nutmeg essential oil or isolated terpenes to rat hepatoma cells and measures Cx43 and cell viability. It supplies no grated spice or depression outcome.
original source context with different preparation, outcome, attribution or population — Oral nutmeg volatile oil changed rat hippocampal measures. No grated nutmeg or depression severity outcome.

original source context with different preparation, outcome, attribution or population — The tested material is commercial eugenol or lab-derived compounds, with nutmeg among possible botanical sources. No nutmeg or depression comparison.

author abstract of the same nutmeg Cx43 assay family — Brief conductance inhibition and longer Cx43 expression changes concern rat hepatoma cells treated with essential oil or three isolated terpenes. The report does not measure the frozen culinary exposure or Parkinson symptom.
oral n-hexane extract and mouse immobility — Forced-swim and tail-suspension immobility fell with extract and spontaneous movement showed no clear change. Clinical depression was unmeasured.
nutmeg extract and mouse immobility — Tail-suspension immobility fell without increased locomotion. The experiment used an extract and no patients.
intranasal essential oil and mouse immobility — Intranasal essential oil lowered immobility in a mouse tail-suspension assay. The route and endpoint differ from the claim.

uncontrolled piperine blend and digestive symptom reports — Piperine, curcumin, virgin coconut oil and counseling. Age subgroup counts are inconsistent and there is no isolated or controlled constipation contrast.

oral isolated piperine and slowed gastric and upper-gut transit in rodents — Oral compound slowed solid gastric emptying and intestinal transit. No clear lower-dose liquid-emptying contrast. Isolated compound and distinct endpoints.

oral black pepper powder and orocecal transit — Upper gut transit 90 ± 51 to 122 ± 88 min (p=.09) with powdered capsules. No stool or clinical constipation result. Distinguish separate red pepper contrast.
crude pepper extract and mixed gut model responses — Stimulatory and inhibitory findings depend on assay. No ordinary cracked pepper or Parkinson constipation rating.
culinary seasonings in a constipation case — Multiple dietary and other interventions leave the contribution of the individual seasoning unresolved.
isolated piperine and bowel proxies in rats — The study assessed fecal water under an isolated constituent in a lesion model, which differs from clinical constipation after cracked black pepper.
Matched cultural or experiential record for black pepper and constipation severity; preserves community/traditional context without controlled efficacy weight.

Oral isolated piperine 100 mg/kg in corn oil increased tolerated paw pressure and reduced ankle-movement vocalizations in rat hyperalgesia/arthritis models (PMID19327174, PMC2688199), while 20 mg/kg had little effect on vocalizations.

The randomized crossover compared matching isolated curcumin capsules with and without isolated piperine. Serum exposure rose, with no pain outcome, no culinary preparation and no Parkinson participants.

Topical clove essential-oil nanogel in rats (PMC9123718) lowered late-phase composite formalin pain but was inconclusive in early-phase formalin and hot-plate assays.
Clove extract was evaluated in a cell screen with biochemical readouts. No ground-spice or pain outcome.

oral sunflower and fish-oil comparator with standardized depression ratings — The author Methods identify sunflower oil with 0.2% fish oil. sunflower food frequency and composite Parkinson symptom burden — The poster reports +2 total PRO-PD points per intake frequency category (95% CI −10 to 13, p=.787). The cross-sectional exposure did not specify an oil grade. It gives no individual depressive symptoms estimate.

oral high-oleic sunflower oil comparator and three depression-related scales — At 26 weeks the sunflower CES-D mean change was −0.4 versus −0.2 and +0.2 under two fish-oil doses, with overall p = .87. sunflower oil comparator and depression ratings after prostatectomy — HADS depression was 3.2 at baseline and 2.3 at 12 months in the sunflower group.
